IN NOVEMBER. Now that the roadside paths-are plashed with mire t I love to dream before the cheery fire Of golden August days we passed together, . Acid moonlit nights when crickets tuned their choir. Wi*out, the meadows and the woodlands lie 3ia ashen sameness 'neath a hueless sky; And biting gusts, foretelling wilder weather, From out the North go hurrying madly by. withered leaves from off the boughs are torn And through the watches of the night are borne Across the Heaven's dark deserted spaces, While piteously the barren branches mourn. [ No song of birds makes glad the morn or night, lie flower looks skyward for a gleam of light, : But everywhere are seen the ruthless traces Of pallid frost, whose fingers blanch and blight. f Yet potent Memory sets Time at naught; Wide leagues I traverse on the wings of thought, And once again with you I mark the glory With which unclouded Summer ea,veg are fraught. Again with you I stroll cool country lanes Fresh with the moisture of abundant rains, Or con the pages of a sweet love story, , er read some merry poet's blithe refrains. Rare happy moments do I gpend, until The blast's rude fingers tap upon the sill And startles me; I find the firelight dying, The house in slumber, and the air grown And so I marvel, much as dreamers do, Now that the nights are long and drear, if you Before the fire, while winds without are sighing, Have visions of the vanished Summer too?

div.head: Tarittits.
div.p: Tarittits.
Bad men excuse their faults, good men will leave

them. Nothing is so credulous as vanity, or so ignorant of what becomes itself. Opinions alter, manners change, creeds rise and fall, but the moral law is written on tablets of eternity. The greatest friend of truth is time, her greatest ecemv is prejudice, and her constant companion is humility. Nothing is more beautiful than a serene, virtuous, happy old age. Such an old age belongs to every indi- vidual's life if he only knows how to build it. The highest use of a friend is his friendship, and in some respects a friendly book is the very best of friends. speech is silver, silence is gold. A book is a bi-metallic friend; it will give you either silver speech or golden silence, as you prefer. Love of novelty, seeking, without due cause, to upset prevailing usages, is no benefactor to the community. The usages have been established by long experience and by common consent, and not until they they can be shown to interfere with some •real good should they be disturbed. To act with common sense, according to the moment, is the best wisdom we know; and the best philosophy to do one's duties, take the world as it comes, submit re- spectfully to one's lot, bless the goodness which has given U 3 much happiness with it, whatever it is, and despise affectation. The following is from a German paper. Corporal to soldier: " Why is the blade of the sabre curved instead of straight ?" Soldier: "It is curved in order to give more force to the blow." Corporal: " Humbug ! The sabre is curved so that it will fit the scabbard. If it were straight, how would it get into the crooked scab- bard, blockhead?" " I—l think I' have stumbled into the wrong office," exclaimed a stranger, who opened the door of a Cincin- nati lawyer's den. "Well, that depends. If you are in business and desire to fail and pay ten cents. on the dollar, this is the right office." " Oh, but I'm one of the creditors of just such a man, and I wanted " " Cer- thinly •, come in. I'll either get you your claim in full or have the scoundrel indicted for fraud." Temptation is a fearful word. It indicates the begin- ning of a possible series of infinite evils. It is the ringing of an alarm bell whose melancholy sound may rever- berate through eternity. Like the sudden, sharp cry of "Fire !" in the night, it should arouse us to instan- taneous activity and brace every muscle to its highest tension. Nothing is more humanising and elevating than the love of flowers and trees. Ridicule it as some men may, there is profit in what they call mere sentiment. When the trees which bear luscious fruit cease to be beautiful, and when nature becomes baldly utilitarian and too miserly for the production of anything but sordid neces- saries, then may man follow. He may shut his eyes to beauty and his ears to melody. Perhaps a gentleman is rarer than many of us think for. Which of us can point out many such in his circle, Men whose aims are generous, whose truth is constant, and not only constant in its kind, but elevated in degree, whose want of meanness makes them simple, who can lbok the world honestly in the face, with an eqtal manly .sympathy for the great and the small. Self-possession is an important element of a successful -manner—" Be self-possessed; that is the only art of life," says Mephistopheles to Faust—and shyness or self-con- sciousness is, more than anything else, detrimental to ease of manner. This commonest of defects, which may be largely increased or counteracted by early in- fluences and training, is, however, in many cases consti- tutional and unconquerable. A Cumosrry OF NUNBERS. - The multiplication of '987,654,321 by 45 gives 44,444,144,445. Reversing the order of the digits and multiplying 123,456,789 by 45, we get the result equally curious, 5,555,555,505. If we take 123,456,789 as a multiplicand, and interchanging the figures of 45, take 54 as the multiplier, we obtain another remarkable product, 6,666,666,606. Returning to the multiplicand first used, 987,654.321, and taking 54 as the multiplier again, we get 53,333,333,334—all threes excepting the first and last figures, which read together 54, the multiplier. Taking the same multiplicand, and using 27, the half of 54 as the multiplier, we get a product of 26,666,666,667—a1l sixes except the first and last figures which read together 27, the multiplier. Next, interchang- ing the figures in he number 27, and using 72 as the mul- tiplier, with 987 ,654,321 as the multiplicand, we obtain a product of 71,111,111,112—all ones except the first and 'lest figures, venich, read together, give 72, the multiplier. Equally cur; .ous results may be obtained by multiplying these written either way, by 9, or by the figures 'ec'vmPe'3lll: 'the multiples of 9 variously interchanged. AFRAID OF BVIZOLAIZS.—" It's a joke on me, of 'course, but I'll give it to you fellows," said a class farm man o a little group, in the City Ha 11.." I have a great ' bed I want to know that

fear 'of burglars. When Igo to ever y door and window is securely fastened. About a nic ,nth ago we changed hired girls; and the new-comer vf as very careless about the doors o' nights. On two or • diree occasions I came downstairs at midnight, to find a window up or the back door unlocked. I cautioned her, but it did no good. I therefore determined to put a job on her. I got some false whiskers, and an old rig, and one night about eleven o'clock, I crept up the back stairs to her room. She was snoringlaway like a trooper, but the minute I struck a match she awoke. I expected a great yelling and screaming, but nothing of the sort took place. She bounced out of bed with a "You villian!" on her lips, seized a chair by the back, and before I had made a move she knocked me'on my knees. Before I

could get out of the room, she struck me again, and it was only after I had tumbled down the back stairs that , she gave the alarm. Then she went through to my room, rapped on the door, and cooly announced, 'Mr. Blank, please get up, I've killed a burglar." IN TUE DAYS OF CHAUCER.—It will easily be seen that the times in which Chaucer lived and the circumstances of his career were peculiarly favourable for a great and original poet, and especially for one with Chaucer's un- rivalled power of catching and reproducing the pecu- liarities in character and habit of classes of men. Border countries are the favourite ground of picturesque writers. Types of character are more strongly marked and more sharply contrasted there than elsewhere. Thus Scott chose for his usual field the border-land between England and Scotland, or the dividing line of highland and lowland. And the age of Chaucer may well be called the border-land between the dark ages and the modern period. In his own great poem he brings together the knight who had fought for the Cross in Prussia with his brethren of the Teutonic order, and the prosperous London merchant and the essentially modern country gentleman; and this Waa a true picture of the times. So in the literature of that age, the formal and learned Gower and the rough and antique satirist Lang- lande were alike contemporaries of Chaucer; while in Italy Petrarch was writing poetry as polished and artis- tic as any that the world has ever seen. This was just the age in which the genius cf Chaucer, with its singu- lar variety of scope, and its power of seizing points of character, would find fullest play; and Chaucer's varied career was entirely in his favour. As soldier, courtier, scholar, diplomatist, and man of business, he must have had unusual opportunities of studying character and learning'the real life of his age. And we find the char- acter of his poetry in this respect just what we 'might expect to find it under these circumstances. He has eft, in such poems as "The Flower and the Leaf," and Thh Court of, Love," perfect specimens of the fair-land in which the Troubadours delighted, with all their?grace but all their fantastic unreality. But the same poet has left that marvellous photograph from real life, :the pro- logue to the "Canterbury Tales ; " and the genuine and simple pathos of the story of Griselda. The variety of character in the poetry of Chaucer keeps 7constantiv before our minds that, though he is rightly called the source from which the stream of English poetry takes its rise, that source itself, like the great lake that feeds the Nile, derives its fulness not only from the springs that arise within its bosom, but from the streams whose waters it collects and makes its own.---The Popular Edu-

"Now, Mr. Witness," said a Columbus lawyer, "are you willing to swear solemnly that the chair was really facing the east? Remember, sir, the awfulness of per- jury." Witness: "Well I won't swear, sir, but I'll bet you ten dollars it was." • How TO WRITE A GOOD LOVE-LETTER.—" Aunt Julia," said a blooming girl of seventeen, " what is necessary in order to write a good love-letter ?" "Well," replied the aunt, 'you must begin without knowing what you mean to say, and finish without knowing what you have

written." - There are no more vicious habits than adopting . measures to "keep awake" or employing artifices—or, still worse, resorting to drugs and other devices—to induce or prolong sleep. Dozing is the very demoralisa- tion of the sleep function, and from this pernicious habit arises much of the so-called sleeplessness—more ac- curately wakefulness—from which multitudes suffer. Every man desires success, and the strength of his desire is shown in the earnestness of his efforts; the difference lies in the objects in which he desires to succeed. Earnestness is good, success is good; what we have to watch is that we are earnest in a worthy cause; then our success will be justly a matter of rejoicing. No cowardice is so great as that found in want of truth. Belief in the rightness of a cause, in the value of a high moral standard, in the supremo righteousness overruling man, self-respect and moral dignity—all go by the board when we condescend to a lie, either spoken or acted, either by suggestion of the false or suppression of the truth. Whatever it may be that we are called to testify or acknowledge we should stand to openly and without wincing. It is the woman who devotes the hours of work most assiduously to employment who will most thoroughly enjoy an evening of social recreation. It is the man who has spent a winter in patient and energetic activity who will best prize and best use his two weeks or two months of summer vacation. It is to him who submits sweetly and cheerfully to the monotony of daily life, with its petty trials, vexations, disappointment, and fatigues, that refreshing changes will come with most delight and bring the truest recreation. There are three things to which man is born—labour and sorrow and joy. Each of these three things, says Mr. Ruskin, has its business and its nobleness. There is base labour and noble labour; there is base sorrow and noble sorrow • there is base joy and noble joy. But you must not think to avoid the corruption of those things by doing without the things themselves. or can any life be right that has not all three. Labour without joy is base; labour without sorrow is base; sorrow without labour is base; joy without labour is base. There are few more potent forces in character or in life than that of the imagination. It has, in fact, a life of its own underlying the actual and visible life, yet secretly and constantly moulding and fashioning it. It has its sins and virtues, its strength and weakness, its develop- ment and repression, all of which tell upon the desires, affect the disposition, and to some extent determine the actions of men. Whoever wishes to be the controller and director of his action must discipline his imagination. It is before the hand is stretched forth to do the unjust deed, before the lips are opened to speak the cruel word, that the sin of injustice or cruelty begins. It is the indulgence of the fancy which pictures the coveted gain and dictates the bitter word. If this be not checked and resisted, there is little hope that the evil deed will be avoided. ) Before Prince Bismarck reconstituted the tnap o 4 _ .

A Yankee once had his carriage stopped at the frontier of a petty prince's country. The Herr Ober C9ntrolleur at the custom house came forward, and, much to his indignation, was received in a nonchalant way. The Yankee was ungentlemanly enough not to get out of the carriage, or even to take off his hat. The Herr Ober sharply demanded the keys of the tourist's trunks, which his subordinates began handling roughly. "Here, hands off !" shouted the Yankee. "I didn't come from the Uuited States of America to be controlled by you. Put those trunks back, I'll not go through you at all. I'll turn back. I'm in no hurry, and don't care for losing a day. You're no country—you're only a spot. I'll go round you." And he did. As host( DIAMOND.-To pass from entomology to mineralogy. Horace Brooke, who is married to a young cousin, or rather (if I may adopt an expression some- times used which points out the relationship more distinctly). Welsh niece of mine, told me of an odd thing that once happened to his mother, Mrs. Brooke. The family residence is on the banks of Lough Earn, and there, as elsewhere in England, Scotland, and Wales, pearls of more or less merit are not uncommon. Mrs. Brooke took to collecting them, and children from the surrounding villages got into the habit of bringing any that were picked up near, receivine, in return a shilling or two for their find. One day a little girl arrived from a greater distance than usual, offering not a pearl but a pebble. Mrs. Brooke, who was only seeking after pearls, declined to buy it. Shortly afterwards the butler, a good-natured man, came up and suggested she should change her mind. "'The little girl," he said, "has had a very long walk, and is crying bitterly at having to go home empty-handed." "Oh, very well," said Mrs. Brooke, "take the stone and give the child what she asks for it." This he did. A month or two afterwards a friend of theirs, a great traveller, who I knew South America well, after ogling the pebble for I some time suddenly broke out thus: "Do you know, if I were in Brazil, I •should be certain that in that bit of , stone you had got hold of a real diamond." The bit of I stone was submitted to a competent jeweller in Dublin, ' who entirely confirmed this "tale :of a traveller ;" and the Lough Earn pebble is now one of Mrs. Brooke's diamond rings. Unluckily, all traces of the little girl and her whereabouts had been lost; she may for aught I know to the contrary, have been a fairy in disguise, so that no inquiry could be made as to whether stones of the same kind had been found in the neighbourhood before or since. If Mr. Gladstone could introduce diamond fields into Ireland as well as Land Acts, both Ireland and England might be all the better for this new opening. I do not say that there is anything impossible in the supposition that native diamonds may be hidden in Ire- land, though it would surprise me to hear that the dis- covery was one of any great value. There is a French rivulet somewhere, in the sands of which Oriental rubies of good quality have, I believe, been found now and again, and in the waters of the Upper Loire there certainly are or were sapphires. I can enly hope that if any steps should be taken in this direction, we may not be dis- appointed in our diamonds as Ciesar must have been in our pearls. Some tradition about the British pearl was one of the lures that drew him on to the first invasion of the country, and there is something touching in his sulky tone when lie tells us that they are all " lividi et subfusci coloris." In fact, like everything, else in this world, as Solomon would have said, they turned out to be "vanity and vexation of spirit." To have organised a costly expedition, to have killed your thousands and burnt ancient citi2s to the ground, yea, more than that, to have flung away precious Roman lives that might have been useful to him on the edge of the Rubicon for the sake of "livid and subfuse pearls," pearls only fit to "cast before swine," must indeed have been a bitter dis- appointment. However, he got his pearls—just as Esau before him got his pottage—and if both gentlemen after- wards grudged the cost, that is their business and not ours.—Reminiscoices of Sir Francis Hastings Doyle. Such plants as Tenweek Stocka-and Grimace. Asters with their annuals are now quite over, and should be clealed. out forthwith. Gladiolus, except in favourable-situations, are best taken up. Tie the tops together, andi hang them for a few days in an open shed, or put them on a shelf in an airy place. We find the coaler they are kept-the better, so long as they are not frozen. After they have been harvested, they may be inserted: ita pots and filled round with moderately dry soil arsand, and placed in a cellar or a similar place. The vacancies left by these and other plants might with advantage be failed up by what are termed spring flowering plants. The following are a few that are likely to be known to the cottaget, and within his reach L—Wallflbwers,Double Daisies, Myosotis (forget-me-not), Arabis, and Primroses. THE Whapow.—After the plants are watered this time of the year the saucersthat the pots stand in should be emptied shortly after,and none should be allowed to re- main from one watering to another. We have met with some whose watering operations are regulated by the absence, or presence of the water in the saucer, ignoring the fact that the wateris for the benefit of the roots in- side the pot, and before it can be ascertained that a plant requires water the soil in the pot must be examined. There is, however, one plant—Arum Lily—that does not object to a little remaining in the saucer continually. Indeed, the plant is almost an aquatic, and the roots, which are thick and fleshy, are liable to perish if per- mitted to get dry. The plant should be watched as to green fly, mad if the pest makes its appearance carry the plant out of doors and brush them off with a feather or syringe the plant with soapy water, laying it on its side whilst it is being done. aa.a,

, a 51.0qC I N G . -- Siiyoking,. at the preeeirt.clave la-welt-nigh as universal a human practice as -eating; drinking, or sleeping. Until very, lately it was hampereaa in this country 1 )y restric- tions annumerable, written and unwritten. , and its votaries were constantlyat oddswithlegitimisl Id by-laws and social -prohibitions limitin,g their indulgence in the fra- ,grant weed to certain localities: and hours of ti ie day:and night in a fidgettyand sometimes -v-exatiou s manner. These restrictions howevenhave in many cases been done ,aviav with altogether, and in ethers so it itelligently modified as at) afford but little solid groun d foe com- plaint to the most inveterate c,onsurner of tot )acco. Not to hark back any. farther. in the history of Bi itish smok- ing than the period , just preceding the Crit nean War— little more than. thirty years:ago, in fact— men still in the prime of life will distinctly remember, ve e doubt not, that at that time it was considered " sno bbisha-athe epithet "had form"' had not then been i nvented—to emoke a cigar-in the • sareet, and an English man bating any pretensions to gentlemanly breeding and position would as soon have thought of crying "Cats' ine,atl." in the Barbican.as-of puffing a meerschaum or cutter on the shady side of Pall-mall. Railway companies made, no special provisions for smokers in connecti onawith their 1 oiling stack: Being on a journey by rail it was only ' possible fort the traveller to smoke -under, tolera- lion of his fellow-passengers, or by bribing a guard Ito lock him up in a compartment by hinnealf. Not only was after-dinner smoking out of the question . e . in private.houses inhabited by ladies, but id was not . allowed in- the principal London resta,urante. , Even: a well-known ordinary, though it sprang from a cigar-ehop and called itself a divan, forbade its guestsate: smoke where they had dined, and sent them upstairs, aftertheir meal, to adismal back room, if they were berae en-toying with a postprandial regalia and cup of coffee OR thepre- mises. There was-not a single London theatre that could boast oaa-smoking saloon within its precincts. nor a public dining-room to which a fumoir was contiously attachect! Men—even those strongly addicted' to the weede—seldom:sraoked in their own housea, the, female prejudice against the-after-scent of tobacco running re- markably ragh, in the early "fifties." They conveyed 1 their pipes and pouches, their "puros" and cigar-cases— cigarettes were all but unknown to Englielasmolters in ' theeprre-Crimean days—to clubs, public and private- billiaadiroornseor the chambers of some baehelorefriend,. for the most regarded with distrust and suspicion by the. partners of tlienejoys and sorrows. At the conclission of their vaporous- orgies, before returning ,to homes un- defiled by the. fumes of burnt bird's-eye or. calcined cavendisla they 'generally made some laudable; if ineffeea: tual;effert to,purify their breath and garrnanta from the rank and lingering nicotian reek. As a, matter of fact, thirty years-ago the majority of married amen belonging to the better classes of English society, smoked, so to speak, under-protest, whilst the parents :and guardians ' of Ceelebs regarded his use of tobacccaas- a: formidable symptom of dissipated habits, although his younger female acquaintances usually contrived to:put up with , it, for reasons best known to themselves., , In the words of Moliere's immortal medical reformer, "-we have, changed all that." Smoking has overcome, one by one, all the social barriers formerly-set up to re- tard. its. triumphal entry into domestic, life, and now assertaitsaway in at least half the iiOlfgPS occupkd by well-to-do-Britons. Cigars appear an the dining-room after—not infrequently before—tleeeladies have left it, and that insinuating libertine, the cig,arette, sometimes makes,his way up to the drawing:room, where he has been even known to undergo affectionate pressure by , the lips of the fairest of the fair. Smokaag is authorised in restaurants, theatres, and railway carriages,, subject to certain provisoes by no meaneronereas or prejudicial , to comfort. Club smokingerooreseance the Ishmaels of . committee-men, shabby, -forlosta and relegated to the! most inconvenient and inaccesaible regions of the club-, house, axe now amongst the niestluxuriously furnished, and decorated apartments iaethe gorgeous palaces a Club-Land. With the exception of churches and come cart-rooms there are few 'subtle places of assembly ;ts which some sort of practical.7eonsideration, taking the . ~form of accommodation, is :bet daeplayed on behalf of : - the inveterate smoker's requirements. Ladies favour the "-soothing practice" as: conspicuously as they were 'once wont to discourage iteathe Deemed and liberal. pre- . ' fessioas all smoke copiouslaeand persistently; the clergy 'no longer denounce tobacee:as an invention of the Evil One, provocative of idleness, tinnatural thirst, . scep- ticism, and all manner of otherbaneful tendencies... Men of the highest rank and' fashion are not in the-least ashamed of being seen- in public places with cigarette, cigar, or even, a glossy briar-root in :their 1 mouths. He who does notsmoke at all is a "cazntite nag* ligeable " in his way—the infinitely rare exception' to a rule obtaining such general observance amongst Englishmen of every social condition that smolting has of late become an intregal habit of our dailyenatioaal. life. We are not, perhaps, as far advanced in the official. countenancing of tobacco smoke as some of our Con- tinental neighbours -whom constituted authorities justify in regarding every locality of public frequentation, and' every vehicle of locomotion, as a place to be smoked in by prescriptive eight, unless conspicuouslys fitted out with prohibitive notices. Germans Austriaas, Italians, Russians, and—ina lesser degree—Frenchmen smoke in. their restaurantsecafes, and railway coaclaes, as a:mattere of course. In the majority of Viennese onmibuses even there is a "Ranch-Coupe," constituting an entire moiety of the portly, and leisurely "Stell-wagen "' that conveys: thousands oPpassengers daily between the: city and the: suburbs of the: Danubian Empire-city.. Though we do: not as yet smoke inside our omnibuses, however, nor in our restaurants, during meal-times, we- may fairly be. reckoned amongst the most steadfast. and profuse con- sumers attobaeco amongst European nation, and have certainly rid ourselves, from a "society."' point of view, of our whilom prejudices against the molt agreeable of stimulmts and sedatives—for both these varieties of comfort are imparted to us by the: judicious use of nicotia--with all the thorough-goingness. of which, every, true Briton is proud as an ancient and approved charac- teristic of his masterful race. Even when those prejudices were most rampant aan.ong us, English institutions specially affected to the accommodation of our aristocracy in their hours of' leisure and recreation exhibited a far kindlier tolerance of smokers' tastes and fancies than has,down to the pre- sent day, been displayed by Continental institutions of a similar character. At no time within our remembrance has the committee of any London club ventured to dic- tate to its members what sort of tobacco they shall incinerate within the four walls of their smoking-room, or what particular description of receptacle they shall . utilise for conveying the growths of Virginia, Maryland, and the Havana to their lips. What Englishman has ever seen posted up on the walls of a club tabagie a notice to the effect that "members are strictlyprohibited from smoking pipes in this room a" Not one, we confi- dently believe; nor do we believe that such an imperti- nent and oppressive regulation would be complied with for a moment by any of our fellow-countrymen. It has, however, obtained in many of the more fashionable clubs abroad ever since those places of rendezvous secured a footing in the leading cities of the European mainland. Although German gentlemen, during the period of their life passed at the university, are almost invariably power- ful and continuous pipe-smokers, they confine their smoking at their clubs, aa a rule, to cigars and cigarettes, and a pipe is never seen, even in the military an sport- ing% casinos of Berlin or Vienna. It is no less uniformly tabooed in the bast clubs of Italy, Spain, and Russia, where the apparition of a meerschaum or "short clay" would scarcely awaken less surprise and consternation than that of a seven-headed' fiery dragon. In Paris, even, the Continental headquarters of English social cus- toms and of fashions attributed to our 6, high-life"— locally pronounced in such sort as to rhyme accurately with fig-leaf—the question whether a man who prefers a pipe to a cigar should be permitted to smoke the former on the premises of his club-house is at present being gravely discussed by the committees of the principal Lutetian " cercles."- In all probability, as we are in- formed, this importart issue will ultimately be decided in favour of the pipe-smoker, who, it seems, has been borne with for some considerable time past in more than one distinguished Parisian club. Great astonishment was manifested on one occasion, four or five years ago,, at the famous Jockey Club, when an English member produced his favourite pipe from his pocket after dinner, calmly lit it, and. proceeded to smoke it with imper- turbable enjoyment. The example set by this insular innovator was not followed to any great extent by the members indigenous to French soil; but it made its mark, and was the starting-point of a languid move- ment in favour of abolishing pipe-disabilities at some future epoch of the club's history. That epoch, it would appear (says the London Telegraiih), has arri'ved, or nearly so e and Englishmen affiliated to Continental clubs, whose name is legion, may look forward, confi- dently to a period when they will be able to smoke, their pipes in Parisian, Roman, Viennese, and Florentinceelubs —we are doubtful about Berlin--without violating any by-law, shocking any native member, or transgressing any understood but unexpressed canon of polite. society.

An " iniPressionist " sent in a " Sunset" picture to the Royal Academy. He carefully marked on the back of the frame which was the right side up; but he added a polite note, "Should rev work ,be placed on your walls upside down, please catalogue it as sunrise.' It is not perhaps much thought of, but it is certainly a very important lesson to learn how to enjoy ordinary life and to be able to relish your being without the tran- sport of some passion or gratification of some appetite. If we would see things aright, we must see them from the point of view of others as well as. from our own. This is the quality we ought to cultivate even if we can never perfect it; and this is the essence•of justice. Sim:mien OF DEATIL—On Monday last, at the Norwich Assizes, George Harmer, aged twenty-six years, plasterer, was indicted for the wilful murder of an old man named Henry Last, on the ICth of August. The body of Last was discovered in the back room of his house covered with sacks. He had apparently been felled by blows delivered frona behind, and the indentions on his bead correspond with a plasterer's hammer found in a box belonging to the prisoner. On the morning of the day the murder was com- mitted prisoner was discharged from gaol, and to an ac- quaintance named Nelson he signified his intention of eob- hing and "doing for old Last." Prisoner subsrquently disposed of property sworn to have been in Last' S pos- session, and then proceeded to London, where be was ap- prehended. He was found guilty and sentenced to death. MR. It was expected that Warrington would be minus one or iliero of their best players last Saturday, be in the end athey -managed to pot a full team in the field. This was rather fortunate, for it took them all theic time to prevent their old ceup tie opponents from reversing the previous result. The [ Aspnll team, like others. has goodand bad.points. Among !its good points is the energy it throws into its play; there is nethinglnkewarm or indifferent about-the Aspull met", forithey one and all work desperately from beginning to end. tiC..,n the other band, it anust•be said that they are un- venally rough, and theytaokle and ecrimmage in.a fashion tbatire hardly becoming in what after all is ,bat a friendly game. Speaking of rough play, a err' is just now being...raised as to therat'ner frequent serious and even fatal accidenis that are taking place on the football field. It is noticeable, how- ever„that elly far the larger proportion of these accidents Iresult fromoinatcbee under Aesociation rtitee. This does not seern to bear out the opinion some people express pretty freely that Ike Association game is more gentlems.nly and less dosgerons than the Rugby. Alter ala these 'things do I not depend-so enuch upon rates as upon tke character and I conductef the players themselvesoand plenty of actidents would occur at R.ugby games did the players demean them- selves in each a way as to make accidents inevitable.. A correspondent signing himself "Warrington'" and who evidently is an :admirer of the premier 'local team, but slightly put out the circumstance he refers to, writes as follows :—"‘Kick eff at three o'clock.' This was the time announced for the match Warrington v. Aspull' on Sater- day. At that hour ecme 4,000 people had assembled wait- ing for the show to begin.' Aspull putting in an appearance shortly after, whilst the Warrington players delayed their arrival until 3-30. Thew was not good enough; old Sol won't be trifled with, so turned down the light before com- pletion of the game. I don't wish to write harshly; we Warringtonians are proud of our teams; they have gained front rank and have reason to feel proud of the means whereby their success has be.en won, and 'more power to them ' say I. Lef me, however, assume the part of 'candid friend' I would say to them—observe at least some decent show of punc,nality; den't take liberties or break faith ith your friends the public in any shape or form. After such splendid results, frem equally splendid efforts, it would be a pity so soon to insert the wedge's thin end en- dangering your prosperity or popularity." Lancashire met Yorkshire on Saturday at Whalley Range. The partisans of both counties had reason to be satisfied with the constitution of the teams. The rivalry that exists between the shires is, though healthy, of the most deter- mined character, and the results of these annual contests of qate years have been to leave each aide in tarn victorious. /..-vast assemblage, estimated at from 15,000 to 20,000, was I present. The greatest enthusiasm was exhibited through- out. The match came fully up to expectations. the interest being kept up to the last moment, when a sensat,ional run by TAckwood, of Yorkshire, snatched the game oat of tke fire laud left the score equal—one goal each. , The new grand stand which we mentioned as about to be erected on the Warrington gr3und will probably be fit for use to-day, though not completed. Messrs. Evans, Ashton, and Warren form the sub-committee who have this matter • in hand, and it is likely that the opening of the stand will t be suitably celebrated. ; Another exciting match may be expected to day between [ Warrington and Rochdale Hornets. Last week the Hornets beat Swinton, and that is proof sufficient that they are not to be trifled with. It may be mentioned that each member of the Warrington first team has been presented with a 0 handsome belt by Mr. Kneen, of Bridge-street. The belts are provided with pockets, in which the players may carry t their "unconsidered trifles."

div.head: SERMON ON FRED. ARCHER.
div.p: SERMON ON FRED. ARCHER.

At Wycliffe Cockhedge Mission Chapel, Brick- street, Warrington, on Sunday evening, the Rev. W. R. Parry preached to a large congregation on the subject" Lessons from the life of Fred Archer, the celebrated jockey." The preacher took for his text the words " So run that ye may obtain " (1 Corinthians. c. 9, v. 24). Having referred to the races of Corinth, he remarked that he had only once attended an English race course, and that was more out of curiosity than anything else, but he should never forget the breathless interest of thousands as they watched the winner of the cup pass the goal post, and the deafening burst of hurrahs they heard when the naming of the winning jockey, Fred. Archer, was proclaimed. It was not his intention, as, indeed, it would. be unnecessary, to give anything like a full account of Archer's life, but he should mark out a few of the good qualities of Archer, and asked them to imitate all that was noble in his character. On the other hand, he should warn them of danger by pointing out the rocks on which he was wrecked. They must take the first lesson from the fact that Archer undertook his profession when young. When Fred. was born his father kept a public-house at Prestbury, near Cheltenham. He also was a jockey and steeple- chase rider, and among the races that he won was the Grand National at Liverpool in 1858. It seemed natural, therefore, that Fred. should be put in the saddle when young, and one writer, an authority on turf matters, said that he showed such aptitude for riding that his father determined to apprentice him to Matthew Dawson, the well-known trainer of Newmarket. He won his first race when eleven years old, and from that time up to his death, at the age of twenty-nine, he won altogether about 2,749 races, and was at the head of the list of jockeys for the last twelve years.. Archer's success in life must be attributed to his early training,. This was one of the lessons that mast be borne in mind, for it was .a . general rule that those who commenced their life's work when young succeeded best. That was so in all matters, but, and this the preacher impressed on his hearers, it was especially so in religion, lie urged all young men and women to enter the Christian race in their youth. Again, Fred Archer was an ambitious man. This was a characteristic feature of his life, and probably one of the causes of his unparalelled suc- cess. It had been asserted by some that ambition was something unworthy, bomething that should be

avoided by Christians, but he should like to know the man who by his own industry had obtained a high position, who had made an impression on the: age in which he lived, or had a hand in the forma- tion of the world's history, of whom it 'could be said that ambition never touched his soul. He believed that such a character was impossible. It was true that, like every other principle, ambition was liable to abuse, but in that case the abuse and not the am- bition was the evil. He was told that Archer was a heavy better, and ambition perverted in that way was liable to censure. He exhorted them all to be as Christians, ambitious. Archer, he proceeded, al- ways went in to win. I always ride to win" was his motto, and that was the aim and ambition of his life. Nothing greater had. ever been accom- plished in the world than had been done by men who had consecrated their powers and abilities in one great thing. Numerous instances of this could be cited. Newton thus discovered the law of gravi- tation, and Luther gave his mighty energy to ex- I pose the falsehoods of Popery, and to diffuse a knowledge of the gospel. The result was the Protestant Reformation, and the work in which Christians were engaged was second to none in magnitude and importance. It was a work in which they must be able to say "This one thing I do." Another feature in the life of Fred Archer was the self-sacrifice he under- went in order to enter a race, by reducing his weight. On one occasion the preacher had read that Archer when in the scales was discpialifted for be- ing a trifle above weight, whereupon, though it was a bitter told day, he rode without his shirt. Self- sacrifice, he reminded them, was also necessary to enter the Christian race. Another lesson from the ' life of Archer was the consequences that inevitably followed the violation of the laws of nature. The result of Archer's enforced privation was a weakened constitution. If people played with the laws of health they must inevitably suffer. Ile maintained that the present system of horse racing was responsible for the death of Fred Archer. There were in Archer many good qualities. He was a generous man who gave freely of his substance, was not puffed up or vain by his suc- cess, and yet there was something unsatisfactory about his life. Moral perhaps, but not religious. He took a profession which almost always led to nun. They had no need to go to Newmarket to see the evils of gambling. There was plenty of it in Warrington, and he was told that in the large works, in the factories, in the workshops, and even among the lads in the streets, gambling was pre- valent. He was told, moreover, that the wave was coming into their churches and Sabbath schools. It was high time this should be put a stop to. Might they all enter into the right race, running with their eyes fixed on the Saviour. Towards the close of the servicerlfr. B. Farrar sang a solo " No- -1 thing but leaves:"

WAN.—The meetirg of these clubs at Runcorn on Saturday attracted fully three thousand spas- tatonr to the Irwell-iane ground, and they were rewarded tiy seeing a hotly-fought match between ‘,I,Jwo evenly balanced teams. Wigan put a strong combination in the field, while the home club played the old and wog-tried contingent which broke a lance With Birkenhead and vanquished Car- diff some few weeks ago. They were again successful in sustaining their reputation against the Wigan lads, and after a gallant ,struggle won the contest by two tries and three _

minors to one try and four minors. Runcorn won the toss. and Bray!, hay etart-d the ball for Wigan. Taw ball landed into touch at the 25 flag, and on being thrown in J. Ander- ton improved matters by pushing his waa- into home quarters. Wainwright by a good bit of dribblingotransferred the game into the home half, where for some time the home team played on the defensive. The WPigan forward& played a brilliant dashing game, and it required all the strength and ekill of the home forwardeto prevent their getting over the line. Once indeed J Andertoa was within a hair's breadth of scoring, but the collaring of Rancorn was very safe. Tight scrimmaging took place in front of the home goal, until Samuels got a splendid position and made a drop at Foal. The ball passed within half a foot of the post, amid a cry of disappointment from the large number of Wigan supporters who were present. The kick resulted in a dead ball to Wigan. The ball hawing been brought out, the Runcorn forwards swooped down upon the Wigan quarter, led by a dribble of Wainwright and Faulkner. Hughes secured pos- session, and made a grand effort to score, but Samuels proved a hard nut to crack. Saving the game at a critical moment, Samuels passed the ball to Anderton, and through a little disorder in the ranks of the Runcorn backs the Wigan front division rushed the ball over the line and com- pelled Cawley to kick dead, thus registering two miner points to the credit of Wigan. The Runcorn team now as- sumed the aggressive, and after a splendid run by Cawley, which transferred the game into the Wigan quarter, the forward rank pressed their opponents very hard. Slevin, Brayshav, Samuels, and Anderton tried hard to re- lieve their lines, but the assault could not be repulsed, and from one of the scrimmages near to the goal Hughes emerged suceessfully and planted the ball behird the posts. Broady made a poor and unsuccessful kick at goal. The visitors now palled themselves together, and after some brilliant play, Anderton succeeded in getting over the line amid a tremendous cheer. The kick at goal failed, and at half time the game stood at Wigan one try and two minor, to Runcorn one try. After a brief interval the game was restarted by Broady, and Wigan again made a vigorous assault on the home quarter. but the tackling of WrigEt, Lewis, Faulkner, Broady, Barnes. and Clarke, and the dribbling of Joule and Wainwright, aided by the saving tactics of Riley and Andrews, and the dodgy runs of Hughes, kept the enemy at a safe distance. Suddenly, from one of the scrimmages, Joule emerged with the ball at his feet. Speakman secured possession and passed toWainvr right, who from his own quarter made a grand run nearly the full length of the field, and grounded the ball at the pest. Woods took the place, but the kick failed. Anderton, the full back, in attempting to collar Wainwright, dislocated shoulder, and had to leave the field. Wardle was taken from the front division to occupy his place. Weakened though they were by the loss of a man, the Wigan forwards continued to play a splendid game, but all their efforts to score were fatile against the strong defence of the home backs and the brilliant play of the forward division, The visitors managed to place two minors to their credit, thanks to Slevin's dashing play. Towards the close of the game Faulkner scored a third try for Runcorn, but as the place was being taken the referee disallowed the point and the game was resumed. From the line out the ball was kicked over the Wigan lines, and a dead ball resulted in favour of Runcorn,the game ending as follows: Runcorn twe tries and three minors, to Wigan one try and four minors. Teams—Runcorn: Woods. back ; Speakman, Riley, and Cawley, three-quarter backs ; Hughes (captain) and Andrews. half-backs; Wright, Lewis, Broady, Clarke, Wainwright, Faulkner, Barnes, Joule, and Gatley, forwards. Umpire. Mr. H. Wright Wigan : Anderton, senr, back; Slevin (captain), J Anderton, and J C Samuels, three-quar- ter backs; Hunter and Morris, half-hacks ; Brayshay, At- kinson, Whittle, Wardle. Grunday, Booth, Dempsey, Kay, and Harris, forwards. Umpire, Mr. T. Leyland. Referee, Mr. F. Parry. The referee on Monday offered the following reason why he disallowed the try claimed by Rancorn*:—

"At the line out, about 15 yards from the Wigan goal, the ball was knocked on. I could. not see any stick up. but the Wigan captain and umpire declare that the stick was up; and on account of the darkness of the evening I gave them the benefit of the doubt." WARRINGTON v. ASPIJLL.

The match between Warrington and Aspull first teams on Saturday drew together on the Warrington ground one of largest gatherings of spectators of this season. The game was one of tke toughest, and, it may be added, one of the roughest that has been played at Warrington, and ended in a draw, a try and a minor being scored by each side. Pilkington opened the proceedings by kicking off on be- half of Aspull, Barnes returning. Massey very quickly showed up prominently by splendidly 'Collaring Bullough with the ball. Lawson putting in a neat kick to touch. Barnes next made a good pass, alter which the Aspull men led off with a loose dribble, and, getting past Buxton, the ball was taken over the line and a try obtained. The try, however, was not improved upon. This point was scored a very few minutes from the start, and it seemed to have the effect of *putting the home team on their mettle, and for some time after they made it very hot for their opponents. From the kick-out Dillon followed up well, and Speakman shortly after put in a good kick to touch. Continuing the advance movement, the Warrington forwards, aided by Speakman, Barnes, and Massey carried the oval to the line, a touchdown resulting. Fair Turner shortly after- wards got hold, got iu a nice ran, and then passed to Massey, who repassed to Barnes, the latter obtaining a try, from which Speakman was unsuccessful at goal. The As- pull team then made a determined spurt, and took the ball to the line, but Frank Turner, Povey, and Gilbert tquickly relieved. Smith.. on the Aspull side, now get hold, and made a good kick and toiler. Until the call of half time, Warrington were slightly pressed. but good play on the part of Gilbert removed the pressure, and when the referee blew his whistle for a short cessation of hostilities play was confined to the centre, the score standing one try and one minor Warringtoe to one try Aspull. Frank Turner re- started the game, and then Speakman got in a tremendous kick. Povey now dribbled well, and Gilbert alsashowed to some advantage. Seddon next put in a good kick, but Massey replied with one equally good. The play now be- came very rough, the *Keill men being determined to win, and Warrington being equally determined to stop them doing so. A good kick by Gilbert was replied to by Smith, play settling down in the Warrington -25. Bullough now got bold, and almost got over, but was checked .in time. Barnes after this made the .best run of the day—half the length of the field—frem a pass intended for Seddon. Some good kicking on both sides was next indulged in, and then Barnes treated the apectators to a nice run and kick. -Aspen then rushed the ball down the field and scored a minor, mak- ing the points equal. Alter this nothing was scored, the game almost entirely consisting of desperate scrimmages, of which the visitors seemed rather fond, and in which they are particularly etrong. As is seen by the result, the contest'was a very evenly- balanced one. At the ,commencement the home team seemed to hardly lay themselves out seriously, and to this was due the fact that a try wasso quickly scored by the visitors. The game was a particularly heavy one for the forwards, the scrimmages being numerous and desperately contested. The Warrington forwards, as usual, did well, Frank Turner, Rigby, Pavey, Littleweod. and Hough being prominent. Behind, it is needless to say that Barnes showed good form, putting in some clever dodgy runs, and Massey also did very good service by Ilia quickness and plucky tackling. Jolley rather epoiled himself by sticking to the ball when passing would have improved matters; but the Aspull men were very quick in 'laving hold. The visitor, apart from their roughness, which was hardly excusable : sometimes, one and all played with an evident determination to win if they could. Teams : —Warrington-: Beck, Baxton ; three-quarter ' backs, Jolley, Barnes, and Massey:; half backs, Gilbert I and Speakman ; forwards 'Fair Turner, 'Frank Turner, IRigby, Littlewood, Hough, Davies. rovey, Dillon, and Ashton (captain). Pond. Referee: Mr.TrevoreSmith.

MOSSLEY.—This match was played at Whines on Saturday, in the presence of about 2000, spectators. Both teems were well represented, and a splendid game was wit. 1 nessed. Widnes played with the wind in their favour dur- ing the first half, but notwithetanding that advantage Mose- ley had the best of the play. Kiddie kicked off, and Ash- worth shortly afterwards securing the ball at the Widnes quarter, ran through the midst of the home team, none of whom tried to atop him, artd secured a try beneath the posts. which Lawton failed to improve. From the kick-out Wid- Ves worked the ball away, some good play being afterwards tentuletel in by Farrell, S. Bingham, Pluenpton, and Hardin for Widnes, and Lawton for Mossley. Farrell, a few min'utete later, made a fine catch at the Mossley quarter, from which Morris landed a splendid goal. Just before the first half Newby was compelled to retire through an injury he received, and until the call of half time Messley played 14 men. Wilkinson, who has not been well of late, ceased play at half time, and . thus the sides were again equalised. Smith, shortly after the change of ends, dribbled well, and just fell short of scoring. He Atempted to pick the ball up, but failed, and what would otherwise, had he continued dribbl- ing, have been a try, only resulted in one of those meaning- less points called minors. Widnes continued to have the upper hand until the close, Farrell running brilliantly from the Mossley quarter to their line, which he placed in con- siderable danger. div.head: HAUNTED HOMES .OF GREAT BRITAIN.
div.p: THE HAUNTED HOMES .OF GREAT BRITAIN.

Mr. J. H. lngram's highly interesting work "The Haunted Homes and Family Traditions of Great Britain" (published by Messrs. W. 11. Allen and Co, iLondon), has now reached a third edition, and it is likely to become increasingly popular the bet- .ter it becomes known. The author has done his .work so well—has covered his ground so completely .--ithat no matter what part of the country the :reader may happen to reside in if he turns to this -substantial volume of over 600 pages he will find Abut the ghost stories of the district have been placed on record. Mr. Ingram as been in a posi- tion to do his work well as a compiler, because he basal° craze or special theory to support. He says —"had he ever entertained any believe whatever in supernatural manifestations—as evidently many able authorities do—the compilation of this work would have effectually cured him of such mental weakness; but it must be added no story has been included the incidents-of which have been proved to have been the resblt of palpable deception, or for which eny natural explanation has been found." We-should add that there is a table of contents .which forms a good index. 60 that there is no diffi- culty in9icking out the records of special places. The following extract from the wark relates to our fmn neighbourhood.

Chapel at Ashton-in-Mak-erfield, where it now is custody of the priest. This holy relic, by which se many marvellous cures have been.wrought„ is most carefully preserved in a white silk bag. We have before us an: account of a case which occurred in August, 187'2; a woman named Catherine Collins, was sent to the Wigan Workhouse a wholly desti- tute. She had been sitting all day on a door-step, after having come out of the workhouse at Salford on leave, and walked all the way from that town to Mackerfield, in order to have the "Holy Hand' ap- plied to her side, which was paralyzed. When her case came before the Wigan Board of Guardians, Mr. Clarke, one of the Guardians for Ashton, in- formed the Board that hundreds of persons visited the township on a similar errand to that of this paralytic woman.

div.head: IN-CE HALL AND THE DEAD HAND.
div.p: IN-CE HALL AND THE DEAD HAND.

;Ince Hall, famous as being connected with one of the most curious beliefs in existence, is an ancient Lancashire dwelling. In Roby and Wilkinson's popular "Lancashire Legends." this old hall is described as one of those curious half-timbered manraons which are now becoming rare in this country. Its six sharply-pointed gables, and its long ranges of mullioned pointed windows, give it an imposing appearance from a distance; and on a nearer approach the remains of a moat are visible, which proves that it had once possessed means of defence. The estate connected with the hall be- longed to the Gerards for upwards of seven hun- dred years; the owners being descended from Walter Fitzothe, Castellon of Windsor, at the time when Domesday Book was compiled." His son William adopted the surname of de Windsor, but another son, Gerard, was contented to bear his or- dinary patronymic, and became the ancestor of the Gerards of Bryn, now represented by Sir Robert Gerard, of Garswood About the year 1368, John, the third son of Sir Peter Gerard, of Bryn, married Ellen, daughter and sole heiress of Richard de Ince, the representative of a very ancient family, dating very nearly, if not quite, from the Conquest. In consequence of this marriage, the township of Ince passed to the Ger- ards, who, for many succeeding generations, resided at the old hall.

The tradition connected with the building now known as Ince Hall, which mansion was not erected till the reign of James the First, is thus related in the "Lancashire Legends" :—" There is a story of wrong attaching to Ince Hall, which has given rise to the legend of 'The Dead Hand.' One of its early possessors lay on his death-bed, and a lawyer was sent for at the last moment to make his will; but before he reached him the man was dead. In this dilemma it was determined to try the effect of a dead man's hand on the corpse, and the attorney's clerk was sent for one to Bryn Hall in all haste. The body of the dead man was rubbed with the holy hand, and it was asserted that he revived suf- ficiently to sign his will. After the funeral a daughter of the deceased produced a will which was not signed, leaving the property to his son and daughter; but the lawyer soon produced another will, signed by the dead hand, which conveyed all the property to himself. The son quarrelled with the attorney, and after wounding him, as he sup- posed mortally, he left the country, and was never heard of more. The daughter also disappeared, but no one knew how or when. After many years the gardener turned up a skull in the garden with his spade, and the secret was revealed. When this took place the hall had long been uninhabited; for the murdered daughter's ghost hung suspended in the air before the dishonest lawyer wherever he went. It is said that he scent the remainder of his days in Wigan, the victim -of remorse and despair. i Tliere is a room in the hall which s said to be haunted by the ghost of a young lady, and her shadowy form is frequently seen by the passers-by hovering over the spot where her remains were buried."
THE DEAD HIND.

The "Dead Hand," or the "Holy Hand," as it is sometimes styled, alluded to in the foregoing tradi- tion, is the centre around which quite a galaxy of marvellous tales have gathered. It is known to have belonged to Father Edmund Arrowsmith, a Jesuit, who suffered the extreme penalty of the law at Lancaster, on the 28th August 1628. The cause of Father Arrowsmith's trial and exe- cution has been variously stated, certain sceptical persons alleging that he had been found guilty of some foul crime, and that the tale of his martyr- dom for the sake of his faith, and the miracles which attest his sanctity, have been invented for the purpose of preventing scandal in the Church. The onus probandi lies, of course, with them, and until these unbelievers in miraculous intervention can adduce any evidence on behalf of their allega- tions, there does not appear to be any reason for refusing to accept the testimony of the Catholics, which is to the following effect. - Arrowsmith was born at llayclock, in the parish of Winwick, Lancashire, in 1585. In 1605 he entered the Jesuit College at Douay, and in 1612 was or- dained priest. The next year he was sent on a mission to England; and in 1623 was apprehended and taken to Lancaster on a charge of being a Romish,priest, contrary to the laws "in .that case made and provided." He was tried for this offence, found guilty, sentenced to death, and executed. After his body was cut down one of his friends or, as other accounts say, his spiritual attendant, cut off his right hand, in compliance with his dying injunctions and to fulfil his dying promise that he should work miraculous cures on those who had

faith in its efficacy. For many years the hand was kept at Bryn Hall, and when that ancient edifice was demolished it was removed to Garswood Hall, Sir Robert Gerard's residence. 13.timate1y it was placed in the Catholic

div.head: SHOCKING DISCOVERY AT ST.
div.p: SHOCKING DISCOVERY AT ST.
HELENS.

An inquest was INild at the Raven Hotel. St. Helens, on Tuesday morning, before Mr. S. Brig- house, coroner, with respect to the death of a newly— horn female child, whose body was found buried in a field at Eccleston under somewhat singular sircum- stances.—Peter Henderson, glaosmaker, of 17, St. Paul-street, stated that on Sunday morning, while walking with his dog in a field belonging to a farmer named Frith, at Eccleston, he found a box containing the body of a newly-bore child, very much decomposed. He was walking by the brookside at the time, and his dog, a bull terrier, smelling something, began to scratch and uncovered the box, which was embedded eight or sins inches in the ground. The box was an old one, and had been used for containing "blue." He gave information to the police.— Dr. J. Masson, assistant to Drs. Twyford and Jamison,. stated that be examined the body, and found it to be that of a female chile'. It was very much decomposed, having probably been born a fortnight ago.—The Coroner pointed out to the jury that the law presumed that every child was born dead until its separate existence was proved.—The jury returned a formal verdict to the effect that they , were unable to say whether the child was born alive or dead.

div.head: SAD DEATH OF A COLLIER,
div.p: SAD DEATH OF A COLLIER,

Mr. Brighouse held an inquest at St. Helens Junc- tion, on Wednesday, on the body of Thomas Griffiths,. aged 48, of Herbert-street, who met with his death at the Ashton Green Colliery, on Monday afternoon. Mr. H. Hall, Government inspector of mines, was pre- sent.—Mrs Griffiths, the widow, who was greatly distressed, gave evidence of the identification.—Patrick Kennedy said he lived in Marsh-street, Park-road, but ' worked with the deceased. They were splitting a pillar of coal, which was eleven yards long and extended from the drawing-road to an old working. They had about three feet to cut through. On Monday afternoon the deceased Was at the face and witness two yards behind him, when they heard a crack. They ran towards the drawing-road, witness first and Griffiths following. Witness had just got out when he heard Griffiths run against the prop nearest the entrance to the place, and heard him sheut "Oh, Pat come and help me." Their lights had gone out with running. Witness shouted for assistance, and seven men came. They entered the place, and found deceased partially covered with dirt and coal, and lying about four feet in. They set to work to get hire' out, and he talked to them while they were doing it. About ten minutes elaescd, when suddenly they heard the roof again breaking, and they ran out just in time to My, themselves from being buried. Deceased was covered and it took half an hour to uncover him, when be was found to be dead. The place had been propped down the centre. There were seven props. —Mr. Lyon, the manager of the pit, said he had been over the place, and found that there were 3 feet of coal standing on each side of the place.—Mr. Hall said he did not think there had been any breach of the rules or any serious ne- glect. There h4d been a little want of timbering more through want of judgment than anything else.—The jury returned a verdict of "Aecittental death," and recommended that in future the splitting of pillars ef ccal should be tim- bered by props and bars.

THE PAYMENT OF CHECKWEIGH- MEN. At Warrington County Court on Thursday a case came before his Honour Judge Foulkes, which is of considerable importance to colliers. It was brought as a test case under Viscount C:ross's Act of 1886, which was passed last June, and deals principally with the payment by colliers of their checkweigh- men, and with the right of relatives to be present at inquests on the deaths of miners who have been killed. Mr. A. Browne, solicitor, Warrington, ap- peared for the plaintiff, who is a checkweighman employed at the Queen Pit, Haydock, and who sued three colliers named Webster, Williams. and Larkin, who worked at the Pit, for the sum of 6s 9d each, being the amount of their respective shares due to him as checkweighman. The case was an adjourned one, and particulars have been previously given. It seems that it is customary for a checkweighman to be paid by the men, each one contributing a fixed sum, and plaintiff was at a meeting of the men appointed checkweighman. All of the fifty or sixty colliers employed at the pit, with the exception of the three defendants paid their respective shares, and the case was brought to recover from them, under the new Act. the money due from them. At the first hearing defendants appeared in person, but on Thursday they were represented by Mr. J. 0. Swift, of St. Helens. His Honour held. that the case was decided a month ago, with the exception that Mr. Browne should produce evidence, independent of the plaintiff's, of his appointment as checkweighman.-- Mr. Browne intimated that he had an independent witness, and, after some con- versation between the solicitors and his Honour, he called Cornelius Davies, collier, Haydock, who said that in 1877 he was present at a meeting of colliers at Haydock, at which, on witness's proposition, plaintiff was appointed check- weighman. About fifty colliers, he said, were present, but, in answer to Mr. Swift, he said he did not remember whether the defendants were present at the meeting, or were summoned to it. His Honour then read a lengthy judgment, but his voice was almost inaudible to those in court. He found that the plaintiff was entitled to recover, and gave judgment for the plaintiff for the amount claimed. Mr. Browne applied for costs on the - higher scale on the ground that a novel point of law was involved. Mr. Swift objected, and remarked that the case was really brought by the Union, of which the defendants were not members. His !Honour granted costs on the higher scale.

ENTERTAINMENT AT LOVTON.—On Wednesday even- ing aboat 30 members of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Tempters were driven to Lowton in a waggonette, where they gave a very successful entertaintneut in the Primitive Methodist School-room, under the auspices of the Band of Hope. The school-room wee crowded by an appreciative audience. Brother George Clarke, W.D.Coure, presided. After an address by the Chair • man, Brother John Taylor sang "Never be weary," Brother John Warburton gave a Lancashire reading, Love and glue," a choir under the cenductorship of Bro. George Clarke sang a melody entitled " The happy hand of hope," Miss C. Jackson sang 'Leaf by leaf the rotes fade," Brother G. E. Warburton recited "Wandering Jim," Sisters E. and J. Clarke gave the duet " A mother's love." Brother John Waddington sang "I'm hiding," Brother A. Warbur- ton recited "Johnny's lost," which was encored. Sister M. Clarke sang "Wandering boy," and Brother John Taylor sang "Have courage. my boy." The xudience mani- fested their appreciation by warm applause. AnTroN FOR INJURIES To A GRETHOUND.—An action it.. teresting to dog fanciers arid coursing men was heard on Wednesday afternoon at the St. Helens County Court, be- fore Judge Thompson. William Dixon, of Back-lane, Winds, sought to recover £lO from Matthew Cant, game- keeper to Colonel Gamble, the Mayor of St. Helens, for wantonly and maliciously causing injuries to a prize grey- hourd. It was stated that on August 25th two men named Gaskell and Swift, and the clog, were going over a footpath leading from Back-lane to Moss Bank. The dog was run- ning on the footpath ahead of them, when two shots were fired, immediately after which the dog limped back, and fell at their feet. Immediately afterwards defendant came up with a gun, hitt denied having shot the dog; there was, however, no one (ASP ahout. The dog was taken to Mr, Henry Taylor, veterinary surgeon. who extracted' several shots front its ribs. Thomas Ashy a said be heard Dixon offered LIO for the animal but he would not sell her. Witness valued her then at £l5.—T the defence Cam said he saw the dog in a potato field A rabbit came out OR to the footpath and be shot at it ' „vice. He heard a yelp, and plaintiff's dog jumped out ,f the hedge and ran up the footpath.—Other witnesses having been called, his Honour sail he suppesed plaintiff's case was that he wantonly shot the dog.—Mr. Riley said th at was so, and be asked his Honour to award the full arno u nt.—The Judge said he never head a man give his ev- deuce wits more appearance of fairness and honest thar defendant did, and he (the judge) believed he had given : very reason- able and intelligent and natural account. TEE Socialists of London hate held another great meeting of the unemployed, in Trafalgar-sq-etare ; and, though everything has this time passed off quietly., it can, hardly be expected that assemblies offsolcack,people can continue to be held withoutserious mis- chief resulting, especially when_languiage is used of the most violent and threatening kind. It is a matter of course to -say that no . Government worthy of the:name could allow, itself to be over-awed by mobs of this kind, but it is, the duty none the less of authorities,, local and-iinperial, to listen to complaints. when they are made, and; to redress griev, ances when redress is within their power. is the complaint of the unemployed that they are unemployed; and it is impossible, not to sympathise with the demand, which 4„.- Is mule "to organise the labour of the unemployed in useful and remunerative work." iThe Rev. G. S. REA.NEY, in a lecture which he gave at Warrington on Tuesday evening, drew I. power ful picture of the poverty and degradation, and misery among the tvio millions of people inhabiting the east end of the metropolis,- He estimated that one hundred thousand people got up evety morning,, in London, without knowing where or how they would get the next meal. He had, he said, attended a meeting of 350 men, lamongst whom aim only were wearing shirts. He had dtributed tickets for food at, the dockyards where men ,were seeking work which they could not ob- tain; and for protection he had been com- pelled to stand behind and push the, tickets lthrough the iron rails—such was the pressure ;and excitement of the hungry crowd. Relief, it need hardly be said, is in such, cases com- mendable; but it is, after all, a temporary ex- pedient, and the question still. arises—Can _anything be done to remedy such a state of' things? The Socialists say—let the local, authorities be empowered to, organise the: labour for the unemployed on useful and re-. munerative work; but this is a task by no. means easy, and might lead to a state of' things which would make matters worse rather than better. How can it be expected that local authorities, who, are after all bodies composed of businessmen, can set about doing: as covorate bodies that which they cannot do as. individual employers "Remunerative work" is, or should be, work which is rerun- nevative to the employer as well as the em- ployed; and if it were always obviously simple to provioe work of this kind we may be qulte sure that the greed of gain would be sufficient to cause la demand for labour without any need to resort to the action of local authori- ties. It may be that the Socialists simply mean by remunerative work, work that shall be remunerative to the worker; but if that involved a loss to the community, it is quite evident that it is an experiment which could not last long. begin to enter into competition with labour of every other kind, with the result that every labourer would feel that he had a right to de- mand that he, too, should be well paid, whether or not his work paid well. And what then ? It may be suggested that everybody would be happy if wages were raised all round, and the hours of labour reduced so as •• to give a turn to every labourer. But there is • such a thing as foreign competition; we are at present being hard pressed in the race; and we should soon be nowhere in it if we were •to handicap ourselves in this fashion. Still, as an experiment, we should like to see the authorities of the metropolis, where the pres- .-sure and danger are, after all, the greatest, take steps to organise the labour of the unem- ployed—for a short time, at any rate, even if it were found to beunremunerative.Mr.CHAmßEß LAIN, some time ago, declared that of some- thing over too unemployed men who gave their names in to commence sweeping the streets at 2S per day, less than one fourth turned up to commence their duties, and the - others soon fell off. Granted that 2S per day is a very small wage, it is better than going •to the Workhouse, or starving in the streets. What requires to be ascertained is the propor- tion to the whole of the unemployed who are willing to work, but, through no fault of their .own, cannot get anything to do. Men of this class might be helped, even at some cost to the State, for it would pay better, in the long run, to give them a helping hand than to let them gradually descend to the level of pau- pers and criminals. If it should be found • that the bulk of those who hang about the streets belong to that idle and thriftless class who prefer to live upon anybody's earnings rather than their own, it would be something gained. The labour test, such as it was, would separate the wheat from the chaff with the result that the wheat would be carefully housed while the el- if was looked to in another way. The n .tion must be prac- tical in matters of this kind rather than sentimental. Beyond some experiment st-ch as we suggest, and that as a means of gain- ing information, we look for a remedy for the pressure in, our large cities and towns, not in charity organisations or State employ- ment, but in such a thorough reform of our antiquated land laws as will ensure a fair field and no favour alike to employer and em- ployed. Our landed gentry are in some cases living in luxury upon rents and " royalties " which they have not by any means earned, and the consequence is that the farmer and the miner are worsted in the struggle for existence. In other cases the remorseless hands of the dead and the moribund hands of the living grasp title deeds in such a way that estates which, if properly divided, might be lands of smiling plenty, are "going to wreck and ruin," and all because of the unnatural divotce of Labour and Capital which stand idly by. How long this anomalous state of things is to last we know not; but until it is altered—nntil our remnants of feudalism are swept away—we shall look in vain for a satisfactory answer to the bitter cry of the striving labourer who begs, and begs in vain, "a brother of the earth to give him leave to toil."

The Fair Traders, and England for the English party, havelat last got something like an opportunity of making a stir in the coun- try, and it will be interesting to observe whether they make good use of it. They ! did not allow tfut grass to grow under their feet when somebody started the idea, whilst ' a Liberal Government was in power, that the material of our post cards was of German manufacture. There was instantly a howl against the POSTMASTER-GENERAL for em- ploying German in preference to English labourt It transpired that the POSTMASTER- GENERAL had nothing to do with the ordering of the post cards; and, further, that the con- tract was really made with an English firm over which, as to the purchase of material, the Government had no control. Still it was for a time a good sort of stick to beat a dog with; but these ultra-patriots have a much better one to hand at the present moment— if they will only use it. The POSTMASTER- GENERAL of the day, Mr. C. H. RAIKES, is not for Staking things as he finds them; he is a bit of a reformer in his way, and he has taken upon himself to " improve " our mail service with America. Hitherto there have I been three mails each week despatched to the United States, Liverpool liners being , employed which called at Queenstown. Under a new edict which the POSTMASTER-GENERAL ; has just issued there is still to be a tri- weekly mail service; but one of the steamers is to go from Southampton, and it has not to call at Queenstown. Another thing— and this is like treading purposely on the corns of the Fair Traders—the South- ampton steamer will not be a Liverpool liner ; it is a steamer in the service of a foreign company; in other words, the Gov- ernment are going to subsidise a German • Company to carry a portion of the English mails. Of course, if it could be shown that what was being done was a great advantage to the commercial world it might be toler- ated ; but it is clear that it will be a great disadvantage to this part of the country, for in his own circular the POSTMASTER-GENERAL says the mail going via Southampton will in- volve" an earlier posting of letters in all places north or west of London." Can we wonder that in view of such a change there is a strong feeling of opposition in Liverpool, and, other commercial centres "north or. west of Lon- don?" We expect to hear of the genuine Fair Trader prptesting from the bottom of his. boots, particularly when he hear that this " un-English " action is being fol- lowed up by the transference of a subsidy of ,troo per month from the British Steamship Company, which has carried mails to Bath- urst, to a French firm which has vessels run- ning between Goree and Bathurst. We say the genuine Fair Trader because there are not a few Fair Traders who are anything but fair. They make it their business to preach Fair Trade when the Tories are in opposition. These spurious politicians have nothing to say when the Tories are in power, and they will have nothing to say now as to the ques- tionable conduct of the Government in subsi- , dising French and German steamship corn- panics at the expense of the British tax- payer.

Mn. GLADSTONE AND THE CHURCH.—Mr. W. E. Gladstone was present at the service held in the Parish Church, llawarden, on Monday morning, and took walking exercise in the course of the day. Mrs. Gladstone, with Lady F. Cavendish, were in Chester in the afternoon. Mr. Gladstone's attention having been called to some extracts from a sermon of the Rev. E. V. Schuster, a Lancashire clergyman, the right honourable gentlernan, in his reply, says: I think congregational councils, if practicable, would be excellent; parochial councils impossible, and, if possible, injurious.
