div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
Princess Beatrice has become a mother, and the Queen is now the grandmother of z 6 children. This is surely a quiver full, and her Majesty is blessed.
General Kaulbars has taken his leave of Bulgaria, and the Bulgarians are disposed to say, with " Hamlet," that he could not take anything which they would more willingly part with.

Lord Salisbury's policy cf twenty years of coercion has commenced ; proceedings have been taken • against M. John Dillon, and a Nationalist meeting at Sligo is pro- claimed. But this policy will not last twenty years; it is rather " the beginning of the end of coercion.

It seems that Mr. Alfred Woods has simply been keeping the seat wafm for Mr. Darby shire, who is, after all, the choice of the electors of Grapnenhall. The Local Govern- ment Board now say that Mr. Darbyshire must take his place on the 'Warrington Board of Guardians. Mr. Woods will retire ; we are glad to see evidence at last of his being a retiring man.

-- Mr. James Lowther is "still harping on my daughter." He suggests that a substitute should be provided for the London coal dues in the shape of a duty upon such foreign manufactured goods as come into competition with home industries. Why don't the Fair Traders take the matter up ? There is a Tory Government in office " Nos,v's the time and now's the hour."

Mr. Adams has over-reached himself in his action against Lord Chief Justice Coleridge He would have been wise to accept the result of the arbitration in his favour. By pursuing his father-in law as he has done, he has caused the tide to turn against him. The jury felt they were witnessing persecution rather than prosecution ; hence the verdict in favour of the defendants—father and son.

A farmer at Weston, who is troubled with trespassers, says he is " puzzled to know what to do." Acting on the advice of the police, he summoned four men who were caught with dogs and guns on his land; but the Bench dismissed the case on the plea that it was all a mistake, As a rule, people have to suffer the consequences of their mis- takes, but in this instance it is the farmer who has had to suffer; he has had to pay I 83 in costs. This is not justice, it is justices' justice, and our advice to the aggrieved farmer is to agitate for a stipendi?ry magistrate.

_ A mad-cap labourer named William Smith was brought before the Bolton magistrates, on Monday, for giving the master of Christ Church Schools a black eye. He was retalia- ting, in his way, for the chastisement of a little girl. It transpired at the hearing of the case that he had got to the wrong schools, and blacked the eves of the wrong master. Singular, very; but. more singular still, the magistrates dismissed the case on the,defen- dant making a public apology. Having got off so easily, he will make tracks for the other schoolmaster, and, finding him, he will feel at liberty to assault him ad lib. The ways of magistrates are curious.,

There are little differences in the best revu- lated families. Lord Claud Hamilton, M.P., speaking at Carpenters' Hall, on Tuesday, said that he was not altogether with Lord Randolph Churchill on the subject of the coal and wine dues. 'Mr. Chaplin, and some others, are not altogether with him on the question of the closure. Others, again, are not altogether with Sir Michael Hicks-Beach as to his causing the withdrawal of Sir Robert Hamilton by giving him a Colonial Governor- ship. Altogether, it may be said that the Con- servatives just now are not altogether.

• --- The Tories who have been clamouring for the removal of Sir Robert Hamilton as the permanent Under Secretary in Ireland have made a " mull" of it, although they have had their way. Even Lord Carnarvon, who was recently Lord Lieutenant of Ireland, is constrained to praise him. He says of Sir Robert:-" He has served in many departments of State, and his experience, both theoretic and administrative, is unusually large." Why should such a valuable servant be withdrawn from Ireland ? Is it because his experience of Ireland has convinced him of the necessity of conceding Home Rule?

Mr. Walter Long, M.P., the Parliamentary Secretary to the Local Government Board, is reported to be engaged on a three-acres-and a-cow bill on behalf of the Government. He adopts the principle of compulsory allotments —to please " our friend Mr. Jesse Collings, you know." According to politics a la Churchill, Mr. Jesse Collings, as a Gladsto- nian, was a fool and a fanatic; as a Liberal who helps to keep a Tory Government in power, he now represents of course the wisdom of the ages. If the wind may change its course, why should not Randolph be allowed to change his mind?

Bishop Gregg, of the Reformed Church, makes the following suggestive statement with regard to Disestablishment : Ten years ago there were two churches of the Establishment in Southend; to-day there is only one; consequently, during that time the churches of that body have here been reduced by one-half. 'A church free from the State takes the place of the other half, and in this free church, amongst a poor people, a sum of £12,000 has been locally raised for and expended upon the successful experiment. The subject, too, of religious equality, from having been locally a dead letter, is now the first in the pro- gramme of local Liberalism, and the one which evokes most enthusiasm.

• THE GOVERNMENT AND THE MAIL CONTRACTS. —A special meeting of the members of the Incor- porated Chamliez of Commerce of Liverpool was held on Thursday to determine what action should be taken with regard to the contraci;s for the con- veyance of the mails to the United States. Sir William Forwood moved a resolution declaring that the arrangement made by the Postmaster-General (Mr. Raikes) will prove highly inconvenient ar d detrimental to the mercantile interests of the North of Englimd, Scotland, and Ireland, will involve a delay of from twelve to twenty-four hours in the correspondence of that portion of the United Ring- dom which is directly interested in the American trade, and by subsidising an already highly subs'-' dised foreign line will very injuriously affect British shipping interests; also that it is desirable to retain , Queenstown as the point of despatch for the Ameri- can mails, as it affords the quickest route from all 11 points north of London. In submitting this resolu- tion, which was carried without opposition, Sir William Forwood remarked that it was a matter of surprise to him to find that a Government which included gentlemen who but a few years ago were posing as the apostles of Fair Trade and reciprocal trade, was at the very first oppor- tunity taking away the carriage' of mails from British shipowners. Subsequent speakers called attention to the great inconvenience and loss likely to be occasioned when goods are sent by faster boats than those which are to be used for the conveyance of the American mails.

div.head: EXAMINER,. SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 27, 188 G.
div.p: THE EXAMINER,. SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 27, 188 G.
LOCAL NEWS

VISIT OF THE MARQUIS OF RIPON TO RUNCORN.—MT. W. Handley, the secretary to the Northwich Division Liberal Association, has almost completed his arrangements for the visit of the Marquis of Ripon on the 6th Decemeer. Full particulars will be found in our announcement column. WrreNEs PARISH CHORAL SOCIETY.—The members of this society, which sprung into being last winter, and created a good reputation, will give their first concert of the season in the National School on Monday evening. An admirable programme has been arranged, and an enjoyable evening may be promised. WinerEs C.E.T.S.—Tbe usual monthly devotional meet- ing in connection with this society was held on Thursday evening, under the presidency of the Vicar. There was a goisd attendance. Daring the evening Miss Lord played several selections on the pianoforte, and Mrs. Wright Williams and the Rev. J. R. Jones sang the duet, " Hearts and hands." Mr. Jones also sang, ‘• My Redeemer liveth " (Meesiah). He also delivered an interesting address on Scriptural characters." HALTog CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE GUILD.— A meeting was held on Friday night in the girls' echool. room, in connection with the Halton Church of England Temperance Guild. The vicar was in the chair, and there was a large attendance. Mr. Adam Still, of Liverpool, ex- hibited a series of limelight views illustrative of a " Trip to America." Amongst other views was one of Halton Castle, another of the Rev. John Lockwood. The American views were of the most iateresting description, and the au- dience were highly delighted. The usual votes of thanks brought a pleasant eveniug to a close. UNITED METHODIST FREE CHURCH. On Sunday last the anniversary of the above place of worship was celebra- ted, when two sermons were preached by the resident min- ister, Rev. E. Hall. On Monday evening there was a pub- lic tea given in the new schoolroom. A goodly number partook of the good things provided by Mr. G. Turton. After tea the secretary's report of the trustees was read, and addresses were delivered by the Revs. E. Hall and A. Hands (ex-president of the ceranexion.) The latter gentleman spoke of the different powers which ought to exist in the churches, viz, muscular power and word power. Mr. R. Wright presided over the proceedings. WIDNES FREE PUBLIC LIBRA.RY.—A. special meeting was held at Alford() Chambers on Thursday. Mr. H. Wade Deacon presided, and there were present Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. B. Lewis, E. Carey, S. Sadler, S. Robinson, and J. T. Allen (clerk to the Local Board). The clerk was direc- ted to acknowledge the receipt of the "Annual Cyclopcedia" from the publishers.—The Chairman remarked that this was the first donation.—The Clerk reported that 249 volumes had been received as a donation from the Record Society. Fourteen of the 16 selected applicants for the position of librarian appeared and were interviewed by the committee. A Widnes person was appointed to the post, subject to several questions being satisfactorily answered by the candidate. SALE OF WORK AT RUNCORN.—The foarth annual sale of work promoted by Mrs. Preston and the members of the Holy Trinity Sewing Class, in aid of the Church Pastoral Aid and Church Missionary Societies, was commenced in the schoolroom on Thursday evening. The articles for sale were of an ornamental and useful character, and were displayed n a large stall which was superintended by Mrs. Preston and Mrs. Bell, and the ladies of the class. A refreshment stall was under the care of Mrs. Lea and Mrs. Whittaker, with the Misses Stubbs and Tyrie. The Rey. W. Preston performed the opening ceremony, and made a brief speech, in which he thanked the donors of goods for their generosity. In the evening concerts were provided for the delectation of the visitors. The sale was also open last evening, and was fairly patronised. INDEpEWDENT ORDER OF RECHABITES, WIDNES.—The members of the "Onward" Tent No. 1,475 of the Indepen- dent Order of Rechahites (Salford Unity) have celebrated the anniversary of their establishment by a tea party and entertainment in Lacey-street school, Widnes. The Rey. R. Bunion occupied the chair, and expressed his pleasure that the Order was about to establish a Juvenile Tent in Widnes, as he held that temperance principles could not be too early instilled into the hearts of the young.—Brother J. Shaw Green, of Warrington, in the course of his speech, stated that the Independent Order of Rechabites was the wealthiest, the healthiest, and unquestionably the best of all other temperance societies. The Order had completed its 50th year; and had a membership of 100,000. (Ap- plause.) Other speeches were delivered, and a musical entertainment was given by the members of the Baptist Chapel choir, under the leadership of Mr. J. Edwards. Miss Passey was the accompanist. CHURCH MISSIONARY SOCIETY AT RUNCORN.—The annual sermons in aid of the Runcorn Association of the Church Missionary Society were preached on Sunday morn- ing at the Parish Church. and in the evening at Trinity Church, by the Rev. R. Palmer. There were good congre- gations. On Monday evening the annual meeting Was held in Holy Trinity Schools, under the presidency of the Rev. W. Preston. There was a moderate attendance. The Chairman remarked that the late Canon Barclay had been president of the Association for 38 years, and he hoped that his successor would occupy the same honourable position. As secretary, Mr. Preston read a report showing that the Runcorn Association, which includes Aston, Weston, and Halton, had during the past year contributed £63 15s. to the parent Society. (Applause.) The Rev. R. Palmer, the depetation, then delivered an address on missionary enter- prise, and he was cordially thanked on the motibn of the Rev. T. P. Bell, seconded by Mr. T. M. Arrnson. TEE NEW VICAR OF RUNCORN.—A Liverpool contem- porary thus writes with regard to the new vicar of Run- corn :—" By the appointment of the Rev. A. Maitland Wood, M.A., of St. Mary's Church, Liscard, to the vicariate of Runcorn, the district of Wallasey loses one of its best, ablest, and most respected clergymen. The rev, gentleman came to the district about 15 years ago from Bristol. Mr. Wood's residence in the district has been marked with much hard and self-sacrificing labour, which, combined with his many personal and Christian qualities, has secured to him the love and admiration of those who have come under his ministrations, as well as the respect and esteem of the pub- lic at large. He is regarded as a'. Broad "Churchman, and belongs to the same school as the Bishop of Manchester. He is a staunch advocate of the free and open Church move- meet; and has taken a lively interest in all questions ap- pertaining to the education of the young. PRESENTATION.—On Friday evening last, the employes of the Singer Manufacturing Company assembled at their office, 21, King-street, Wigan, to do honour to Mr. J. B. Dooley, who is leaving the district to take charge of the Runcorn Branch Office, under the same firm. The manager and employes. with whem he bad worked for the last 51 years comfortably and successfully, very much regretted the connection being severed, and to show their esteem and kindly feeling they met together for the purpose of present- ing him with a marble timepiece, with the following in- scription engraved en a silver plate :—" Presented to J. B. Dooley, as a small token of respect and esteem, by the em- ployes of the Singer Manufacturing Company on his leaving the Wigan district. October 22nd, 1886." The manager, Mr. Clare, made the presentation in a neat and appropriate speech, which was supported by Messrs. Salmon, Green, Parr, Williamson, Lace, and Chadwick; and Mr. J. B. Dooley replied in very feeling terms.— Wilan Observer. CONCERT AT WIDNES.—A concert in aid of the proposed new Catholic Church to be erected at Moss Bank was on Tuesday evening held in the Volunteer Hall, Widnes. In the absence of the Rev. James Clarke, the chair was occu- pied by the Rev. J. Oldham. There was a large audience. The nrogrammea opened with the selection, "The Bohemian Girl," by the League of the Cross Brass Band, which was fairly well played. Owing to Miss Jameson not being able to appear. the trio "Those Distant Chimes" had to be sung by Miss ()Aden and Miss Hewitt alone. Notwith- standing this disadvantage, it was a moderate rendition. In the humorous duet "The Two Cousins "the same vocal- ists were very successful. Mr. A. J. McCormack was en- cored for his fine interpretation of "Molly Bawn," and re- ceived well-merited applause for "The Storm Fiend." "Nora, the Pride of Kildare," and "My Beautiful Flower of Kilkenny" were fairly rendered by Mr. Finn. The over- ture and the waltz "Fairy Voices," by the string band or- chestra, nude- the conductorship of Mr. James Gordon, were very good. Miss Kiddie officiated on the second vio- lin. Mr. T. A. Barrett gave a pianoforte solo. The treats of the evening were the humorous selections by Mr. Lester Barrett, of Manchester, who kept the audience in roars of laughter. The monologue "The Boy George," and the songs "The Tipperary Christening," " The Professor of Alchology," "Fairly gone," and "Just what was wanted," were laughable in the extreme. Miss Cullen and Mr. T. A. Barrett discharged the duties of accornpanyists in a very creditable manner. SATURDAY POPULAR CONCERTS AT RUNCORN.—An audi- ence of most encouraging proportions assembled in Bethesda Schoolroom on Saturday evening to listen to the second concert of the series introduced by the Mill Brow Brass Band. A capital quartette of vocalists had been engaged in Miss Maud Dennett (soprano), Mr. Percy Barton (tenor), Mr. Fred Dennett (bass), and Mr. W. G. Foreman (comic). Miss Dennett, who possesses a voice of pleasing quality, contributed" Going to market " and "Tell me my heart," which she sang with cultured taste, and was loudly applau- ded for each effort. Mr. Barton has inherited his father's voice and ability, and his success on Saturday evening was most marked. In chosing for interpretation " Come into the garden, Maud," "My pretty Jane," and "When other lips," he made possible a comparison between several of out greatest tenors, and it is not too much to say that he came out of the ordeal with more than credit. To a voice of great beauty and ample range he adds appropriate expres- sion, and an attractive presence, and be was vociferously en- cored for each effort. Mr. Fred. Derma is a vocalist of considerable power and expression and his rendering of "The yeoman's wedding," and "True till death " were highly enjoyable. The artistes were associated in a duet and trio that were listened to with satisfaction. The humour- one part of the programme was admirably carried out by Mr. Foreman, and be was twice recalled. The Mill Brow Brass Band played three selections in a style that calls for cordial praise. During the evening Mr. R. W. Pierpoint, in thanking the audience for their patronage and support, an- nounced that in future the concerts would be held in the Public Hall, and the back gallery wonld be thrown open at a penny each. A good programme was promised, which will include a clever performance by Mons Henri Hellier, the celebrated conjurer. Every pair of Beets at HAYNES'S greatly reduced in price —42 and 44, Horsemarket-street.—Advf. HAYerEs's Great Clearance Sale is now on-42 and 44, Horeemarket-street.—Advt.

GRAPHIC CHRISTMAS NUMBER.—In Our advertis- ing columns will be found some particulars of the contents of the Christmas Number of "The Graphic" for 1886, which is, in many respects, the most extraordinary yet published. Each copy of the edition of 500,000 contains, in addition to the large presentation plate and the letterpress, 16 pages of coloured illustrations; and as every num- ber has to be passed through the press 56 times, there is a total of 28,000,000 printings, an enormous increase over those of any previous year. We under- stand that the printing was commenced in January last, 20 presses and 130 men being employed. For the last five months the work has beeq carried on continuously, day and night. Of the enormous edi- tion of 500,000, 80,000 are already on the way to the Colonies. A number of eminent artists have painted pictures specially for this number, and the stories are by two of the most celebrated writers of the day, Messrs, William Black and D. Christie Murray. THE GUARDIAN FOR GRAPPENHALL : Mn. WOODS UNSEATED.—It will be remembered that the Local
THE NEW IIASTEII.

Mr. Dansey informed the members that the name of the guarantee soo!ety given by Mr. Cannel), the new master, was not one recognised by the Local Government Board. He understood, however, that Mr. Cunnah was prepared to submit another, or even to find personal sureties. It was also against the rule that the master should hold any other official appointment, and Mr. Cunnah was the assistant over- seer for Dutton.—Some discussion took place upon the lat- ter subject, and Mr. Dansey having conferred with Mr. Cunnab, said he had promised to resign the overseorship at once.—Mr. Dansey also spoke with regard to the arrange- ments made for the maintenance of the master's four child- ren. The master's salary and the maintenance of the child- ren should be kept separate and distinct. The master must always repay the cost of the children's maintenance to the Guardians. The rule of the Local Government Board was that 5s per week should be paid for a child between the age of 6 and 14 years of age, and a maximum of 2s 61 for chil- dren under the' age of 6 years. If the master's salary was too little with these payments deducted the Guardians could increase it. At the rate of 5s per week for the eldest and 21 per week for tbe youngest children, the master would have to pay a total sun of £24 14s or 14s more than be paid at present.—lt was decided that this subject should be considered a month hence, when the superannua- tion awards were gene into.—There was no other business ef public interest.

Government Board li-O-Ne been called upon to Mae two inquiries into the validity of certain votes tendered during the election of Guardian for the Grappenhall district of the Warrington Union. Mr. Alfred Woods was in the first instance declared elected as against Mr. William Darbyshire, who had occupied a seat on the Board for many years. As a result of the inquiries which Mr. _Henley and Mr. Stevens made on behalf of the Local Government

Board, Mr. Darbyshire has received an official com- munication which goes into detail as to the votes on each side, allowed and disallowed. The letter concludes as follows :—" Deducting then the votes of McHugh, Woolmer, Lally, Burrows, and Ditch-. field from Mr. Woods' total, it is reduced to 81; whilst your total, after deducting the votes of Jones, Friar, and the doubtful vote of William Wicks, is reduced to 83. This leaves you a majority of two votes, and you would still be in a majority of one if one of Mr. Bragg's votes were allowed to Mr. Woods. The Board must therefore decide that

Mr. Woods was incorrectly returned as Guardian, and that you should be returned as duly-elected Guardian in his stead. They will shortly proceed to issue an order accordingly." This, of course, means that Mr. Woods is unseated, and that Mr.
barbyshire will take his rightful place on the Board.

BRIGHTON ELECTION.—The interest in the Brighton elec- tion increases. At a meeting of Liberals on Wednesday night it was unanimously resolved to invite Sir Jeorge Trevelyan to contest the seat. The invitation was made by Gladstonians and Unionists combined. At the same time the Conservatives met and enthusiastically ratified their choice of Mr. Tindall Robertson, who has the support ' of Lord Salisbury and Lsrd R. Churchill. On Thursday Sir G. Trevelyan,who is on his way home from Rome. tele. graphed to Mr. Willett, at Brighton :—" Here papers an- nounce that I consent to stand. Contradict that clearly," Mr. Munster, who at first came forward as a Liberal Unionist, but retired from that position, has again come forward as an Independent Liberal. div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting was held on Tuesdoy at Dut- ton Workhouse. Lieut.-Colonel Ashton presided, and there were present the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner. J. Lock- wood, T. Whitley. Messrs Hadfield, Brandreth, Aaron, Lewis. Mclntyre, Parr, Lowe, Warburton, Percival, H. Linaker (clerk), W. la. Linaker (law clerk), and J. Far- rington (nuisance inspector). THE MERSEY SALT AND BRINE Co.--The Law Clerk reported that the Bridgewater Navigation Company had forwarded the grant of wayleave for the new sewer across land at Weston Point. The proportion of the cost to be paid by the Mersey Salt and Brine Company was over £66, but when he asked them for payment six months ago they 'aid they would rather wait till grant of wayleave was completed. He wrote to them a week ago, but had had no reply.—Mr. Aaron said this matter had been in abeyance long enough, and he moved that the law clerk take legal proceedings against the Mersey Salt and Brine Company. The Brine Company would never pay the money nntil they were forced. The company bad no right to hold the rate- payers' money so long.—The Law Clerk : We paid the money six months ago.—Mr. Aaron: And toev have been written to time after time. Why should they keep the rate- payers' money six months ?—The LAW Clerk remarked that the Brine Company had acknowledged the grant but had made no rgerence to the money.—lt was resolved, on the suggestion of Mr. Mclntyre, that the Mersey Salt and 'Brine Company be given notice that legal proceedings would be taken for the recovery of the money in ten days. masefdoilciaolwosffi:Lelr 0 f H health,ea LTt presented sTeHntEedDlhSTisßl quarterlycr .—Dr. AredpaTrst, have to report that during the quarter ending+September 30th,1886, the registrars returns record 154 births and 77 deaths in the four registration sub-districts of the Runcorn Union. Of the births, 48 were males and 76 females. The birth rate was 7.7 per 1,000 per quarter, against 141 births with a rate of 7.0 per 1,000 per quarter in the corresponding quarter of 1885. Of the deaths, 43 were males and 34 females; death rate, 3 8 per 1,000 per quarter. against 94 deaths with a death rate of 4.7 pei 1,000 per quarter in the corresponding quarter of 1885. Of the deaths, 19 occurred in persons under one year of age, 11 in persons between one and five years old, 28 in persons between five and 60 years low death rate of 38 per 1,000 per quarter, or 15.2 pet . old, and 19 in persons of CO years of age and upwards. The

1,000 per annum, is very gratifying. The Medical Officer also presented a special report of a death from typhoid fever at Sandy Lane, Weston Point. The premises had been disinfected since the death occurred. Ha also reported a case of typhoid fever at The Uplands,Frodsham. Several sanitary defects had been remedied. No fresh cases had occarred. Measles has broken out at Walton Inferior, Stockton Heath, and Wilderspool, and he should visit these localities as early as possible.-The reports were then adopted.
A NIGEIT IN A RUNCORN BAR-ROOll.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. Charles Reynolds, William Treverton, landlord of the Blue Ball Inn,Fryer-street, was charged with permitting drunkenness to take place on his premises. The defendant, for whom Mr. W. H. Linaker appeared, pleaded not guilty.—P.S. Blair stated that about 7-30 on the even- ing of baturday, the 13th inst., he visited the Blue Ball. He was accompanied by P.C. May. In the vaults he saw Thos. Lydiate, John Hart, and two other men whose names he had been unable to ascertain. drunk. Hart was drinking a glass of beer, and there was a glass of beer before Lydiate. He pointed the men out to the landlord, who made no reply.ll The landlord was under the influence of drink. There were also five or six women Of ill-fatne in the vaults more or less under the influence of drink. He went out with May into, the street, and immediately heard a light going on in the vaul's. They returned, and found Lydiate and another man unknown fighting, and knocking each other down. The landlord shouted " Let them alone," and came from behind the bar into the vaults, where a man lifted up his hand and knocked him down. Toe hOIISO was in a disorderly state, and the landiord never attempted to quell the disturbance. —F.t. May corroborated —Mr. Linaker contended that there was no time between the row commencing and the appearance of the police for the landlord to quell the distur- bance. The landlord laboured under great difficulties in conducting his business. The neighbourhood in which the house was situated was a low one, the class of customers were not of the most respectable, and it was easy to under- stand that in this house there was more noise and disturb- ance, even when seber, than a house in a better neighbour. hoc I with a better class of customers. The defendant did all he could to conduct the business in a proper manner, and if such a disturbance occurred three or four times a year, he deserved the sympathy of those in authority rather than to be baited and run after in the manner he was.—The defendant was also charged with permitting quarrelsome and riotous conduct, and the same evidence was accepted.— Supt. Hollingsworth stated tnat the defendant was fined and costs in May for pernfttting drunkenness.—Mr. Brundrit said they considered both cases proved, aud there were no palliating circumstances. When he took the house there were premises of better conduct, but the house* did not seem to go any better under his superintendence, and he had made the matter worse by being drunk. 'The Bench had determined to impose a fine of 40s and costs us 6d in the first case, and 404 and costs 93 61 in the second case,end the license would also he endorsed.

WIDNES CRICKET CLUB. The annual meeting of the members was held on Thurs- day evening at the Central Hotel, under the presidency of Mr. James White. There was a fair attendance. The treasurer (Mr. H. W. Deacon) submitted the statement of accounts, which showed that the receipts amounted to £126 85 sd, and after paying all expenses there was a balance in hand of £4 Ils 8;1A Mr. R. G. Upw,ird, the secretary, read the annual report. which expressed satisfaction at the finan- cial position of the club, and mentioned that the cricket ground and bowling green were in gool condition. Daring' the past season the club from various causes had not been so successful as could have been wished, and the committee would like to see the members take a greater interest in the club. The report was adopted on the motion of the secretary, seconded by the Chairman. Mr. Kyle read the report of the average sub-committee. It stated that in their opinion the comparative bad results of the season's matches is mainly owing to defective fielding. The captains of the respective teams ought to endeavour to get more collective practice.—Mr. Bayne read the report of the Sports Committee. The receipts had amounted to £122 359 d, and the exoenditure had been £lB9 13s 31, leaving a deficit of £67 95 61 This loss had been principally in- curred by removing and reconstructing the pavil- ion, erecting a grand stand, and making a run- ning track. It was decided that the cricket club's proportion of the deficit should )e raised by subscriptions, and £ll 15s 6d was promised in the room.— The question as to whether the sports should be agaia held was referred to the Committee.—Mr. Deacon presented cricket bats to Mr. Robert Moore and Mr. W. Reay, the champion batter and bowler, respectively, of the first eleven. The bat won by Mr. Kershaw, as the best average man in the second eleven, had not arrived.--A gentleman promised to present a bat to Mr. Callon, who was second best.—Mr. F. H. Gossage was re-elected president of the club, and' Mr. H. W. Deacon was re-appointed treasurer. Mr. Colquitt and Mr. Oakden were elected secretaries. The Committee is composed as follows :—Dr. McCambridge, Messrs. I. Carr, G. E. Saya, W. Upward, J. Wright, R. Scott, R. Moore, J. Callon, sen., F. Young. W. S. Pritchard, and J. Ashall.— The proceedings terminated with a vote of thanks to the chairman.
NEWTOWN MISSION CHURCH RUNCORN.-REV. R.

EDW A R DS' FAREWELL. The annual gathering of the congregation of Newtown Mission Church took place on Wednesday evening. The proceedings commenced with a tea, at which there were a good number present. Subsequfeitly a crowded audience assembled to listen to ;in excellent entertainment arranged by Mr. C. Pownall, the organist and choirmaster. The Rev. R. Edwards, curate in charge, occupied the chair, and in his opening address made an affecting reference to the late Canon Barclay. He was glad be had been at Runcorn, be- cause he had had a good training from the late vicar that he should appreciate all the days of his life. (Applause.)— The Rev. T. M. Armson proposed a vote of thanks to the lay readers in connection with the mission, and also to the wardens, Mr. G. Surnmerfield and Mr. Robert Wilson. The motion was carried by acclamatiou.—Mr. Surnmerfield, in replying, observed that during the past year the communi- cants had increased in numbers, the weekly offertories were well supported, and the Sunday evening con- gregation had assumed much larger preportions. They laboured under great disadvantages, but hay- :.ng made great progress under them all, how much more would they have made could they have held their services in the new church, which he hoped they would soon be able to dn. (Applause.) Alluding to the late vicar, he expressed the hope that the town and congregations would raise a suitable monument to his memory. (Ap• planes.) He expressed his regret that all the curates had to depart. Ho had got to know and like them. He was sure he was speaking the unanimous voice of all the officers and Sunday school and congregation when he said they deeply regretted that Mr. Edwards was about to leave them. He might take it as a consolation that he left the church more flourishing than he found it.—Mr. Wilson also made a few appropriate remarks, and on kis proposal thanks were accorded to those who had contributed tables, and who had in any Way assisted in pro- viding the tee. —At the conclusion of the programme, the Chairman said thaot WAS the last time he should take part in their pleasurable entertainments. He wag sorry for more persons than one that he had to leave them, and he could not help thanking all these kind friends for the sympathy, courtesy, and amiability that they had shown to him during the whole period of his residence in Runcorn. He left with the best feelings towards every- body. He read a letter he had received from Miss Edith A. Barclay explaining that the family did not feel equal to being present that evening. Her mother and herself wished to take that opportunity of thanking all the workers in con- nection with Newtown Mission for their past kindness and assistance during the long period of her father's ministry in Runcorn. In conclusion the letter thanked Mr. E lwar.ds for his devotion to the work of the mission in which her father took so eeeat an interest. (Applause.)—Daring the evening the choir sang several part-songs in capital style. Mr. R. Moore gave a spirited rendering of "Time gallants of England," and he was associated with Mr. A. PROPOSED GYMN-ISIIII.I FOR WIDNF3.—MR. T. C. EDWARDS MOSS ON ATHLETICS. For some titre past there have been numerous opinions expressed in favour of the establishment of a gymnasium for IVidnes. In a letter ceceorly addressed to this journal. Mr. Alexander, the celebeated athlete of Liverpool, offered to form a aymn i8iI117) in the town under the auspices of the National Phys,cal flezreation Society, which he took a pro- minent part in forming. Last evening a well-attended meeting was held in the officers' room at the Drill Hall. ' Mr. Alexaoci.r presided, and mention,d tbat Mr. T. C. Ed- wards-Moss a short time ago asked him to assist iu provid- ing a gymnasium for Widnes, and he promised to do so if there was any prospect of success. He read a letter he had received from Mr. H. Wade Deacon, who said he should be glad to assist a gymnasium to be attended by working-men. Mr. T. C. Edwards-Moss, M.P., wrote from Slane Castle, County Mea h :—I am glad to see by your letter of November 18 that yen have taken the initiative with re- gard to the establishment of a gymnasium at Widnes, and that you have called a public meeting together to discuss the proposal. I much regret.that the meeting has been fixed for a day on which it is impossible for me personally to attend, but I am writing these few lines to assure you of my hearty sympathy in the scheme. I take a great in- terest in it not only on account of my former connection with the athletic world, and my present position with re- spect to Widnes, but also because I believe, from informa- tion I have received, that the want of a gymnasium is really felt in the tswu. The people of Widnes have a natural

• taste for athletics and sport of all kinds. They have several first-class foetbell, cricket, and other athletic clubs ; they held an aunual athletic meeting at Fernworth, which is second to none in the north of Engl ind, and if the . promoters of these clubs will kindly lend their 'assistance, and if the leading gentlemen of Widnes will kindly give their support, I feel sure that au efficient gymnasium worthy of the town could he easily established wnich would be a boon and a bieswiug to a very large number of people. It would specially benefit those whose busimess keeps them tied all day to their work, and whose leisure hours during the winter even- ings might be well employed in developing their muscles, and so improving their physique. You will no doubt point out to those who attend the meeting the great advantages both moral and physical of a course of gymnastic training, and you may inform them that for my part I shall be most happy •to give any assistance I can to promote a scheme which, if carried out, will be so conducive to the general welfare of the inhabitants of Widues." (Applause.)—The Chairman then descaPted upon the advantages and pleasure to be derived from the practice of calisthenics, and invited discussion.—Dr. Cooper, Mr. Baflow. Mr. A. Brown (secre- tary to the Football CluO, end Mr. J. Morrison spoke upon the subject The latter gentleman mentioned that there was a likelihood that the baths hired on a lease for the season , would be at liberty, And his firm would no doubt be willing to allow the building to be used ler a gymnasiem on very easy terms. He suggested £1 for two evenings each week.—ln reply to a question, the Chairman seid the cost of apparatus would be £5O. an expenditure which would not occur efter the first year. The selery of an instructor would be £23 for 23 weeks, and there would be the hire of the room.—After some further obeervetions had been made, Mr. Alexander promised that he would commence a gymnasium under the auspices of the National Physical Recreation So- ciety, on the condition that 100 members at rei each were eueranteed—(epelause)—and a suitable building Was found., —Eventually, on the suggestion of G. E. Savce, seconded by Mr. S. Owens, Mr. A. Brown and Mr. W. E. Oakclen, the secretaries of the foothill and cricket clubs respectively, agreed to receive the names Of intending members and col- lect subseriptions.—Mr. C. E. Barlow promised a subscrip- tion of £5, and Mr. Andersen a subscription of £2 2s.—A 'Kota uf thanks to the cheirtnan conclud‘d the'preceedings.

div.head: BOAMG FATALITY AT WARRINGTON. THREE LIVES LOST.
div.p: BOAMG FATALITY AT WAR- RINGTON. THREE LIVES LOST.

- - -- A deplorable accident, by which three lives were lost, happened at Warrington between twelve and one o'clock on Wednesday afternoon. For some days past a number of workmen who are in the employ of the London and North-Western Railway Company have been working at the iron bridge spanning the Mersey at Arpley, which it had been found required some repair. A couple of boats were kept handy while the work was going on, irt case of any emergency, and on Wednesday, during the time allowed for the men to have dinner, four of them and a lad entered one of the boats, a flat- bottomed one of small dimensions, and proceeded to row up the river. They got on all right until near the weir at Latchford, and when going too close to the weir the boat was literally sucked in by the whirl of the water there, and the occupants were thrown into the river. The lad could not swim, but the men, like most who are employed in repairing bridges spanning water, were good swimmers, and two of them succeeded in reaching land, one swim- ming to the Cheshire and the other to the Lanca- shire side of the water. The boy and the other two men were drowned. Information of the occurrence rapidly spread, and caused considerable excitement. In a short time a grappling party were at work, but their efforts were of no avail until yesterday, when a little after eleven o'clock two bodies, clasped to- gether, were recovered near the wear. The names of the two men who swam ashore are William. Bur- ton, sailor, thirty-four years of age, who belongs to Liverpool, and Jqlin Garlick, a joiner, who lives at 28, Wendell-street, Edgehill, Liverpool. The follow- ing were drowned:—

Joint Woods, aged 15, Slutcher's Lane,Warrington. Richard Daintith, age 22, timekeeper, Bank Quay. Warrington. Thomas Carty, aged about 30, sailor, 43, Whittier— street, off Smithdown-road, Liverpool. The two latter were married men, and much com— miseration is felt for the bereaved families. RECOVERY OF BODIES.

The efforts of the grappling party were yesterday partially successful, as the bodies of two of the persons drowned were recovered by means of the grappling irons at 11-15 in the morning. They were those of John Woods, the Warrington lad, and Thomas Carty, the Liverpool sailor. .The bodies were in water of a depth of over twenty feet, and they were locked together in such a position as to indicate that they had sank and died together. It is thought that Carty, who, being a sailor, was a good swimmer,was encumbered with the lad, whom he and Burton, one of the men who escaped, endeavoured to save him, and that, being un- able to free himself, he was pulled down, and thus both were drowned. The bodies were brought down the river in a boat and taken to Arpley-station, whence they were conveyed to the Patten Arms Hotel, near Bank Quay station. They were deposited in an outbuilding in connec- tion with the hotel, where it is expected that they will remain pending the holding of a coroner's in- quiry into the circumstances of their death. When it became known that two of the bodies had been recovered a lifrge crowd gathered, and the space of ground on the Lancashire side of the river, leading into Bridge-street, was crowded when the bodies were taken on to the railway company's premises. Grappling for the third body was afterwards re- sumed.

div.head: SURVIVOR'S NARRATIVE.
div.p: A SURVIVOR'S NARRATIVE.

Yesterday afternoon, one of the men who swam ashore—William Burton, sailor, Liverpool—made a statement in conversation with one of our reporters, in regard to the circumstances of the accident. In the course of it he remarked, "We left the iron bridge at about 12-20, and started to row up the river. We got towards the weir, and when nearing it thought we might go a bit closer, and there we found ourselves getting sucked in by a backwater.' One of them here remarked "Push out for very life," and then they found that the boat was begin- ning to fill with water. "She then," said the nar- rator, "went down from under our feet. I got hold of 'Johnnie Woody' (Woods). We asked the ques- tion of each other if we could all swim, and all an- swered Yes,' but Woody.' I said to young 'Woody,' I'll take care of you.' As the boat was settling down young 'Woody' got hold ot me and said Take care of me.' While I was assisting young 'Woody' Dick Daintit li, got hold hold of me by the neck, and he very near done mo—as close as a toucher. I was struggling in the water for a bit with Dick Daintith, and then he got excited, and I had to get clear, or I would have been fixed myself. I should. have been done as sure as fate, for I was jut going to give it up myself. Then I tried to swim for the shore. The water was rush- ing me up towards the weir, and it was as much as I could do to keep away. The more you try to get out of it the more you seem to get into it. I had a tough struggle. I have had many a hard struggle at sea, but yesterday's near upset met. When I got to the top of the water I said Dick, let go,' but 'he would not, and became helpless. I got hold of the bottom of the boat and held on for a bit and breathed, and then struck out for a swim. The • boat stuck there with the strength of the water. When I went down I could feel the slimy stones at the bottom, and I thought to myself I'll never get out of this.' When I came up on my back the water was falling by my feet, and I knew I was in the stream. I got hold of the keel of the boat, and was quite done." Burton then again re- ferred to the moment when the boat filled and went down. He got hold, he said, of the deceased Woods, Daintith got hold of him, and all three went down together. Woods let go hia hold, and must afterwards have caught hold of Carty, in whose grasp his body was yesterday re- covered. Tom Carty, he said, was a splendid swim- mer. "Could he beat you ?" "lie might beat me in a short distance, for quickness, but he has not got the strength. He was only a very light chap. When I got ashore I began to throw up water like a. good 'an. If I had taken much more water I should have been done. When I saw G-arlick swim to the Cheshire side, I said to myself You are all right, Jack, but Tom's done.' Young Woods must have been clinging to the lower part of him (Tom), and prevented him working his legs." As might be expected, the sad event is the chief topic of conversation in the town.

SUDDEN DEATH AT S HELENS JUNCTION. Mr. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest on Wednesday at St. Helens Junction on the body of Edward Foenev, 23 years of age, of 25, Watery-lane, who died suddrnly at five o'c'ock that morning. Deceased complained of being ill on Monday, and Dr. Casey gave him a bottle of medicine, but the deceased became worse, and died as stated. A verdict of "Death from natural causes" was returned.

DIE PARE WOITNDING CASE.—At the Town Hall, on Monday, before Alderman J. Meßryde, and Mr. B. Hi- ram, James Seddon, a young man, who has been several times remanded,was again charged with unlawfully wound- ing Joseph Pennington, under circumstances previously reported.—Mr. R. W. H. Thomas appeared to prosecute,and Mr. Swift represented the prisoner. Mr. Thomas said the Injured man was still unable te appear, and 12:. asked for tbe prisoner, who had been out on bail, to be farther remanded.. The prisoner was accordingly remanded for a week.

div.head: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.

div.head: AMATEUR THEATRICALS AT NEWTON.
div.p: AMATEUR THEATRICALS AT NEWTON.

A new feature in regard to local entertainments was wit- nessed at Newton Town Hall on Tuesday and Wednesday evenings, when in aid of the fund for the improvement 0 the grounds of the Newton Cricket and Bowling Club an amateur dramatic performance was given by local gentle-f men and ladies. The piece performed each evening was' the well-known three-act comedy "The serious family; and the characters were sustained by Captain A. D. Beton, Lientenant-Calonel Morrison, T. Stone Esq, Captain H. M Thompson, rs Clare Royse, Mrs John Jones, Mrs Handy. side, Mrs Seton, and Miss Peel. As might only be expected the affair created wide-spread interest and on each evening; , the Town Hall was deraely packed by ab enthusiastic audi- ience. The performance was under the immediate patron- age of Lord Gerard, Colonel W. J. Legh, Mr. T. W. Legh,, M.P., Messrs T. J. Gillespie, J.P., W. F. Gooch. J.P., R. Houghton, J.P., G. McCorqnodale, D.L., J.P., A. C. McCor- quodale, JP., J. Pearson, J.P., C. Pilkington, J.P., and Capt Withington, J.P. At one end of the hall an appropriate stage with the requisite scenery, side wings, dee had been erected under the personal euperintentendence of Commander R. C. Royse, R.N.. who officiated with marked ability as stage manager, while the scenery, Jac., was kindly supplied by the Latchford Dramatic Society. Mr. Birch Brown, of Warring- ton, supplied wigs and costumes. The draperies for the stage were designed and erected under the directions of Mrs. Royse. The performances in every respect passed off re- markably well, and the apparent accuracy with which the various parts were represented occasioned the greatest sad,- faction to the audience. The characters were taken as un- der :—" Charles Torrens." Mr. Seton ; " Captain Murphy Maguire," Mr. Morrison; 1. Frank Viecent," Mr. Stone; " Aminadab Sleek," Captain Thomson; "Danvers," Mr. Mac Adam ; "Lady Sowerby Creamier," Mrs. Clare Royser "Mrs. Charles Torrene," Mrs. John Jones; "Emma To; rene," Mrs. Handyside; "Mrs. Ormsby Delmaine," Mrs' Seton; "Graham," Miss Peel. Mr. T. Pearson very effi- ciently carried out his duties as the prompter, but they were only light, consequent upon the careful rehearsals iv bleb had taken plies prior to the performance.

A LIVERPOOL Glra, AT ST. HELEN3.—Before Alder- man J. Mcßryde and Mr. B. Birarn, at the Town Hall, en Monday, Catherine Davies, a young woman hailing from Liverpool, was charged with being drunk and disorderly on Saturday morning, and farther with committing wilful damage to window panes and drinking glasses to the amount of £3, the property of Sir Andrew B. Walker, Bart. Prisoner pleaded guilty to the charge of drunkenness, mad said she did not recollect anything about the damage.—P.C. Ratcliffe said on Saturday forenoon he received the prisoner into custody from the manager of the Parr Vaults. She was then drunk.—Mr. Bennett, manager of the Parr Vaults, deposed that on Saturday forenoon the prisoner was drunk in the vaults, and declined to leave when requested. He turned her out, but she entered by another door and ran her arm across the counter, sweeping off all the glasses. He again put her out, whereupon she " hammered " at one of the doors until she smashed its glass panes. She was then , given into cugtodv. The damage amounled to about The Bench inflicted a fine of 53 and costs for the drunken- ness, and for the wiltul damage imposed a further penalty of 2s 6d and costs, with an order for the payment of £.3 as damages; in default of payment, one month's imprison- ment.

WESLEYAN MISSIONARY MEETTIXG.—At the annual meet- ing on Tuesday, which was he'.d in the 'Wesleyan Chapel, the Revs. J. Shi,pham and -.i. Kent delivered addresses, followed by the Rev. James, Johnston (Congregationalist), who remarked that the o ary Society included,: .perations of the Wesleyan Mission- m addition to the European stations, werea- ;lan Ited in India, China, Ceylon, the West thoselnd which e B,the Gold Coast, South Afripa, and Fiji. With the exception of. Europe and China, the majority of the coun- tries ocvapied were under British rule, which gave them a special claim upon the hearts of Englishmen. The directors of the Wesleyan Suiety were desirous of maintaining their ' present ground, and, further, of making extension. In days \ when it was as common as fashionable to see countries making wholesale annexations on the plea of commercial advantage and military prestige the servants of Christ should make corresponding exertions ir, the name of Chris- tendom. He asked who contributed more towards the labolition of slavery in the West Indies in 1834 than the Wesleyans established there ? They suffered, and resisted, for long years at the hands of the planters in combating the unhallowed traffic. He alluded to the spread of Chris- tianity during the present century, and said it was great, yet much remained unaccotnplished. After careful esti- mates had been made, it was supposed that there are 1,000 millions heathen and Mahommedians, for whore conversion they gave throughout England and America two millions sterling. He compared this with the expenditure upon military armaments, and prayed that the Lord would In- crease His labourers and open their hearts to noble service and sacrifice.

BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held at the Union Workhouse on Tnursday fore- noon. In the absenceSf the chairman, the Deputy Chair- man (Mr. James Fisher) presidei. There were also present the Rey. Thomas Chambers, Rev. Father Finegan, Messrs. John W. Wareing, John Matthews, William Tyrer, James Buckley, Joseah Jackson, William Gore Ashton, James Bur- chall, William Middlehurst, C. B. Johnson, Wm. Gerrard, James Rowson, William Swift, T. Eatock, Edward Syder, John Leatherbarrow, Joseph Griffiths, J. Ellison, W. Daine,

and S. H. Hartley (clerk). RELIEF RETURNS.—The Workhouse Master reported there were 465 inmates of the house, against 458 last week, and a similar number in the corresponding week of last year. There were 211 boys and girls in the school. THE GUARDIANS AND THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD. —A reply to a communication from the Guardians as to whether it would be competent for them to pay 6s per week for the maintenance of a girl named Anders in the Indus- trial School for Girls, Liverpool, the Local Government Board wrote it was not in accordance with the practice of the Board to as§etit t 9 Slç 2. Muse eaVe id veiy exceptional The Board wished to be infotmtd if it was an excep- tional case, and under what eirtttnistances the child was transferred from the West Derby Orphanage to the Indus- trial School.—The Clerk Suggested that the matter should be left in his hands, and he would again press the matter upon the Local Government Board and point out that it Iwas an exceptional case.—This course was adopted. THE WORKHOUSE INSURANCE.—.The Clerk reported That in accordance with the wishes of the Board, the Workhouse premises had been re-surveyed by the insurance company, and the estimated amount for insurance was £27,350, an increase of about £6,000. which was due to the new vagrant ward and new chapel.—Mr. Wareing : Is there anything for the protection of the inmates ?—The Clerk : I am sorry there is not.--Mr. Wareing : That is the most important thing to me.—The Clerk said he did not wish to raise the question of the water supply at that moment, and suggested that the matter should be referred to the Finance Committee. —lt was decided to refer the matter to the Finance Com- mittee. THE PAYMENTS FOR CONTRACT WORK. -- Messrs. G. Waizhom and Son, builder and contractor, and carrying out the erection of new bakehouse, &c., at the Workhouse, wrote for a cheque of £250 on account of contract.—Tee Rev. T. Finegan suggested that the matter shi.uld be re- ferred to theßuilding Committee, and Mr. Wareing seconded the motion.—The Rev. T. Chambers moved an amend- ment that a cheque for the sum of £l5O be drawn, and, sub- ject to the decision of the Building Committee at their next meeting, be paid to the contractors.—Mr. Daine seconded the amendment.—After some discussion, 6 voted for the amendment and 11 for the motion, the latter being carried. THE LATE Manx SUPPLY.—The Clerk read the following letter from the late contractor for the supply of milk to the Workhouse Halsnead Farm, 23rd November, 1886. Dear Sir.—Please bring before your Board on Thursday first the balance .of our account. You were served honour- tOly and fairly by us. July and August are two worst months in year for milk; to deduct such a large amount is very unfair—Yours most respectfully, 0. WARD."—Mr. Daine : Has he not been paid yet ?—Tho Clerk : He has been paid in accordance with the contract, but if he is to be paid in any other manner yon must give instructions for it. —ln reply to Mr. Middlehurst, the clerk said the amount of deductions by the committee was £lB lie Bd, and the amount of the contract was £93.—The question was referred to the House Committee. THE DISTRESS IN PRESCOT.

Th 3 Clerk remarked that at the last meeting of the Board he was instructed to draw up a form of memorial to the board of Trade in reference to the exceptional distress in the Prescot district,and he had done so in the following manlier: "The Memoi ial of the Board of Guardians of the Prescot Poor Law Union. in the county of Lancaster. Sbeweth, That the Union aforesaid is compri-ed of twenty townships, having a population in 1881 of 117.938 persons, and a rate- able value of £631,698 at the present time. That the town- ship of Prescot, with a pop alation of nearly 6,000, and a rateable value of £12,000, is one of the Town- ships forming the said Union. That the chief in- dustry of the inhabitants of Preecot is connected with the manufacture of watch movements, rte. That for a lengthened period considerable depression in the manufacture of these articles in this locality has been ex- perienced, and has caused deep distress and poverty among the skilled artisans and others. That the present deplorable state of the watch trade is largely owing to the practice, which has sprung up in recent years, of placing foreign movements in English hall-marked gold end silver cases, such cases being both of English and foreign manufacture, thereby causing the public to believe that they were pur- chasing watches of English make and design. That those engaged in the several branches of watchmaking, namely, movement making, finishing, caser making, (ie., have re- solved to co-operate in asking the Board of Trade to formu- late and to lay before Parliament and there to support a measure calculated to prevent the fraud being further perpetrated upon the public by goods of foreign manufacture being soli to them as of home make. That it is believed your department contemplate preparing a bill dealing with fraudulent marks, and that now negotia- tions are proceeding with the French, German, end other Governments, for an additional agreement under which the use of fraudulent marks shall become punishable by the confiscation of the goods and the prosecution of the maker and the vendor thereof. That if this.belief is well founded, your memorialists consides this an opportune moment to urge upon you the necessity for inserting clauses in such bill as will preclude any foreign-made watch case being Hall-marked at a British or Irish Assay Office, and will prevent the placing of any watch movement of foreign manufacture in a British or Irish Hall-marked case. That the evidence obtained by the Select Committee of the House of Commons ton gold and silver (Hall-marking) in July, 1878, amply justifies the passing into law of a measure con- taining the provisions indicated. That your memorielists do not regard this as a question of Free Trade or of Protection, but as one to render impossible the continuation of the fraud on the subjects of Her Ma- jesty in Great Britain, Ireland, and other Britieli possessions. Your memorialists therefore pray that you, as President of the Board of Trade, will, in any bill which may be sub- mitted to Parliament dealing with fraudulent marls, have earnest regard to the due and proper safeguarding of the public from fraud by introducing such provisions therm n as will effectually carry out the prayer of your memorialists." .-:-The Clerk said he purposed sending a copy of the memo- rial. to !very member of Parliament, another copy to every Union in England and Wales. If they could by any means support the Board of Trade in their bill its passage might mean some .hundreds of pounds to the ratepayers of the Prescot Union. If the watch industry in Priecot was to die out, it would simply mean that they would have to keep the people, and it would be a charge upon the whole of- the Union.—Mr. C. B. Johnson, in moving that the seal of the Board be affixed to the petition, said it was not a political matter at all, and the strongest advocates of free trade were supporting the movement, which was merely • a movement to stop the fraudulent practice of placing foreign wwch movements in English hall marked cases.—Mr. Tyrer. in seconding the mo-gon, said the colonies suffered greatly by .foreign watches being foisted on them as English made, while the only thing End- lish about them was the hall mark:—Mr. Ranson and Mr. Daine supported the resolution which was unanimously passed.—The Clerk then read a cope, of a letter be proposed to send to each Board of Guardians in England and Wales, drawing attention to the distress among the skilled artisans of Prescot, and the fraudulent practices which deprived them of their livelihood, and asking their assistance in the matter by adopting a similar petition.—On the motion of the Rev. T. Chambers the Clerk was instructed to send a copy of the letter to each Board of Guardians, and .alse a copy of a letter to each member of Parliament asking for his support in the matter. THE Poore _Lew CONFERBNCE.—In accordance with notice given at the last meeting. Mr. Wareing moved the appointment of Mr. C. B. Johnson and the clerk (Mr. liertley) as a deputation to represent that Union at the meeting of the Central Poor Law Conference to be held at London on the Bth prox.—Mr. Matthews seconded the reso- lution, which was passed. Tone Tem MISTRIISS.—On the motion of Mr. Wareing, seconded by Mr. Leetherbarrow, Francis McCulloch was appointed task mistress at the Workhouse at a salary of £25 per annum, with rations, Jim This was the principal business.

By a dynamite explosion which took place on Saturday at Luxulgan, Cornwall, a piece of rock work weighing half a ton was blown among some workmen, killing one on the spot and severely injuring others. The Press Association is informed that Lord Coleridge is likely to be the defendant in another action at an early date, his daughter, Mrs. Adams, being the plaintiff. The nature of the action has not yet been divulged. It is set down for trial before a special jury. THS LIBBRAL PARTY.—A correspondent states that dur- ing next month Mr. John Morley, Earl Spencer, and prob- ably the Marquis of Ripon will visit Hawarden Castle, and that before Parliament meets informal gatherings of Liberal leaders will be held at Hawarden Castle. FATAL GABOTTING CASH.—An elderly man, named John Withers, while returning home froen the Leeds Mar- ket on the 13th instant, was assaulted by four roughs, who stole his purse and other valuables. He remained uncon- scieus after the assault, and died ow Saturday. His assail.

ants are at large. A POACHER SHOT DBAD.—A. TOUEV man named Cotter was shot dead on Monday sight whilst poaching with two companions in the mountainous ,sdistrict bordering Cork and Kerry. The party were met by a gamekeeper, who called on them to desist. The keeper was fired upon and returned the

fire, killing Cotter. ENCOUNTER WITH POICHERS.—Six colliers Were awe- bonded at Leigh on Thursday morning, on a charge of as- saulting several of the Earl of Ellesmere's keepers. They were encountered while poaching on the previous night, and offered a stout resistance, fighting with sticks; an Thomas Rudd, head keeper, lies in a dangerous state. SHOCKING COLLIERY ACCIDHNT.—Two men named Har- ris and Clayton were descending the shaft of the Aldwarke Main Colliery, Rotherham, on Monday to join a.party of visi- tors who had gone down to view the workings, when the cage "tilted," and its occupants fell about three hundred yards

10 OE2 t.;(ltoin 9f the shaft. They were of cogree inetanta- neonsly killed FEARFUL Cobra2lll itcrnESTT.—A shocking colliery ac- cident was bebotted on Saturday from Maesteg,South Wales. While a number of workmen were engaged in the mine, Mr. F'altner, oversman, and James Seagel, collier, were embedded by a fall of roof and killed instantaneously. Mr. W. Plum- ber, the manager, was standing near at the time, and nar- rowly escaped. DISCHARGES AT THE DOCKYARDS.—AR appeal having been made to the Chancellor of the Exchequer for a supple- mentary grant to avoid dockyard discharges, Lord Randolph Churchill writes to Sir Samuel Wilson, M.P.. that he cannot interfere with the action of the Admiralty who would, he feels sure, make no dockyard reductions that were not imperatively demanded in the vinterests of the public service. FATAL EXPLOSION.—The Glasgow fire brigade were on Wednesday called to the premises of Messrs. Shaw and Co., where a cask of naphtha had exploded. After extinguishing the flames several firemen remained in the steep, and a second explosion occurred through a lamp coming in con- tact with some benzoline. A fireman named Morris was instantly killed by the shock, and two of his comrades were seriously burned. MUNIFICENT OFVER.—Mr. Thomas Porter, a Manchester merchant, has promised a donation Of £50,000 to the Cross- ley Orphan Home and School, Halifax—an institution founded and endowed by members of the well-known firm of carpet manufacturers—on condition that the name be al- tered to "The Crossley and Porter Orphan Home and School." Application will be made to Council for permis- sion to make the alteration. BIRMINGHAM Concests.—At the Warwickshire Assizes, on Wednesday, Mr. Justice Grantham passed sentence of twenty years' penal servitude on William Oram, who was convicted of coining at Birmingham, and whom his Lord- ship described as a most notorious criminal. Elizabeth Thompson and Charles Tonks, found guilty of engaging in coining operations, also in Birmingham, were each sentenced to five years' penal servitude. THE WELBII TITHE Wart.—At Lledrod. Cardiganshire, the farmers and tithe payers have sent intimations to the Earl of Lisburne, the trustees of Sir Arthur Chichester, Bart, and the rector of the parish, that unless 25 per cent is conceded on the present tithe-rent charge nothing whatever will be paid. The anti-tithe agitation has now spread to Pembrokeshire, and reductions varying from 10 to 25 per cent have been demanded in nearly every parish. LORD RANDOLPH CHURCHILL AND HIS CONSTITTENTS. —A deputation of subscribers waited upon Lord Randolph Churchill, M.P., on Saturday, to present s cheque for the amount raised among his constituents to reimburse his lordship the expense to which be was put in contesting the seat for the Southern Division of Paddington at the general election in July last, owing to the opposition of Mr. Page Hoppa. which they deemed frivolous and vexa- tious. THE SOCIALISTS.—Lord Salisbury has informed the Soc;al I'emocrate who sent a memorial to Arlington-street on Sun- day from their meeting in Trafalgar-square that the pro- posals contained in it, which involve extensive legislative changes, will doubtless be duly considered by Parliament if they are laid before it; but he is unable to adopt or sup- port them, as he is convinced that they would cause addi- tional distress and suffering far in excess of that which at present prevails. ANOTEER WIFE MURDERER SENTENCED TO DEATH.— Mr. Justice Field, on Tuesday, at Norwich Assizes. passed sentence of death on Harper Riches, fish hawker, of Beccle's, for murdering his wife, in the Norwich Market-place, on the Bth mast, by cutting her throat with a knife. Deceased had left him, and he traced her to Norwich, and, in the presence of his own father, who tried to hold him back, committed the crime. The jury etrengly recommended him to mercy on account of the provocation by his wife's conduct. SUPPOSED MANSLAUGHTER AT MANCHESTER. An in- quest Was held at Manchester, on Monday, on the body of Bridget Maguire, whose husband is in custody on suspicion of causing her death. Evidence was given that the deceased and the prisoner quarreled about money, and the deceased was found on the floor dying by a lodger. The prisoner said she fell down in her excitement. The medical evi- dence was that death was caused by fright or excitement. A verdict of "manslaughter " was returned against the deceased's husband. ACCOUCHEMENT OP PRINCESS BEATRICE. Princess Henry of Batteeberg was safely delivered of asson at five o'clock on Tuesday morning. Both her Royal Highness and the infant are doing well. The following official bulle- tin was issued on Tuesday afternoon t—Wiedsor Castle. November 23rd.—Her Royal Highness Princess Beatrice (Princess Henry of Battenberg) was safely delivered of a Prince this morning at five o'clock. Her Royal Highness and the infant Prince are doing well. (Signed) JOHN WILLIAMS, M.D., WILLIAM JENNER, M.D., JOHN REID, M.D. MINERS' CONFERENCE.—The Miners' Conference was re- sumed at Manchester on Tuesday, when Mr. Burt, M.P., delivered the opening address, He referred to the improved position of the union in Scotland, which, he said, was a matter for much satisfaction. He also spoke of the various subjects which will come under the discussion of the Con- ference, and described the London coal dues as an iniquitous tax. He advised that the Union should formulate its de- mands in reasonable language, and insist on their accept- ance by the House of Commons. On Wednesday. a motion was adopted in favour of starting with the least possible delay "an organised restriction of labour of considerable extent throughout the principal coal-producing districts." faunal, MEETING IN MANCHESTER.—Mr. Labouchere, was the principal speaker at a great meeting, held in St. James's lßall, Manchester, on Wednesday evening in support of the principle of Home Rule for Ireland. Mr.l Proven& M.P., moved a resolution declaring that the beat interests bath of Great Britain and Ireland imperatively re- quire that the great effort to give a better government to Ireland should be firmly persevered in until a durable settle- ment was arrived at, and that the only plan which would satisfy the justice or the policy of the case was that of an Irish legislative body for the management of what Parlia- ment shall decide to be distinctly Irish affairs. Mr. Caleb Wright, M.P. seconded the resolution. In supporting the resolution 114. Labonchere. M.P., said that ever since we swept away the separate Irish Parliament we had been en• gaged in a foolish attempt to convert Irishmen into English- men. Would it not be wise of us to give up this war against nature, which had been attended with so little success ? The absurdity of the war was admitted by their opponents, who, however, would not consent to Home Rule because they thought Home Rule was antagonistic to their own class in- terests. He condemned as impudent and arrogant the at- tetapt of the Liberal Unionists to force Home Rulers into the adoption of their views by calling in the aid of the Tories, declaring that to do such a thing would be to place the Liberal party at the mercy of any Liberals who went to the Toriee for aid. He predicted that notwithstanding all the secessions that might take place, the Liberal party would continue to live and move. It was, to his mind, idle to talk ef other reforms until the Home Rule .question was dec;cled upon the lines laid down by Mr. Gladstone. They were told that the decision of the last election was final, but their enemies need not flatter themselves that it would be final. No reform would ever have been passed had its sup- porters been dismayed at a first defeat or at half a dozen defeats. The resolution was adopted. erfLORO•EINSEED Cotten LOZENGES, a medicated hr seed fxtrAct, ; postsge 2d. Kay, Bros., Stockport, and all Onemitta.--Adet.

THE ADAMS-COLERIDGE CASE. On the reassembling of the Court, on Thursday morning, in the case of Adams v. Coleridge, which had been under hearing all the week, Mr. Justice Denman resumed his summing up to the jury. In conclusion, he pointed out the serious nature of the allegations made against Lord Coleridge and his son. If they found that the documents had been laid before the arbitrator with the intention of in- fluencing his mind, then they must give a verdict for the plaintiff. On the other hand, if they found that that was disproved, and that the plea which the defendants had put on record was a true one, he should tell them they ought to find for the de- fendants. If they found for the plaintiff the dam- ages ought not to be stingy or small, for it would then have been established that defend- ants had, with malicious intent, attempted to pervert the true course of arbitration, and they must mark their sense of this dishonour- able conduct—all the more dishotrable because committed by persons in the position of such high standing as Mr. Bernard Coleridge, and more than all a man who presided in one of the highest courts in the realm, and was a Peer.—The jury retired at twenty-five minutes to one o'clock to consider their verdict.—As soon as the jurymen left the court, Sir Henry James said he thought that the convenient time to mention the points of law involved in the case. He had to submit that there was no evidence to support the alleged cause of action against the defendants, and that there had been no proof of publication.—The Judge said he had practically told the jury all that the counsel suggested.—Sir Charles Russell said that at the proper time he should submit, as a legal proposition, that the defen- dants had the right to send in any documents they thought fit, however libellous. In the course of conversation between the learned counsel and his lordship, it was agreed that the legal arguments could be taken, if necessary, before himself or the Divisional Court,—Mr, Justice Denman remarked that the point was an important one, well worthy of argument, and suggested to the plaintiff that he ought to obtain the assistance of the ablest coun- sel at the Bar.—The jury returned into court at a quarter to two, after an absence of an hour and ten minutes, and gave a verdict for the defendants, the foreman of the jury then proceeding to read a paper drawn up by the jury, in which they ex- pressed the opinion that this action had been caused by the careless and highly reprehensible manner in which Mr. Harrison sent in papers, and;considering Mr. Harrison had taken on himself all responsibility, thought the plaintiff should be held free from cost in the action.—The Judge: You have nothing to do with costs. I give judgment for defendants, with costs. This announcement was followed by some slight applause in court,which was at once suppressed.

WARRINGTON FARMERS' CLUB. A special meeting of the members of this club was held at the White Bull Inn, Horsemarket-street, on Wednesday evening, when there was a good attendance. Mr. John Marsh occupied the chair.— The SECRETARY (Mr. J. L. Stelfox) read minutes passed at several committee meetings, which con- tained memorials that had been sent to landowners and tithe owners. That to the landowners asked for 'further concessions by means of reduction of rent, to meet the exigencies of the times, and that to the tithe owners asked for the remission of the whole, or the greater part of the tithes, now and hereafter to be collected by the persons to whom it was addressed. A letter had also been sent to the Welsh farmers, sympathising with them in their agitation against the tithe charge. A reply to the rent memorial was received from Sir George Chet- wode, who said that he had already met his tenan- try by reductions, but preferred to deal with indi- vidual cases as they arose, and Mr. Smith Barry simply acknowledged receipt of the memorial. Mr. Howell Gee, writing from Denbigh, said that such expressions of sympathy as had been sent by the club to the Welsh farmers, coming as they did from brother farmers in adversity, were very gratifying and encouraging. The letter added that the immediate necessity for a good land act was felt in Wales, even more keenly than the immediate necessity for disestablishment, as the farmers could not hold out much longer under present conditions; Wales I would be satisfied with nothing less than the three Fs, with sliding scal. The following had also been passed by the committee :—(1) "Resolved, that in these days of low prices it behoves farmers everywhere to combine with the object of arresting any further fall in prices, and of effecting economies in the cost of production and distribution of farm produce. That co-operation or combination is the best means of obtaining that object, as it can be clearly shown that considerable economies may be thereby effected in the sale of produce, railway carriage, porterage, &c., besides securing for farmers a ready sale for the whole of their production. That the members of the Warrington Farmers' Club ear- nestly appeal to all farmers to come forward and join them in the pursuit of the afore-named objects, because a full benefit can only be obtained by means of a thorough union and combination." And (2) "Re- solved, that it is evident that the present low prices for milk are largely due to the disorganized manner in which milk producers effect the sale and distri- bution of milk, whereby they force down prices by competition with one another, and place themselves at the mercy of organised bodies of milk dealers. That it is desirable to organize milk producers in this and the neighbouring counties in pursuit of such definite objects as the maintenance of the wholesale price of milk, the assurance of a ready market for the whole milk production, the avoid- ance of had debts, and the general promotion of the milk industry. That the members of the Warring- ton Farmers Club ask all milk producers to join the Club, in order that, by means of a central organiza- tion, the above-named objects may be secured." —A discussion followed the reading of the minutes. In the coursd of it Mr. DAVIDSON urged upon far- mers the necessity of combination. If the farmers of England would unite, their demands would be conceded. But they did not unite. If the same condition of things went on for another year, half of the farmers in this country would be ruined. —Mr. T. STELFOX also spoke of the prospects of farmers. The children of 'farmers. he said, at ten years of age got up in the morning just as the land- lord was drawing a costly quilt over his head, and, "in certain state," trying to get asleep. Who, he said, was as great a slave in this country as the farmer's wife? No one. The husband was the next slave, and then came the sons and daughters. People talked about farmers' daughters and pianos, but if a farmer's daughter worked hard all day why should not she on an evening rattle her fingers over the piano ?—The Chairman, referring to tithes, said that the club did not desire to touch one stone in the Church. They simply objected to the Church drawing its support from a wrong channel. —The discussion was continued by Messrs. W. Darbyshire, John Darbyshire, and Percival.—Mr. DAVIES read a compilation of figures regarding the tithe rent charge of the township of Bollington, and said that he had addressed a letter on the subject to Lord Egerton.—The minutes were passed,. and afterwards it was resolved to send out further me- morials asking for reductions of 30 per cent. in rent and 10 per cent. in tithes.—A discussion sub- sequently took place regarding a case recently be- fore a County Court judge, in which heavy dam- ages were recovered from a farmer, whose son had shot a valuable dog that he supposed was suffer- ing from rabies, and from which he apprehended danger to the stock. The Club decided to ask mem- bers of Parliament to support an alteration of the law affecting such matters.—This was all the busi- ness.
