A police patrol came in contact with a body of " moon- lighters "on Tuesday near Castleisland, Kerry. Shots were fired by the men, but without effect; and the police cap- tured nine prison..rs, seven of whom have been identified. They were all armed. COLLIERY EXPLOSION IN WALES —THREE MEN KILLED. —An alarming explosion has occurred at Trimsaran Col- liery, near Kidwelly. One man, named David John, was killed, and two others so shockingly burnt that they suc- cumbed to their injuries. In a letter addressed te a Stockport alderman, Mr. Bright says that when he was asked by an American if he thought it possible to return to Protection in .England be replied that it was not impossible, bat it would not come until the United Stares restored slavery. GOOD TEMPLARY.—The weekly session of the Hope of Earlestovvn Lodge of Good Templars was held on Mon- day evening, when there was a very full attendance. Bro. John Taylor, W.C.T., presided. Three candidates were initiated and several others proposed for membership. The digest of business for a meeting of the District Lodge at Warrington was considered and the lodge representatives in- structed thereon. The evening's programme was " Enter- tainment and Ode practice," and a pleasant entertainment of songs, readings, <tc., was interspersed with the singing of odes by the members. .

LECTURE ON LONDON LIFE BY THE REV. G. S. REANEY. On Tuesday evening the Rev. G. S. Reaney, of London, but formerly pastor of Wycliffe Church, Warrington, gave a lecture on "Scenes in London Life—Rotten Row and Ratcliffe Highway," in Wycliffe Hall, Warrington,' under the auspices of the Mutual Improvement Society connected with W ycliffe Church. The chair was taken by Mr. J. G. J.P., and there were also on the plat- form the Rev. J. Yonge and Mr. S. Rigby. There was a very large attendance, the ball being com- pletely filled. The CHAIRMAN said he need not introduce Mr. Reaney to them, because he was well known to all of them. (Hear, hear.) And he need not assure Mr. Reaney that they entertained those feelings of cordial affection towards him which they enter- tained years ago, and rejoiced most of all that they saw his face once more, because he knew it without one word from him (the chairman). (Applause.) The Rev. G. S. REANEY, who was received with loud applause, said the very kind remarks made about him by the chairman had not lessened the difficulty which he felt in talking to them that night, many of whom he recognised as the friends of the earlier days of his ministry, and friends in whose affection he lived for some years, the memory of which often helped him in moments of depression and in hours of perplexity. (Applause.) He was very glad to find that Mr. McMinnies' right witty band had not lost its cunning, and that his dear friend Mr. Rigby was as naughty as ever. (Laughter and applause.) ' In speaking to them upon Rotten Row ' and Ratcliffe Highway very likely some of them would ask why did he select such a sub- ject to talk to them upon down in Lan- cashire. Well, the object of his lecture—he would be very frank with them—was two-fold. He wanted to make a little money, and he was, not singular in that desire. (Laughter). There was a member of the House he regretted the chairman was not now a member of—(hear. hear)—who said on one occasion, in a moment of unpremeditated frankness, "Mr. Speaker, there is not a gentleman here to whom a .£5O note at this moment would not be a God-send." (Laughter.) Well, he had a few little schemes not purely of a personal character in his work at the East End, for which he wanted to get something approaching £5O. He had asked people to give him the money and they did not, so he thought he would try to earn it himself. (Ap- plause.) The second object in selecting a subject like that was that he was very profoundly con- vinced that the solution of some of the great social questions of the day must be made in London. Lon- don turned up at the feet of their statesmen or men they called' statesmen all the problems of modern life, and if they could solve these problems in Lon- don, they would be solved for the whole country, and indirectly for the whole world. (Hear, hear,) The title he had chosen was not a mere matter of alliteration. They knew London was a city of two cities, which they might divide into the city of the west and the city of the east. They never could understand the east unless they knew something about the west, and they never could righteously judge the west unless they knew something of the east. Rotten Row and the Ladies Mile were a kind of drive in Hyde Park, where, on a May-day after- noon, they might see all the nobles and all the no- tabilities of that great empire which they called Greater Britain. They were there sure to see what was sometimes aptly called a "returned emp- ty "—that was a Colonial bishop. (Laughter.) They were not sure to see a dissenting parson. Rotten Row, therefore, was a kind of simulcram of the city of the west, while Ratcliffe Highway, which lay far away from all parts and most scenes of pleasure, was an ordinary London street, dim in the sunlight of a summer's day, dark in the fog of a No- vember noon. Each of these places in this great city had a history, Rotten Row taking them back to the time of the Stuarts and of Charles the second, , but the only eventful thing he could call to mind in the history of Ratcliffe Highway was a murder. The murderer was buried at the crossing of the roads, and the other day his body, with a stake through it, was taken up. Just off Ratcliffe High- way another memory was this. that Swedenborg, one of the great dreamers of the human race, was buried. Rotten Row he called the highway of the City of Ease. It was a splendid sight on a sum- mer's afternoon to go and stand there by the Ladies' Mile, or walk just across to Rotten Row. There they saw everybody that was worth seeing in the great , London and the empire; and if they knew all who I rode by they would be astonished to find that the shabbily-dressed man on that wretched hack was a iduke. One of the things, indeed, that he was most impressed with WAS the bad looks of tbe people. (Laughter.) They knew it was very often said that if the judge was put in the dock they would condemn him without any evidence whatever. (Laughter.) If they would change their dresses he would guarantee to find in the East End 500 men who on the whole would look as much like peers as those of the House of Lords, and 500 women who, dressed up and bedizened in the manner in which West End tailors and tailoresses at- tired the ladies, would look quite as much like duchesses and viscountesses as the ladies who nursed poodles. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) In the West End they never seemed to have babies, but sometimes he thought they wore all babies at the East End. Why did not these people nurse their own babies instead of poodles? (Hear, hear, and laughter.) Sernetimes the people of Ratcliffe Highway came amongst the people of Rotten Row and then there was a scare. It was really a funny thing to see the West End frightened, to see all those retired officers in a "funk," and to see all tbe young blue bloods going along the street at the double march. (Laughter.) The prevailing odour in the East End was fried fish ; the people there seemed to be always eating fried fish. To the poor tired worker who had had nothing but bread for 12 or 14 hours this was the most savoury morsel he could buy. (Hear, hear.) Giving other illustrations of life in the East End, Mr. Heaney said he had been at a meeting at which there were 350 men and only six of them had shirts. And yet it was said there was over-productien. There was not over produc- tion of shirts in the east end. (Hear, hear.) There was not over-production of anything but of that epidemic of life, for it was an epidemic. In Ratcliffe Highway they could see the whole world pass along, except the west-ender. On one occasion at two o'clock in the morning, he met a countess there, and in reply to a question, she 3A.id she was used to come out four nights in the week to seek the poor lost girls of the east-end of London and take them to a home. Not many of that kind, however, came to the east- end. There were some came whom they called" slumrners." or "philanthropists in a fuddle." (Laughter.) Lome of these once asked him to show them the poor people, but, "No," he said, they did not show them. (Applause.) He did not care for those who appeared as though they could not give any pity, help, or sympatlayoor even a motherly or sisterly love, unless they saw the people in their misery, temptation, and filth. (Hear, hear.) Tnere were women who worked twelve hours a day and earned Is. They had to be their own carters, and those poor women and girls went struggling along the streets with their great bundles and worked for one penny per hour, finding their own cart- age and their own cotton and needles. Seeing one of these women looking through a window at some bonnets, he asked her if she was going to buy . one, but she replied that she had never bought a new bonnet in her life. He asked the ladies present to think of that. These people lived any way, and in. many cases it was impossible to say where they did live. At the Guild Hall banquet the other day there were 1000 men whose dinner cost £2,500, or £2 5s a head, but he provided a dinner for one hundred men for £1 Gs. (Hear, hoar.) What, therefore, could have been done with the amount spent at the Guild Hall. (Hear, hear.) In the City they ate and drank every year £lOO,OOO, and that of itself would give them free education. The lecturer then mentioned various acts of kindness which the people of the East End did for each other ; and to illustrate the hard- ships imposed on parents by the exaction of school fees, gave an instance of a poor woman having to borrow a pair of shoes in which to go to plead for the school fees of her child. What wonderful places the lodging-houses were in London. There were shops in them in which you could buy anything you waked, and something you did not want. (Laughter.) They would find one person cooking his two- eyed beefsteak, another a bit of eel, and perhaps a third washing everything he possessed. Talk to them, and they wanted to,know who you were, and it sometimes took a week to find out people's names, they had so many. He knew of sOme people that had names as long as their arms almost—and ever so many aliases, and one hardly knew what name they bad got On that week. (Laughter.) Ihe problem of the East End was to be solved by sympathy, not patronage, and not preaching in the pulpit about dam- nation which these men did not care for and did not fear, Once a man got down in a crowd he was down for ever, and .Londbn was a great crowd that would trample down Mr. Gladstone, Lord Salisbury, Cardinal Manning, and Christ himself if he got down. What had the West End people done for the great city of the East ? Could they remem- ber any debate in the House of Commons with respect to the East End ? Mr. McMinnies would, perhaps, remember a debate that took place in the House of Commons about spending £40,000 in one year on Hyde Park corner to make it more convenient for the rich, whilst thousands of little children of the Fast did not live within two miles of a park and had no play ground but the streets. The West End people had been the rulers, and Mr. McMirnies knew how difficult it was to get wiee laws passed, no matter what might be the pressure outside. How great bad been the privileges of the House of Lords, but greater still had been the responsibility of those rich people of the West End— the city of the East. of culture, and of splendid luxury. (Hear, hear.) They had a State Church that had not been the church of the poor in its management. For 200 years what had it done ? And what had the sects done P Stock men up in the pulpit to bid the world come and hear the Gospel and charging 78 GJ per annum as a starting point for the Baying of their souls. (Hear, hear.) The question of

the land lay behind the question of the city. If there were not men of understanding amongst their rulers of to-day, men who could repopulate the depopulated vil- leges of the country, then the problem would get deeper and deeper. They wanted industrial education in their schools and they wanted Lancashire people to keep their Lancashire lads amongst them. They wanted to drive back upon English fields the men who ought to live out of Eng- lard's fruitful land. (Applause.) He felt deeply that un- less something was done fur the masses of the East End of London, they would do something for them- selves. He had great hope in Lord Salisbury and he had great hope in Joseph Chamberlain, He knew both these men felt this question most deeply. He had seen semething more than cold sympathy in the face of Joseph Chamberlain when he had talked to him about the people of ;he East End. Lord Salisbury had said, and spoke with deep emotion when he said it, " I notice the sinister and evil ten- dencies of the time." D d they think the authori- ties in London had been scared by nothing; he knew they had not. There was a new phase coming over the poor of the East End. The physical-force Socialist was amongst them, the Red Cap, the Continental Revolutionary rose be- befo-e them like a spectre. The Cockney Irishmen, with lurid imagination and desperate aims, WAS becoming the leader of the discontented Englishmen ; the old feeling be- tween master and man was going from the workshop. A deep half-conscious sense of the injustice of life was becoming the creed of men who cursed the God of toe churches and the rich. They were groping their way slowly to their own sdlution of the questions that lay at their hearts night and day. They were thinking in silence to-day with faces like that of lelind Sampson. but to-morrow they might grasp in their terrible might those columns of state on which our prosperity and freedom had been built up. (Loud ap- lause.) A hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Heaney was moved by Mr. G. WALLINGTON, seconded by Mr. S. RIGBY. and warmly accorded. Mr. J. WALKER suggested that it might meet the wishes of many in the audience if an opportunity was given them as they left the Hall to contribute in aid of Mr. Reaney's work in London. This suggestion was adopted, and about £5 was contributed. The proceedings were brought to a close by a cordial vote of thanks to 'the chairman, moved by Mr. H. ROBERTS, and seconded by the Rev. J. YONGE.

HONOUR TO A NRWTON-LE- WILLOWS T ENT. Mr. Harold Ernest Watkins, son of Dr. Watkins, of Newton- le-Willows, has been aisarded the first prize for practical chemistry in the medical department (last Summer Session) of Owens College, Manchester. MARRIAGE AT ST. JAMES'S CHURCH. —On Saturday morning a considerable number of people assembled in St James's Church, Havdock, to witness the wedding of Mr.. James Canliffe and Miss Mary Houghton. Being members of the choir, the service was musical throughout, the organist of the church officiating at the organ. The Rev. H. Kearney, the vicar, performed the ceremony, and during the signing of tFe registers, the organist played appropriate music, and the church bell was rung until the wedding party left the church. It is usual at this church, when practic- able, to have a service with as much music as possible when members of the choir are married. _ _

CAPTURRD WHILE TRESPA.S9ING.—Between eight and nine o'clock on Sunday morning, while Mr. Thomas Stone, of Newton Pack, along with a man in his employ named Pennington were walking along the former's estate, they noticed two men engaged in " ferreting" in a wood on the farm occupied by Mr. James Kerfoot. The two men, de- camped, but they were pursued, and one, who gave his name as John Handley, a labourer, of the Vulcan, was caught. Mr. Stone also found a ferret in one of the bur- rows, while a net with one rabbit were also discovered. The second man succeeded in effecting his escape. Handley was taken to the police station at Wargrave, but he was subsequently released when it was ascertained that he had given the right name and address. The case will be heard at the Newton Petty Sessions to-day (Saturday.) Egnir.R.STOWN BAPTIST CHAPEL : SERMONS AND TM& MEETING.—The anniversary sermons in connection with the Baptist Chapel, Market-street, Earl estown, were preached in. that place of worship on Sunday morning and evening, by the Rev. W. Batbgate, of Liverpool. There was a fair attendance in the morning, and in the evening the chapel was filled. Collections in aid of the church funds realised about £4. The annual tea meeting was held in the chapel on Monday ea ening. About 150 persons sat down to a sub- stantial repast, the tables being presided over by Mesdames Tayler (wife of the pastor), Starkie, E. Davies, Davies (Oxford-street), Peake, Clare, Shalcross, Mullins, Hardman, Simond, Pimblett, Mulray, Green, Cronin, Rice, and Pickup. At the subsequent proceedings the chair was occupied by the Pastor, the Rev. W. C. Taylee. -An enjoyable pro- gramme of songs, recitations, was rendered by the scholars, and Mr. G. F. Aveline was warmly applauced for a song. The lost chord ;" Miss Edith Jackson finely sang " The better land; and Mr. John Waddington's song, " Can I e'er forget the valley," was highly appreciated. Readings by Mr. B. Harrison (Lancashire dialect) and Mr. Harry Aveline created considerabls enthusiasm. During the even- ing the choir, conducted by Mr. A. Holdsworth effectively sang several anthems and glees. . AN EARLEsTOWN GIRL us TROUBLEL—SaraIt Hickey, a young woman, residing at Earlestown, was charged at the St. Helens Town Hall, on Friday, before Mr. W. Pilkingten, Dr. Gaskell, and Mr. W. Blinkhorn, with stealing a shawl, value 10s, from the shop of Mr. Joseph Ka', 12, Peter-st., on the 10th iust.—Margaret Thompson, the stepdaughter of the prosecutor, said she saw the shawl (produced) in the shop. She hail occasion to go into the kitchen, and on re- turning she missed the shawl. Margaret Hyena, Crab- street, said•that about three o'clock on the afternoon of the 10th met, she was standing close to Mr. Meson's pawnshop in Claughton-street. The prisoner accosted her and asked her to pawn the shawl, which she alleged was her own. She stated that she did not like to go into the shop, as her mother had once given Mr. Moxon a "good cursing." At first she refused to do so, but eventually consented and got 5s upon it, which she handed to the prisoner.—P.C. Barker said be apprehended the prisoner at Yarlestown. She said she knew nothing about the thef t.— The prisoner pleaded not guilty, and stated that an old man unknown to her bad given her sixpence for pawning the shawl.—lnspector Whittaker remarked that the girl told him quite a different story.—Mr. Pilkington said the wit- ness Hyam did a very foolish thing in pawning the shawl, and she had run into considerable danger.—The prisoner had been several times previously convicted, and she was sent to gaol for twe months, with bard labour.

EARLESTOWN DISTRICT TEMPERANCE UNION. The annual meeting of representatives in connection with the Earlestown District Band of Hope and Temperance Union was held in the Good Tempters Lodge Room, Bridge- street, on Friday evening. The chair was occupied by Mr. J. H. Graham, president, and there was a good attendance. The report of the secretary, Mr. R. Higgins, a summary of which has been previously published, was adopted ; and the report of the treasurer, Mr. George Clarke, supplemented by a report from the auditors, Messrs. J. Judson di W. Pear- son, was read and unanimously passed on the motion of Mr. Mullins, seconded by Mr. Jameson. A conversation ensued upon the various reports, and the position and future pros- pects of the Union, which were considered of an encouraging character. Cordial thanks were tendered to the officers of the past year for their services, and Mr. Graham acknow- ledged the compliment. The meeting next considered the general reports and positions of the following societies com- prised in the Union :--The Good Tempters, Baptist Band of Hope, Primitive Methodist Band of Hope, Wesleyan Band of Hope, the Congregational Band of Hope, the Blue Ribbon Mission, and the Sons of Temperance Friendly Society. The officers for the ensuing year were appointed as follows :—President, Mr. J. H. Graham; vice- president, Mr. John Taylor; treasurer, Mr. George Clarke ; secretary, Mr. William Pearson ; aseistant secretaries, Mr. 0. Picket and Mr. E. Newman ; auditors, Messrs. J. Judson and W. Clare. The Executive Committee was elected as follows :—Messrs. F. Urea (Good Templars), 0. Pickett (Wesleyan), J. Taylor (Primitive Methodist), Mullins (Baptist), J. Hughes (Congregational), J. Judson (Sons of Temperance), and J. Nicholls (Blue Ribbon Mission), with the president, secretary, and treasurer. Various arrange- ments for the ensuing year were decided upon, including the taking part in a cenopetitive examination under the aus- pices of the Lancashire and Cheshire Division of the United Kingdom Band of Hope Union.

THE REV. ROBERT CARR ON "SELF KNOWLEDGE." A meeting in connect ion with the primitive Methodist Mutual Improvement Class was held in the Primitive Methodist schoolroom, Earlestown, on Monday, when over 30 members assembled to hear a paper by the Rev. Robert Carr, resident minister and president of the society, on "Self Knowledge." The chair was occupied by Mr. J. Hollyock. The Rev. Robert Carr gave a definition of the word knowledge, and said a man's knowledge embraced all his ideas about everything. But knowledge might either per- tain to the innumerable objects outside the knowing mind, or it might pertain to the knowing mind itself. In the lat- ter case it was self knowledge, in opposition and in contra- distinction to the innumerable objects outside. The impor- tance of such knowledge could net be over-estimated, and it was essential that a young man above all others should have an accurate knowledge of his own c,ipabilities, of the parts in which he was lacking. Ignorance of self was often fatal. Many a fine young fellow had suffered a disastrous defeat and been hopelessly crushed, not because he had not parts which would have gained him distinction, but because he essayed to do a work for which he was not competent. The importance of self-knowledge had attracted the notice of all thoughtful men more or less, and " know thyself" was one of the three precepts which were described with golden letters above the doorway of the magnificent temple at Delphas. It was considered such an embodiment of wis- dom that the ancients regarded it as divine. Self-knowle4e was important if it only enabled them to see themselves as others saw them, and it did more—it took a man into the nner chamber of his own soul, where he could see every- thing as it was, whereas others could only look at them as they appeared. He pointed out the mlny phases in which the subject might be consklered, and stating that he must necessarily restrict the limits in a small paper, he pro- ceeded te urge that self-knowl edge made a man , conversant with his own capabilities, and taught I him to discriminate the degree of excellence pecu- liar to each faculty. It also taught a man

THE AlirEnicarl alems.—At a largely-attended meeting of representatives of the Liverpool provision trade, held on Tuesday, to consider the alteration in the American mail system, all the speeches were strongly condemnatory of the action taken by the Government, and resolutions were unani- mously adopted protesting against the change which had been made. Loss OF 140 LIVES.—A Plymouth correspondent says a search instituted in the South Seas, on behalf of the Government, has failed to obtain any news of the schooner Young Dick, which was on a voyage. with 140 persons on board, chiefly labourers from 11.3 w Zealand, whoa° term of servipe bad expired. SHE NEVER HAD ONE.—Mistress (to servant girl) : Your name is what ?—Girl: Mary, mum—Mistress: Yes, but what is your surname ?—Girl: My sir name? Why, mum, I never had any. I'm not a man. • It isn't always a desire to embrace religion that leads young men to attend evening prayer-meeting. What they want is to embrace the religious during the moon- light walk home after the exercises. Captain Jawkins : /Co, I'm not exactly engaged, but I have the refusal of two or three girls.—Miss Ethel: What a capital way of putting it ! I suppose you mean you mean you have asked them, and they have said ".No," Hs Krum IT.—The husband was an exceptionally mean man. His wife said to him: "My dear, it is time we were thinking about the education of our Jules." "Oh ! it costs too much." "Don't you know of a cheap school ?" "Yes." "Which is it ?" "The school of ad- versity." IMMEDIATELY AGREED.—" Bailiff," said an Arkansas judge one day last week to • the officer in charge of the jury, "will you please inform the jury that there will be a horse race in Merrick's pasture at three o'clock ?" The jury had been out for forty-eight hours, but in less than thirty minutes they came into court with a verdict. WHAT WAS WRONG WITH HIM.—At a mission-hall in Pollokshields the clergyman's wife was kindly question- ing at the close of a meeting a woman whose husband had been long ailing. "What is his trouble, Margaret ?" said she. "Wed, ye see, mem, it's no very muckle o' ony kin' o' trouble. It is jest a kin' o' general ability." Drunkman : Professor, 'fessor ! Come here—hic— secon'. You're 'nequcated man. 'Portant question wants to ask ye. Want to ask ye—shay—hic—is th' earth round 2—Professor: It is approximately round, friend. It is what scientific men call an oblate spheroid, but in ordinary, common-place everyday conversation it is perfectly proper to speak of it as round.—Drunk- man: That settles it.—Professor: Settles what, my friend P—Drunkman: Sholves the problem, splains the riddle, loocidates the mystery. Explanation perfec'ly sas'factory-, sir. 'Everythin' splained bootfully. Knew- suthin' matter the earth. Can't stan' up on the blamed thing. S'round. 'Counts for it. Can't stan' up on a blame roun' thing !—Lynn Union. Sir Francis Doyle tells a capital story of Sir Robert Peel. He was, when Irish Secretary, examining a national school in Ireland, and putting questions on the Old Testament. "Tell me," he said, "what was the reason why Moses left the land of Egypt ?" The older boys passed it, but a little boy on the back seats held out his hand, with "I know, yer honour !" "Come to the front and tell us all about it," said Sir Robert Peel. The boy obeyed, and, when he got to the front, he looked Sir Robert full in the face, and explained the matter thus: "Please, yer honour, he shot a Peeler !" Paddy had merely Hibernicised the land of Egypt.

WARRINGTON BOA.RD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of this Board was hell at the Workhouze on Wednesday morning. There were present the Rev. G. F. Roberts (chairman), Messrs. Bonnell, Brown, Isherwood, katcliffe, Balharry, Voisey, Jolley, Clark, Heston, W. Houghton, Hibbert, Wright, Eckersley, J. Houghton, Gibson, Blackhurst, Woods, Humphries, Grange, Strange, Harrison, Greening, Swinton, Kilshall, J. C. Sutton. (clerk), and S. Button (assistant clerk). ILLNESS OF A MEMBER. The CHAIRMAN said that befoie the desk read the minutes he should like to say a word or two. He felt sure that lee would have their sympathy when he expressed regret ttiat a member of that Board whom they all held in high es- teem had been taken seriously ill. He referred to Dr Mackie, who was taken ill en Sunday. They would be glad to hear that that morning he called at Or. -Mackie's house and was informed that he was no worse. SCHOOLS COMMITTEE. This Committee reported that the school children had been invited by Mr. Poole to witness his myriorama at the 'Public Hall, and that the invitation had been accepted. The Committee also recommended that Mr. and Miss Gib- bon, of Warrington, be appointed tailor and mistress of one of the homes at the schools, and after these two candidates had been before the Board, the mintites were confirmed, on the motion of Mr. JOLLEY. SCHOOL FEES. The School Fees Committee reported that fees had been all Owed in 80 cases, 72 of which were old and 8 new cases. —Mr. BLACKHURST moved, and Mr.' HARRISON seconded. the adoption of the minutes.—Mr ISHERWOOD proposed that a return be made of the names of persons who had been summoned before the magistrates in connection with school matters.—Mr. BLACKHURST said there was no doubt that the school fees were on the increas a, and he was sorry to say that they were likely to go on increasing as long as the state sif trade remained as at present.—Mr. HARRISON : And it is not peculiar to Warrington.—Tbe CHAIRMAN was afraid that the suggestion of Mr. Isherwood was impractic- able, because the summonses were issued bv the Town Council, and not by the Guardians.—Mr. HARRISON had no doubt that Mr. Isherwood would obtain all the informa- tion he required if he would apply to Mr. Riley, the school attendance officer.—Mr. Isnerawoon said his reason for wishing for a return was that the names of some of those who were fined at the borough court on Mondays seemed to have a resem- blance to those who received school fees. And, besides, he had noticed that £llO had been paid in the half-year for school fees, while no more than £l6O had been paid for relief, and he thought, therefore, that It was time some steps were taken. He also mentioned that he could give an instance In which sixteen puddlers had been granted school fees.—The CLERK pointed out that Mr. Isherwood had made a mistake as to the cost of the re- lief afforded, because they were giving something like .Dl6O at each Board meetirag.—Mr. Blitowx said that although that Board was net directly connected with prosecutions, vet they were indirectly, and as some of the parents who Lad fees allowed them were most negligent, the committee might by putting pressure upon them do good in two ways, first by insisting upon more regular attendance of children, and second by making the pareros more economical. He feared they were going on in too lax a manner, both as re- garded school fees and other things.—Mr. GREENING said it was a fact that parents who had school fees allowed were brought before the borough magistrates and succeeded in Berne way or other in paying their 55 fines, but how they did so was a mystery to most people. lii many cases too these people spent their money in drink or in some way they ought not to do while their children were running about the streets in a disgraceful fashion. But with that they had nothing to do; all they had to do was to adminis- ter the school fees and they looked after these as closely as possible. Mr. Isherwood had referred to paddlers being allowed school fees, and the committee had some of them before them the previous day, and they seemed to have next to nothing coming in. One man told them that he had had only one turn the previous week, and the payment for that was all he had to keep six or seven children. The committee were administering the fees very closely, more closely indeed than he himself should like to do, but under the circumstances they felt bound to be what he considered a bit hard in many cases. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. JOLLEY said the School Fees Committee was one that ought to command the respect and confidence of that Board, and it should be borne in mind that the money for the school fees was not given to the parents themselves, but paid over directly to the teachers so that it could not be spent in drink. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. HARRISON said every precaution was taken to avoid imposture in allowing scheol fees.—Mr. BLACKHURST also mentioned that many who called themselves puddlers were men who only had odd jobs, and their wages often did not run 105 a week.—The co m- rnittee's minutes were then confirmed. THE CANCELLED CONTRACTS. The CLERK mentioned that he had written to the con- tractors for the supply of groceries with regard to the un- satisfactory nature of the articles supplied to the school and Workhouse, and informing them that the Board had decided to cancel the contracts. He had received a letter in reply which be read, and in which the contractors asked that the goods might be specified which it was alleged were not in accordance with the quality desired. The quality of the cheese had been complained of by the master of the Work- house, and that had been immediately changed, and that was the only complaint they had received. At present, the letter stated, they were supplying, and ba4 been for a con- siderable time, institutions larger than those of the G oar- Mans with precisely the tame class of goods, and instead of receiving complaints they had been recommended for the superiority of goods supplied. Attention was also called to the condition of the contraots, and they made a formal ap- plication for the appointment of an arbitrator. The Clerk having read his reply to this communication, remarked that he did not think there was any need for a discussion on the matter.—The subject then dropped. THE WORKHOUSE MASTER'S CASE. Mr. YOISEY referred to the letter which bad been read from the Local Government Board at the previous meeting of the Board, in which it was requested that the Workhouse- master (Mr. Mackey) should be called upon to resign, owing to certain erasures having been made on an account sent in by Mr. Hedgcock, plumber, ttc. Having referred to the various circumstances in connection with this matter that I have from time to time come before the Board, and con- tended that it was not of so serious a nature as to merit so I severe a punishment, he pointed out that the only purpose that could have been served by the erasure was simply the saving of a little trouble to the clerk or somebody else about I the Workhouse. Mr. Mackey was charged with untruth- fulness in regard to the circumstance that it was alleged I that while he knew of the erasure be disclaimed any know- , ledge of it to the auditor, but he (Mr. Voisey) would like to I be quite sure on the point. He would say at once that he I thought Mr. Mackey was reprehensible in not baying brought the matter before the Board, but he should like to know whether Mr. Mackey stood alone in that matter. He said that if anybody else bad any know- ledge of it they were quite as culpable as Mr. Mackey. (Hear, hear.) It had been brought to his knowledge that somebody from Mr. Sutton's office bad approached Mr. Hedgcock almost immediately after the delivery of the bill, as to whether the bill had been tam- 'pared with.—The CLERK said that when the auditor (in January last) discovered that the account had been altered be turned to his (Mr. Sutton's) son and told him to go to Mr. leledgcock.—Mr. VOISEY said that was not the time he was referring to. Did not, in the early part of August, some one go from the clerk's office and ask Mr. Hedgcock pointedly if the account had been tampered with.—The

CLERK said that was a charge of the most serious deicfip- tion, and the person who made it ought to he in a position to say who the pereon was that went to Mr. Hedgcock.— - Mr. VOISEY said that he had received his information from Mr. Heaton.—At the request of the clerk, Mr. S. SUTTON (eesistant clerk) was asked if he had ever gone to Mr. Fedgceek with the account between the 11th July and the 29th September last year, and he replied that he had not, and he had no knowledge whatever of the alteration till the auditor called his attention to it in January last. He was also quite sure that no one had gone from the clerk's office with the account about the time referred to.—Mr. VoISRY then said he would leave it to Mr. Heaton, and if his infor- mation was not correct he would instantly withdraw every word he had based upon it.—Mr. HEATON said he had gone to Mr. Hedgcock, who stated to him that shortly after he sent the bill in a clerk came to him from Mr, Sutton's office and asked him if the bill had been altered.—The CHAIRMAN: What date was that ?—Mr HBATON : He could not tell me •=-(" oh, oh ")—but he believed it was in August.—The CHAIRMAN eaid it was not dispeted that Mr. S. Sutton went to Mr. riedgcock ; what was disputed was the time of that visit.—Mr. HEATON : Mr. Hedgcock told me it was in August or September.—Mr. VOISBY said he had been told that the visit eves in August.—The CHAIRMAN : Mr. Sutton says he did go to Mr. Hedecock's, but it was at the instance of the auditor, in January,—hir. Votsay said that if it were true that nobody went to Mr. Hedgcock before the audit he, of course, instently withdrew everything that had been said in regard to it, having been misled by the information put into his hands.—The CLERK mentioned that before the audit he had only bad the invoice in his possession a few hours, after which it was in the possession of the workhouse master.—Mr. Voisav then went en to say that he should like to know exactly what did take place between Mr. ' Mackey and the auditor in January, 1886, be- cause it was stated that Mr. Mackey had said he had no knowledge of the e.asure. He wished to know if it was within the knowledge of , any guardian what passed.—The CLERK said it was the 'auditor who said that Mr. Mackey denied knowing anything about the alteration, and it was the auditor who sent his son, who took Mr. Shearer with him, to Mr. Hedgcock. If somebody had aimitted knowing about the erasure why should the aaditor send down to Mr. Hedgcock ? The audi- tor had said nothing to him (the clerk) about it, and not having been in the room at the time he was not in a poei- . tion to say what Mr. Mackay said.—The CHAIRMAN said he was called into the room by the auditor who was in a , state of excitement and indignation with regard to the ac- count, and the question being put to Mr. Mrckey, he said he did not know anything About it.—Mr. VOISaY said he had been going to ask for the production of the whole of the correspondence, but he thought he would now let the mat- ter rest. It was a lernentable feature of the case that Mr. , Mackey after so iromy years should forget himself in a pal- try matter of that kind. (Hear, hear.) He should like to know whether it wtis the general wish of the Board that Mr. Mackey should be eel led upon to carry out the step re- quired by the Local Government Board.—The CHAIRMAN did not think any motion of that Board would have the effect of making the Local Government .Board alter their mind, unless, indeed; they could show them that come of the facts upon which they based tbeir decision were wrong, —Mr. VotsF.7 said that was not a matter of fraud, but simply of saving other people trouble.—Mr. HARRISON said that Mr. Voieey having referred to the charecter of the lie, be might remind them that Queen Elizabeth said a lie 'was only an intellectuel mode of getting out of a difficult situation." (Laughter.) He believed that the lie, if there be a lie in that matter, was very much of that character— be believed it originated from a desire to avoid a disagree- able situation, and to would unnecessary trouble. He then asked if the chairman could afford him any information as to whether Mr. Mackey admitted to the Guardians having made the alteration in the account.—The CHAIRMAN Ido not know.—Mr. BROWN thought that the Local Government Board were acting on the assumption that Mr. Mackie had made that admission. Suet), however, was not the case.— Mr. VOISKY said it seemed to him that the Local Govern- ment Board had made a great matter of it. Was it one of those cases for which a man who had spent his best years under the Guardians should lose the credit of all his past services? He had grown grey in the service of the Guardians, and were they going to say he should lose all the benefit of this because of this error, which he (Mr. Voisey) did not see in that grave and seri- ous light some people had seen it.—Mr. GIBSON asked if the auditer had found fault in other ways with Mr. Mackey's conduct.—Mr. VOISEY objected to this question, and after- wards moved "That after a full discussion of the complaint made against the master, the Guardians declare it to be a case where they would be disposed to support an appeal by the master to the Local Government Board to have his irreg- ularity or other fault overlooked, and that a letter be address- ed from this Board to the Local Government Board according- ly.—M r. BROWN seconded this proposal; which was also sup- ported by Mr. Harrison.—Mr. Ginsore repeated his ques- tion, and asked if Mr. Mackey had been surcharged for three weeks' wagee.—This question was also objected to and not answered.—Mr. Jolley and Mr. Blackhutse spoke against the resolution.—Mr. GREENING referred to the charge brought against the clerk's department, which, he said, was an attempt to push blame off one set of shoulders on to another. Mr. Voisey, Mr. Greening went on to say, had ki ought forward the matter in a straightforward manner, no doubt believing-the information he bed was sufficient to prove it ; but he judged, from the finish of Mr. Voisey's speech, that, in his opinion, the information he had received from certain patties did not substantiate what it had been thought it would do. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Voisey had then very properly and gentlemanly said he weuld withdraw everything he could not salistantiate.—Mr. Ws,l'B mot ion was soon after put to the meeting and negatived by 14 votes to CLERK then said that as the charges which had been made against his department were very serious ones, he should ask the Local Government Board to inquire into them'. (Hear, hear.) The relief cases were then proceeded with.

WOMEN'S CLUB AND THE FREE LIBRARY QUESTION. The annual dinner of the committee of this club was held on Saturday evening at the Warrington Conservative Club. Councillor Mackie, the Mayor, occupied, as president, the position of chairman, and Mr. J. Potter was vice-ehairman. Amongst those present were the ex-Mayor (Alderman Harri- son), Messrs: Thomas Morris, Thomas Robinson, A. B. Mackie, George Riley, I. Leeson, T. Hollings- worth, W. E. Stout, T. H. Ashcroft, •J. Bayley, A. Daniels, W. Ford, J. Godfrey, T. Heywood, W. Rus- sell, T. Sanson, R. E. Ellis, W. Sanson, and R. Pen- nington. The dinner, which was given by the Mayor, as provided by Mr. T. 0. Speakman, the manager of the Conservative Club, and gave satis- faction to all. Various toasts were honoured after the repast, and the MAYOR, in a short speech, hav- ing referred to the satisfactory prospects of the club, suggested that steps should be taken to make it free for working-men, to be admitted by vote, in commemoration of the jubilee year. They had, he said, spent £llOO on the club, every penny of which was honestly 'obtained, even at the bazaars, and he should like to put it in M. Morris's power at the coming meeting of the ratepayers to consider the question of the free lending library to say that the Workmen's Club was free to all the working-men of Warrington. (Cheers.) If Mr. Morris could not get the money he wanted in large sums of £5OO or £lOOO, there was, he felt sure, sufficient life and spirit left in the working-men of Warrington to ob- tain a free lending library by the ordinary opera- tions of an active and zealous committee. If £2OOO could be raised by the working-men of War- rington, the bona fide working-men repre- sented by their own club, he had no doubt the other £2OOO required would come tumbling in from the richer men. (Applause.)-- Mr. Tuomis Moßms, in responding to the toast ' "The town and trade of Warrington," said that the free lending library was a matter which, he sup- posed, he had got on the brain—(laughter)—and he wanted them to assist him. It was only a question of ways and means, and he believed there were numbers of men in and around Warrington who if they would put their hands in their pockets would materially assist and enable them to carry out a useful work. (Applause.) Air. Morris pointed out that there were free lending libraries in &Ron, Stockport, Blackburn, St. Helens, and Wigan, all manufacturing towns, and two in St. Helens. Run- corn, notwithstanding that it was composed of sea- faring men and had a migratory population, also possessed a free library which was going on mag- nificently. In conclusion, he said he should want all the help he could get from them, and he had no doubt it would be willingly given. (Cheers.)—Mr. ASHCROFT, who proposed the health of the President, denied the assertion which had been made that the free lending library movement was confined to a few Radicals.— Mr. _MORRIS, in corroboration of the statement made by Mr. Ashcroft, said he did not think there was a more honest and sterling Conservative in Warring- ton than Mr. John Roberts, and he was with him heart and soul in the free library movement; so were thousands of Conservative workingmen. Only that day they were going to a few wealthy Conser- vatives and Liberals to ask their aid in this move- ment, but Mr. Roberts had made a prior arrange- menttand could not go with him. (Applause.)—The MAYOR, in reply, said he was very anxious, to put Mr. Morris in a position to be able to say at the Free' Lending Library meeting what the Workmen's Club had done, and the sympathy they showed to- wards the movement. (Applause.) He had seen the Town Clerk that day, and he had arranged for them to have their meeting in the Circus next Thursday but one; and he hoped the Tories, the Radicals, and all, classes would attend, and show their interest in the movement, and he was sure they would then succeed (applause)—but he would not as Mayor pledge the Town Council. Songs were afterwards given, and a pleasant even- ing was spent.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, THURSDAY. The manner in which Lord Salisbury has taken his nephew into the Cabinet has been very freely criticized; but, after all, the fewer ceremonials we have the better. The whole thing was very quietly done, almost as quietly as the Guinness boom, and almost as suddenly as the disendowment of the White Star and Cunard lines. One might have expected a little more trumpeting and a few addi- tional puffs preliminary, but when Parliament was not sitting little more could be done. There is a recognition of the claims of Scotland in the appoint- ment, which is all very well in its way. I hope Mr. Balfour will he able to shed a little of that lazy dilletantism which spoils him for the seriousness of official life. Lord Randolph has shown himself by no means dilletante, and again faithful Tories are asking whether he is likely to shed his views first, or his party to shed him. The "Standard" of course has its opportunity and takes it. It really seems to dislike Lord Randolph almost as much as it used to dislike Lord Beaconsfield. But its power is not now what it was, or, rather, Lord Randolph's power is much greater. The party must do -With him, be- cause it has come to this, that it can't do without him. Somehow or other things are turning out very strangely in the camp. There is poor Sir William Hart Dyke, who had everything to expect a little time ago, and who has everything to expect still— at least, who has got none of the things he did expect. He is not to be Governor of Hong Kong. He has not refused it, because it was not offered to him. And yet he was model lieutenant, doing everything he was told, and asking no questions. Did any Irish Secretary ever take office at a time when he might have made his own terms so easily, and yet was content to be so forbearing and to play on so small a fiddle? The old-fashioned Tories are complaining. The Conservatives have come into power, and the Tories are not in it. Certainly the Postmaster-General has got himself into a hornet's nest about the American mails. There is something yet to come out. Is it a game of brag between him and the eliminated companies? There are wheels within wheels in such matters. I can readily understand that an outsider's view of the question would be that the contract should be given to the company who could best perform it. The Inman and the Guion are to supplant the White Star and the Cunard. It takes five ships to do the service, and you must test the strength of the chain by its weakest link. The best vessels of the Inman, the Cities of Chicago and Berlin, would make New York from Queenstown in about 84 days, the City of Montreal, the slowest, in about 10 days. Then, of course, there are the Union boats. This company started the Arizona, which became the greyhound of the Atlantic, bounding across in about 74 days. Thsn came the Alaska, which carried off the palm even from the Arizona. Here, indeed, are two strong links on the new cable, but we have to look to the weak ones. The Wisconsin is scarcely faster than the Montreal. It is a ten days boat. The Ne- vada and the Wyoming are from 9to 94. How are these to be matched against the Cunard with its Servia and Aurania running in 71 days, and the Etruria and Umbria, the fastest vessels on the ocean, the present greyhounds of the Atlantic doing the distance in 64 days? Then, under the new arrangement, Southampton is to have one of the three mails. Is this the thin end of the wedge? Can it be that a Tory Government, the advocates of Protection, are arranging to deflect a lot of Government money into the hands of a Ger- man firm? For let us, for a moment, compare the Liverpool rorte and the Southampton route. Early in the week the Alaska brought the New York mail via Queenstown and Liverpool, and the bags were in the custody of the London Post Office eight days and four hours after they left the New York Post- master. The Treves, belonging to the rival company, was meanwhile also conveying the mails, but via Southampton. The Treves is one of the latest, if not the latest, of the German fleet. The mails were in London by their route eight days and eleven hours after they had left New York, and arrived the Post Office unsorted. Of course, by the Queens- town route, all the time of the journey up to Dub- lin and all the time of the journey from Liverpool to Euston is available, and is employed in sorting the letters. Thus Liverpool gets its mail at once, and Manchester, Leeds, Warrington, Bradford. Pres- ton, Leicester, and all the great towns in the north get their letters before London. The truth is that here the conduct of the Postmaster is treated as a mystery. There is some motive at work of which the public know nothing. I cannot believe that Mr. Raikes is in league with Prince Bismarck, and yet it seems as if he is retarding the American mails to put money in the pockets of a German firm. At last Mr. Boehm's new statue of the Duke of Wellington may be seen and criticised. A plaster cast is not a bronze, but it sometimes looks better than a bronze. Perched on its high pedestal oppo- site Hyde Park Corner, I think the first criticism that is suggested is that the Duke is very large and the horse is very small. lam sure Mr. Boehm has accwately reproduced Copenhagen's proportions still the famous charger does not look much. The Duke's dress is the familiar conventional costume— the frock coat, the Hessian boots, the, telescope and the cocked hat; but lam happy to 'say it has not been thought necessary to extinguish him with the conventional military cloak. The Prince of Wales told Mr. Boehm that he thought it "excellent" and the Duke of Cambridge went a step further, and pronounced it "most excellent." The cast will be taken down in a few days, and in due time we shall have an addition to the list of London common- places. Of course it is not as bad as our famous Griffin and our more famous Byron (its neighbour). Mr. Boehm is always an artist, but he is very rarely a genius. We have H.R.H. for treasurer at the Middle Tem- ple for the coming year. The treasurer has to head the procession of the Benchers up the hall, to take in the principal guest on Grand Day, to read grace, and to have his name figure as host on the invita- tion cards when the Hon. Society gives a dinner. The duties are not cumbrous, and only one other of them remains unmentioned. He has to make the little speeches which fall to the customary lot of a chairman or president. In all these I think our Prince will hold his own with any other Queen's Counsel on that bench. A crowd round the law courts from four o'clock out has now got to be quite a recognised feature of the Strand in the early evening. One cause celebre follows another, and litigants and witnesses are watched with prying eyes. Lord Coleridge of course escapes notice. He comes in at the judges entrance, and then, though he is a remarkable-looking man, he is not, outside the profession, a well-known man. Sir James Stephen or Sir Henry Hawkins are as well know to the ordinary Londoner as Mr. Irving or Mr.Spurgeon,but the Lord Chief Justice is seen very little about, and does not look the.least in black cloth I like what he looks in red silk. But the plaintiff's face and figure have got to be very familiar. Mr. Cotter Adams is a giant in height, and by no means a knock-kneed giant either, but square shouldered and burly. His manner in court has throughout been courageous and defiant. No greater contrast could be imagined than exists between Lord Cole- ridge and his son-in-law. The former has a singular trick of blushing like an innocent young girl, and then turning white and then blushing again. One is almost reminded of a lighthouse with revolving lights. Mr. Adams' sallow face never shows the slightest tinge of that rose-coloured suffusion which would make Lord Coleridge so interesting if he were a young girl of nineteen. The interest in the other case is greater still. I suppose Lady Colin is one of the most beautiful women in England. Anxiety, and the illness which attacked her in Rome and brought her to death's door in Florence, have, of course, left their inevit-
e _

able trace on a face that only two years ago was radiant with youth, and health, and beauty. She is very tall, stately, and graceful. Her complexion I is dark and rich, her eyes brilliant, and a wonderful I smils lights up her face from time to time. In talking, her animation is extreme. Born in Ireland, and of Irish ancestry, her face does not in the least suggest her country. But for her stature you ' might be sure she was Italian, and anyone who had heard her sing "Santa Lucia," or any of the Nea- politan songs which she delights in, might well fancy her one of the beauties of Capri. Lord Colin is in sorry contrast to Lady Campbell. Short, stout, and thickset, there is nothing very aristo- cratic in his appearance. The crusade against the Academy seems to have subsided and to have left matters very much as they I were. Poor Mr. Hart retired and regrets it. It is said he will send in his customary eight. He will probably receive them all back again. It is curious I that the crusade seems to have told not on the R.A., I but on the other institutions which supplement and I seek to move it. The Society of British Artists has ' for years represented the lowest ebb of the painters' craft. They made Mr. Whistler one of their num- ber some years ago, and everyone wondered that he lent his strength to so feeble a concern. The worst , painted pictures always got in. This year a new I leaf is turned over. Of 400 works sent in only 75 were definitely accepted. Meanwhile the institu- tion in Piccadilly has been even more exclusive. Of course it deals with greater reputations and very much larger figures. The Waterloo House has been for some weeks sell- ing off. The sale still continues and everything is to be disposed of. The explanation is more inter- esting than the fact. This block of buildings is to be thrown down. The Board of Works is at last awakening to the value of the site. Trafalgar- square will be enlarged, and there will be an unin- terrupted view from her Majesty's down to Northumberland Avenue and the Grand Hotel. The international yacht race will become an inter- national institution. Next year Scotland will be re- presented across the Atlantic. On the Clyde they are going to build, or they are going to attempt to build, something that shall surpass the performances of the Genesta. The yacht is already on the stocks. She is to be called the Thistle, will be manned by a Scotch crew, sailed by a Scotch skipper, and owned by a Scotch gentleman. The Glasgow Club will take a proud place in the table of yachting clubs of the kingdom,if the craft that flies her colours should win the race. But yachting men are now con- stantly thinking that it is time this race should be run in British waters. Let the Yankees send one of their cutters over here. Let them cross the Atlantic and meet us in our own waters—one cannot say ground—and the conditions.of the race will be more equal. The Mikado has been running so long that it really seemed as if the Directors of the Savoy had forgotten to take it off. But it won't run much longer. Its nights are numbered, and, unless it should unaccountably start into Sudden and re- newed popularity, its nights are few. There has been a good deal of mystery about its successor. Mr. Gilbert delights in mystery. Of the forthcom- ing opera it is known, however, that the subject and scenery will be Eastern. Costume, and a pecu- liar charaoter of music, are the two points to which the directors now pay most attention. I don't like a loncr word, but there is a homogeneity about all the Sullivan music. Pinafore breathed of the sea. The patter of Fairy feet was heard all through lolanthe. The Mikado has character stamped on every bar of its music. In taking an Egyptian subject, Mr. Gilbert will command' the advantage of a new and characteristic wardrobe, and Sir Arthur will find themes for his melodies in which Verdi's Aida will be his only rival.

div.head: MARKETS
div.p: MARKETS

MANCHESTER TRADE, FRIDAY.—The market is tame all round, and in no de, artment is there an average trade going through. Yarns are quiet. THE IXAMINER. SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 27, 1886_

A. RATHBONE. 43, Arpley-street, Warrington, 24th November, 1886. :Our correspondent will see from another portion of the paper that in consequence of the sudden and serious ill- ness of the Mayor it has been deemed desirable to post- pone the Town's Meeting which had been fixed for hursday night next.—En. Ex.]

SERIOUS ILLNESS OF 'IRE MAYOR. It is with regret that we announce that the Mayor (Dr. Mackie) was early on Sunday morning suddenly attacked with illness. He recovered during the day, but on Monday morning he was again seized, and since then he has been very seri- ously affected with partial paralysis. During the week the illness has been of a somewhat fluctuat- ing Character. A consultation was held on Wed- nesday evening with Sir William Roberts, of Man- chester, who took a hopeful view of the case, and recommended perfect immunity from all public and business engagements, and on the return of con- valescence a visit to Llandudno. Unfortunately, a bad night was spent on Thursday night, and an alarming relapse took place yesterday afternoon. Deep sympathy is expressed on every hand with his worship, and general regret is felt that so soon after election to the office of Jubilee Mayor of the borough he should have been incapacitated, for the time being at all events, from engaging in the im- portant work to which it was known he intended to devote himself. From inquiries made late last night we under- stand that the condition of the Mayor remained such as to cause grave anxiety. It may be mentioned that the town's meeting in connection with the movement for freeing the lend- ing library,. which had been fixed for Thursday night next, at the suggestion of the Mayor, has been postponed, the Deputy-Mayor (Alderman Harrison) wisely considering that the best course to adopt under the circumstances. THE JUBILEE YEAR AND THE IMPERIAL

INSTITUTE. The following important letter (which is believed to be from the pen of Dr. Mackie) appears in the " Times " with the signature of "A Lancashire Mayor" :---In common with the mayors of all other towns, I suppose, in the three kingdoms, and the chairman of Local Boards, I received a circular signed by his Royal Highness the Prince of Wales a day or two after my election, commending very strongly the proposed Imperial Institute of the Colonies and India as the memorial of her Majesty's jubilee by her subjects, and asking me to lay it be- fore our Town Council at the earliest opportunity. I veiy much fear that this scheme, when urged from such a high quarter, will most seriously interfere with the many local pro- jects of jubilee benevolence which are in course of formation. Every town has its own peculiar wants, and it was generally raderstood advantage would be taken of the jubilee year to raise such a sum as would enable something to be done locally, and of a permanent form. I know that in our town we have gone a long way in agreeing to have a Jubilee Free Lending Library. A Victoria Free School, and new baths to be called after our Queen, are also high in popular favour. I have no doubt that these can be secured if we are not burdened by calls from other quarters, and es- pecially from quarters so high as those represented by the Prince of Wales. Is it not possible for Lon- don and the colonies and India to secure an Im- perial Institute out of their own proper funds? It will be but a poor result of the rejoicings of the jubilee year if all that can be shown of a substantial kind is a huge hall, however chaste in its architpc- ture and magnificent in its fittings. Leave the pro- vinces alone, and they will have no difficulty, even in the smallest hamlet, in raising some memorial, if only a fountain of Water which shall bear the name for ever and ever of her Most gracious Majesty Queen Victoria. / •

THE WARRINGTON HARRIERS.—The above club had their usual cross-country run on Saturday from the head-quarters, Legh-street, ten members taking part in it. The 'hAres, A. M. Cohen and J. Water- worth, were despatched with the bags at 3-30, the I pack following at 3-45,-with J. Burke acting as pace. j A. and G. Ratcliffe, D. Walsh, G. Stokes, J.-Bellian, jH. Maddock, and R. Sherlock also ran, the last j named acting as whip. The trail lay along Bold- street, Knutsford-road, as far as the Cheshire Cheese. , It then lay across the fields to the left, and through j the meadows near Morris Brook Farm. Here the fields were partly flooded, and all tasted the sweets" of cross-country running. The trail then lay along the road at Thelwall and on to Grappen- , hall. Here the hares waited upon the pack and I joined in the run home, where they arrived at 4-55. ' the distance run being about eight miles. ENTERTAINMENT AT LATCHFORD. On Monday evening the fourth of the series of entertainments j in connection with Christ Church, Latchford, was I held in the school, Wash-lane. There was a good ; attendance, and the following programme was sue- ' cessfully rendered, viz :—Song, "I dreamed a dream,' Miss Nixon ; glee' "Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled pepper," Messrs. Green, HankeY• and Grounds; recitation, The lifeboat," Mr. Ash- ' ley; song, "The postilion," Mr. 11. Broadbent ; i J violin solo, Mr. E. Atkin; song, " Thady O'Flynnt j Mr. Longbottom ; song, Mr. E. Reynolds; song' ; Auntie,' Miss Parry; glee, Christ Church choir; song, "Do they think of me at home," Miss Ashley; encore song, "Ye banks and braes," Mr. Ti. Cross- ley ; glee, "The bells o`. St. Michael's tower," , Messrs Monks and Grounds and Master W. Knight; song, j Irish comic (encored), Mr. T. Acton; recitation, j "Cure for toothache," Mr. Brierley. The programme theramme was interspersed with humourous pieces I vicar, the Rev. B. B. Prescot, under whose direction ; the entertainment was given. • WARRINGTON UNION SCHOOL ATTENDANCE CoM- MITTEE.—TIIe monthly meeting of this conitmittee was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday. There I were present Messrs. Jolley- (in the chair), Green- ing, J. Houghton, Brown, and Bonnell. Mr. Shearer, j school attendance officer, reported that the attend- ance at the schools in his district was fair consider- ing the time of the year, being one per cent under I the average of the last three months. Ile also re" J ported several cases of children up to eleven years jof age who were attendihg a school at Sankey I Bridges which was not a certified efficient school, and that the Board School at Great SankeY would I still accommodate 150 more children, the fees there being low. The officer was instructed to use every ; endeavour to obtain the attendance of the children lat a duly certified school. Mr. Garnett, attendance officer, reported that the attendances of the chil- dren at Padgate National School had fallen off one- half owing to an epidemic ot measles in the district, and he thought it would become a ' question with the Sanitary Authority whether the schools should Ibe closed for a time. With that exception the at- , tehdance at the schools in his district had con- tinued very fair.—The rest of the business was routine.

I 1 WARRINGTON BRITISH WORKMAN puI3LIC HOUSE 1 COMPANY, LIMITED.— Last evening the annual ; general meeting of the shareholders of this com- pany was held at the Ilorsemarket-street House. and there . Roberts) and showed amongst other items that the cash received during the year for refreshments, beds, &c. amounted to £2,868 12s 2d, and the profits to £134, 8s sd. The directors re- commended that a dividend of 7i. per cent, be paid !to the shareholders, and that after Providing for i 1 the payment of income tax, auditors fees, direc- tors' honorarium, &c., the balance be written off plant account for depreciation. ' , This recomraenda- tion was adopted by the meeting. The following gentlemen were re-elected directors, Messrs. John Critchley, C. Broadbent, and P. Clare ; and Mr. J. 'W. Hayward was elected as a director in place of Mr. I. Hayward, deceased. Messrs. J. W. Bouchier and G. A hearty vote of thanks was passed to the chairnitan, directors, and secretary for their services.

During the week two new companies have been brought not, the raison d'etre of which it is difficult to discover. div.head: IttterS to the editor.
div.p: IttterS to the editor.

THE JUBILEE YEAR—ANOTHER SUGGESTION. Sir.—As there are so many suggestions flying about as to the best way in which to commemorate the Jubilee Year, perhaps you will permit that I, through your columns, should make mine. It occurred to me after hearing one made by the Rector of Warrington in his sermon on Mayor's Day. My suggestion is that a Refuge for Discharged Curates be es- tablished, and I feel sure it is a suggestion that will sot:a- mend itself to the mind of the Rector.—Yours, A SYMPATHISER WITH THE DISTRESSED. Warrington, Nov. 1886.

LIGHT WANTED. Sir,—Please permit me through your columns to call attention to the urgent need of a lamp, or some means of lighting, near the end of Bewsey-street, leading to Horsemarket-street, where the road has recently been widened, and other alterations are in pro-; grees. As vet the road is but roughly formed. and it is in total darkness. Last night I was passing along it, and, after meeting several policemen, I saw, about twenty yards further on, a man sitting in the middle of the road, enjoying a pipe of tobacco. He was, apparently, under the influen6s of the " potent," but the instincts of humanity prompted me, and a,nother person who was passing at the time, to lift him up, and deposit him in a standing posture against the nearest wall. That was the extent of our benevolence. No doubt the fellow's unfortunate position was his own fault, but the fact remains that, doubtless owing to the darknees that surrounds the spot, he was passed by several police officers, who, had they seen him, would not have allowed him to remain in the middle of the road, to be run over by the next vehicle that passed that way.—Yours, Sze., Warrington, Nov. 24, 1686. B.

div.head: BETTING PROSECUTIONS.
div.p: THE BETTING PROSECUTIONS.

Sir,—l see by your report of the recent betting prosecu- tions at Warrington that John Mather was fined £25 and costs for keeping a betting house, and in connectioa with that case I would like to draw attention to a matter that is a little beyond my comprehension. Anyhow, it requires explanation. It is well known that summonses had been issued, returnable on the some day, against three other persons, but on Thursday in last week, the day fixed for the cases to be beard, it was announced that those against cer- tain persons had been withdrawn. The urns day an even- ing paper announced that the persons referred to had paid costs, and in addition bad made a donation to the poor box. It is genetally rumoured that the donations were of no tri- fling amount. Now, sir, to me this does not seem fair play. There is a strong scent of favouritism about it. If it be true that certain defendants paid these costs and donations it is a natural inference that they preferred not to test the case, and, in fact, admitted themselves in the wrong. Those responsible for the prosecution may have acted within their rights, bat would it not be better that the public should know the reason why one was treated so differently to the others? It is like allowing people to evade the law by putting a moiety of their profits in the poor box.—Yours, Warrington, November 22nd, 1886. INQUIRER.

div.head: RUNCORN MAGISTRATES.
div.p: THE RUNCORN MAGISTRATES.

Sir,—Will you permit me to call attention to a case which appeared in your issue of the 13th, in which I was prosecutor. I am annoyed and and harassed exceedingly by men carrying guns, and accompanied by dog-, trespassing in search of the rabbits and birds upon my farm. I have fre- quently spoken to the police and they advised me to catch and prosecute coe of the offenders if I wishe4 to have the nuisance abated. Os the let November my son and P.C. Blease saw four men with two guns and two retriever dogs working the land, and, as they were caught in the act, I took out a summons against them, not to prosecute, but merely to obtain a conviction, and so put a stop to the annoyance. The case was clearly proved; the men admit- ting being there, but giving the excuse that they wers shooting small birds with the consent of the adjoining far- mer, and had got on ray land in mistake. This was really too absurd. Cam anyone imagine that two retriever dogs are required to hunt up small birds, and yet (though I told the bench that one of the men had been there before) OR this flimsy excuse the magistrates dismissed the case, and to instruct me in the uncertainty of the law, mulcted me in 18$ costs. lam puzzled to know what to do. I have taken the advice of the police, and done all that I could to help ' myself, aid vet lam worse off, for the magistrates have allowed an excuse se open' that anyone may use it, and in addition I have the costs to pay.—Yours truly, HENRY ACKERLEY. Weston, 23rd November, 1886.

134,-Bince you have thought fit to insert a paragraph ooncerning me taken from the "Preston Guardian," you will, I hope, permit me to correct some inaccuracies con- tained in it. (1) It was the chairman that with justifiable warmth, refused to allow a speech to be made when a ques- tion only bad been called for. (2) The accusation of" ignor- ance" was made against me and not by me. It was that of being ignorant of Greek, in reply to which I "stated that I knew Greek," kc, &c. (3) I said the gentleman was trying to entangle rue in issues not touched upon in my lecture, to which alone questions were to apply. It would surely be more fair not to report me at all than to falsify facts so shamefully. I may add that the gentleman with whom I am said to have had the "warm recrimination" moved the vote of thanks, and the gentleman who hinted at my pos- sible ignorance of Greek seconded it with an assurance that he bad nct meant to eay anything that could offend.—l am, air, yours truly,

We had no reason to believe when we quoted from the Pres. ton Guardian " that the paragraph was other than a fair summary of the proceedings, as the paper in question is in high repute for its general accuracy and impartiality. —En.
