div.head: SUNDAY SCHOOL AND THE THEATRE.
div.p: THE SUNDAY SCHOOL AND THE THEATRE.

Sir,—There is such extreme juvenility about the letters of " W.E.5.," that I almost blush to find myself replying to them, being at the present date "something over 21." I have waded through two or three written by him, and it is a toss up (I hope this word is not unorthodox!) whether their puerility or bad grammar is most apparent. Still, I think the slaughter of the Queen's English carries the palm. Now, in the last brilliant sample I am told that my re- marks respecting "J. B. Isaac" are spiteful and personal. I don't regret (though it may be my loss) that I don't know "J. B. Isaac" any more than I know " W.E.5.," and (more regretable still, perhaps) I don't care a pinch of inferior ' snuff for either, and on these very grounds I don't like to , be told I am" personal," even when allowing considerable latitude to one of tender years. If! had wished to be spite- ful I should have said J. B. Isaac" was a person who quoted Scripture for personal ends, who attacked a subject (the theatre) that he was in gross ignorance of ; and wbose teaching of the young on this matter, especially when de- nouncing it, must of necessity be grossly prejudiced, and in the end fouud out and scouted.

In no way desiring to be spiteful to " W.E.5.," though be offers a fair field for it. I will merely advise him, whilst still young, to study Lindley Murray, to rush into print less frequently. and to stir up no more mud uutil be knows the rudiments of orthography better. .1 A man that's fond precociously cf stirring, Must be a spoon "—Hood. NOY. 22nd, 1380. GARRICK.

div.head: PROPOSED LIBERAL LEAGUE.
div.p: PROPOSED LIBERAL LEAGUE.

Sir,—At a meeting of representative Liberals held at the National Liberal Club this evening, it was resolved to estab- lish a Liberal League for the association of men and women in Liberal work, such league being formed for the purpose of counteracting the influence of the Primrose League, and for promoting Liberal principles throughout the British Em- pire. It was stated that such league was intended to include and combine all Liberals of every section, irrespective of sex, throughout the empire; to be a means of communica- tion for all Liberals between themselves and between them- selves and the leaders of their party ; to initiate non-exis- tent and develop existing Liberal clubs and organizations; to assist in providing halls and rooms in various parts of the country for political meetings ; mad by all legitimate means to promote political edncatien and progressive legis- lation.

It was stated that letters promising support to such a league had been received from influential Liberals in all parts of the country, especially in county constituencies. A committee was appointed to draw up a constitution and rules for the league, to be submitted to a future meet- ing. Representatiyes of existing women's associations were present, and protnised to co-operate and affiliate their secie- ties with this national movement. It is proposed to estab- lish lodges, county and divisional councils, and a grand coun- cil, and to extend the operations of the league beyond the United Kingdom. Will you permit me through your columns to ask any Liberal or Radical of either sex, who approves the establish- ment of the league and would be willing to co-operate ia its formation in this district, to send me as early as convenient their names and addresses, and to give any suggestions, which shall be duly considered.—Yours faithfully, JAMES DRAKE DIGBY. Secretary pro. tent. Cambridge House, Weston Park, Crouch End, N., Nov. 16th, 1886.

div.head: SPIRITUALISM V. CONJURING.
div.p: SPIRITUALISM V. CONJURING.

Sir,—Your correspondent "Beta" seems to be in earnest. Wishing to rush in, he quite forgets that the angels, in whose company he at present is, fear to tread; the ground may be holy. I have no doubt, sir, that you would allow members of those" families in whose homes such phenomen are being obtained " to give a few sketches of their interesting inter- views with the shadeless shadows of the silent land. But what then? Medium or no medium, we don't seem to have much to gain. Mr. Acton might gain a wrinkle or two, and that would be However much in earnest " Beta " may be, he is quite outdone by " Just ic e." who, in his anxiety to "get at truth," is willing to rust, on to any platform, so that be may come in contact with "facts." Just so, but what as to the facts? Beware of credulity, my friend; "facts" have for a few thousand years now come in very questionable !shape.

_ Now as to the "double slate, locked, and sealed, with a small piece of slate pencil inside," why put the pencil in- side at all? Surely the power that could work such won- ders with a sealed slate would have no difficulty in provid- ing writing material. And as to the writing, "Justice" does well to say "Intelligent messages are written therein." I don't know about this. I have seen several fae similes of such writings, and cannot bear shoal testimony as to the in- telligence of the message. But n w let a supp se that we have this spiritualistic seance, and all comes off successful, what then? Those who do not see it would not believe our testimony. Even those who did see the " conjuring " would not rest satisfied unless told how it was done ; the world abounds with doubt- ing Thomases. It seems to, me that the chief trouble in this spiritual matter is with the medium. Psychological, and physio- logical derangements, are best treated by specialists, who, understanding the agents required by the patient, may easily mediomania. My friends may, after this, say I am an incorrigible materialist. Perhaps this is true. I know this, that the library shelves teem with volumes which tell us that this world of ours has been over-run with half- naked dancers, flaaellants,witches, and sorcerers; that in past ages the world abounded with saints, and that priests and inquisitors tormented mankind. I have sat in what were called religious meetings, and have watched the credulous believers in faith-healing hope to receive special and spiritual response to their wild pleadings. What then? These visitations trouble mankind in a less and less degree as we grow more enlightened in matters pertaining to the pathological treatment of the system, and the educational requirPtnents of the human mind. Have we not the wild imaginations of vegetarians, and anti-vaccinators, to cope with? These two alone seem to me quite sufficient to find work for all who like to have a tilt now and again at wind- mill sails. Now, sir, I beg " Beta " and " Justice" to believe me, when I say that if they will make—arrangements for a dis- play of spiritualism, I shall have pleasure in attending, and I will try to bring myself into such a frame of mind as Hamlet speaks of when he says— There at e more things in heaven and earth. Horatio,

Than are dreamt of in our philosophy." I 811411 have no more to say on this subject till such time as your correspondents have given me an opportunity of speak- ing as one having experience. Then I may be able to re- port that" Justice" and " Beta" have played Such fantastic tricks before high heaven As make the angels weep aided, of course, by

div.head: CLIFFORD DIX.
div.p: CLIFFORD DIX.

Sir —A. proposition appeared in last week's paper signed "Justice," in which he challenges me to prove that spirit- writing is a trick. I accept it, and, in prove of this, I leave £5 with you as my deposit: but as "Justice" does not see why he or any other spiritualist should trouble to bring a medium to Warrington, I don't see why he should force that duty on me. If he knows Spiritualism to be truth, it is his duty to give a helping band to get a medium to come te Warrington. Now, I propose that "Justice" deposits £5 along with that which I have already deposited. We will then try to arrange for a medium to come to Warrington, the medium to be paid "so much" for his services on cone dition that spirit-writing is performed, and it turns out to be a genuine phenomena. We will then arrange for a com- mittee of Warrington gentlemen. I will write a question on a paper, and give it to one of the committee in a sealed envelope. The question shall be so simple that n:nety-nine persons out of every hundred can answer it; hat no one but myself shall know the contents. I shall be allowed to examine the elate on which the answer is to be received, and apply such tests as I think proper to guard against decep- tion. If an answer to the question which I shall have written is obtained, and I fail to prove that it has been got by a trick, my deposit of £5 goes towards paying the mediure's fee; but if he fails to obtain a suitable answer, or if he obtains an answer, and I prove that it is a trick, then " Justice's " -..E5 goes to some charitable purpose in War- rington. If we fail to arrange for a seance in Warrington, we will then try for one in London, to take place under the above conditions; but, in failing to accomplish this, " Jus- tice's " £5 go,s towards some charitable purpose, just the same as if a seance had been arranged and the medium had failed in his objet, for unless something like this is done this subiett may go on for ever, and no arrangement be made I will allow "Justice" two months to arrange matters from the time he makes the deposit; but if his de- posit is not made within 14 days from the publication of this letter, I shall consider he has] withdrawn his chal- lenge. "Justice," in giving the evidence of a number of well- known gentlemen, alludes to Harry Keller, a conjurer. He says that he failed to prove that spirit-writing was a trick. This may be, as there are many different ways of per- forming it. Supposing Harry Keller to be the cleverest conjurer in the world, so ;far as sleight-of-hand and mechanism is concerned, what would this avail him if the medium used a chemical mode of performance, in which science Harry Keller might have been ignorant. Or ef what use would the knowledge of all the chemists or mechanics in the world be if the medium used sleight-of hand? I can perform it a dozen differs-it ways, and I say that if a question is written on a piece of paper, of which the medium is ignorant, an answer cannot be obtained with- out trickery. " Justice" also said that he had had experience of Spiritualism, and that I had none. If he means going to a seance with my eyes shut and believing all that is said, I have had none; but if looking at things as I find them, tak- ing the evidence of spiritualists without doubting their word, trying litte experiments, and then trying to find out a cause—ii this is experience, I have had it for the last twenty years, for I believed in certain phenomena when I was a ; boy, and still believe, but not in the light of a spiritualist. And now, if you will allow me a little more space in this paper, I will go farther into this matter and give my views ef It. If we place a needle on a smooth surface and put.
The Mayor of Macclesfield has constituted a movement for the restoration of the privileges of the sclasduled voters of 1880

The latest telegraphic news from Windsor Castle is that everything is going well with the Princess Beatrice and the Queen's latest grandson. Owing to the depression in the iron trade, the Winger- worth Iron Company in Chesterfield have decided to blow out all their furnaces for the present. The Queen held a council at Windsor on Friday after- noon, which was attended by Lord Cranbrook, Lord Cross, and Lord Stanley of Preston, with Mr. Peel, clerk of the Council. DEATH SENTENCE.—At Warwick Assizes, on Friday, Jus- tice Graham passed sentence of death on John Norbury for the wilful murder of his wife at Birmingham. The woman was of drunken dissolute habits.

TUNNEL BETWEEN SCOTLAND AND IRELAND.—The Lon- don and North-Western Railway Company have despatched an engineer to Donaghadee to follow up soundings taken during the past summer in connection with the proposed tunnel between Scotland and Ireland. Tus IMPERIAL INSTITUTE.—The "Australian Times" says it has been finally settled that the site for the Imperial Institute will be South Kensington. The institute will in- clude a Free Library, and a great hall suitable for the dis- cussion of papers of interest before large audiences. SAD DROWNING CASE.—On Thursday night, as a party of gentlemen were driving from Sandbach to Middlewich, Mr. Mears, of the Middlewich Milk Factory, alighted near the Shropshire Union Canal, and the night being very dark be fell into the water and was drowned before his com- panions could rescue him.

A TROOPSHIP AGROUND.—The Euphrates, troopship, on leaving harbour at Portsmouth at 12 o'clock on Friday, with the 7th Hussars for Bombay, went aground after pro. carding a few hundred yards and remained fixed twenty- five minutes. Altogether over a thousand troops were on board, and much anxiety was felt lest she should remain there till the tide ebbed.

- -- GREAT Fuzzis BELFAST.—An alarming fire broke out at noon on Friday in the extensive premises of Messrs. Clot- worthy and Company, wholesale druggists and oil mer- chants, Bridge-street, Belfast. The flames spread with great rapidity to the stores at the rear of the premises, and from thence to some private residence on the other side of the street, from which several were carried in a fainting condition. The premises were completely gutted. The

- - damage is estimated at £4,000. • THE IRISH POLICY OF THIS GOVERNMENT.—IS is stated that the Irish Government are making arrangements for the despatch of troops to various points in Ireland, where im- portant action in reference to the rent agitation is contem- plated by the authorities. A correspondent telegraphing from Dublin says :—lt is reported on good authority that the Government have resolved to institute prosecution against Mr. Dillon, M.P., and Mr. William O'Brien, and that the League meeting summoned for Sun- day, near Irishtown, county Mayo, will be proclaimed. A:Dublin correspondent of the -Central News telegraphs (later) that a summons was on Friday served on Mr. John Dillon, M.P.. calling upoa him to show cause in Queen's Bench, Dublin, on Mondly, why criminal information should , not be taken against him for having, at a meeting at Loughrea ' used intimidating language with regard to Lord Clanricard and his tenants. The greatest excitement prevails amongst Nationalists, owing to the proclamation of the proposed de- monstration in Sligo on Sunday. They say they will give a banquet to Messrs. Dillon, O'Brien, and other InembPrs, since they are not allowed to hold an open-air meeting. It is stated that a large force of military are ordered to Sligo.
THE BULGARIAN DIFFICULTY. PLOT TO MURDER THE REGENT'S.

SOFIA, WEDNESDAY, 9-45 P.M (delayed in transmission).— A new conspiracy against the Government has been dis- covered in this city through the instrumentality of Major Pojoff, commander of the garrison. The plot was organised by two officers who are inspectors in the Military school, and one of whom is a Russian. These, with two other officers, gained over a dozen cadets belonging to the batch of forty who took part in the seizure of Prince Alexander, and who were lately released and allowed to re-enter the Military School. •file plan of the conspirators was to kill Colonel Nicolaeff (the Minister of War), Major Popoff, and the Regents, to-morrow (Thursday) morning at five o'clock. Last night, however. Major Popoff with some troops en- tered the school and had all arms removed, and this morn- ing the four officers implicated were arrested. The con- spirators will be tried by court martial within a few days. The Central news learns that private telegrams received in London from Madagascar indicate that the relations be- tween the HMIS Government and France will shortly lead to an open rupture.
LIBERAL CLUB DEBATING SOCIETY.

The usual weekly meeting of this society was held at the Liberal Club last evening, when the chair was occupied by Mr. D. Davies, the vice- president. Mr. Neild was not able to be present to read his paper on "Thrift and Co-operation," but in his stead, Mr. Bromley read one on Disestablish- ment. Ile said that if by disestablishment nothing further was meant than the severance of religion from State control, the clergy w,,uld be about the most enthusiastic of Liberationists. It was dises- dowment that they dreaded. Having referred to tithes and the valious sources of revenue to the Church, and to the action of the clergy in past times on important political questions, Mr. Bromley said that, prior to any legislation on the question of dis- establishment, there should be an inquiry into the origin, nature, and extent of the property and revenues appropriated by the Church of England. No one could doubt that ownership and vested in- terests would be fully considered. It was only likely that a nation would act more liberally to them than they had done to the nation. When the time came for the disestablishment and disendow- ment of the Church of England, all the talk about robbery would be as so much windy for a nation could no more rob it- self than En individual could rob himself. A discussion followed, which was commenced by Mr. S. BARLOW, who said that, although he was born a Churchman, he was a thorough and a strong opponent of the Church of England as by law established. To call it the national Church, he ar- gued, was a piece of stupidity, as there really was no such church. Nine-tenths of the tithes and the connections of this country with the Church were with the Church of Rome in former times. The majority of the people of this country were opposed to the Church of England, and never went to church. The Church of England, as by law established, was not fit to live—the sooner it died the better. Of course,he was not speaking of the faith of the Church, but of the mode of governing it.—Mr. F. MONKS, J.P., in the course of a few well-chosen remarks, said there should be some discrimination between the money given to the Church as a religious institu- tion, and as a political institution. The Church, he thought, could claim the money given it since it was an Episcopalian Church, and what it inherited from what they might call old Catholic times should be appropriated by the nation either for educational purposes or for assisting other forms of religion.— Mr. H. WHITECAM deprecated the question being so much looked upon as one of past history. The question should be looked upon to-day as it bears upon the people of to-day. The political power of the Church trammelled them at every point, and stood in the way of reform. The Disestablishment Bill should be made the one thing to be now gone in for by the Liberal party.—Messrs. Kenyon, Sut- cliffe, A. Browne, R. Roberts, G. Wallington, and Duffin also took part in a very interesting debate, and Mr. Bromley afterwards replied. The meeting concluded with votes of thanks to the reader of the paper, and to Mr. Davies for presiding. Next week Mr. C. Plinston introduces the important question of Home Rule.

The hares also appeared to be very partial to high fences, showing a marked preference for spiked fenc- ing, to judge from the quantity that was encountered dur- ing the run. The bares started at 3-15, and after cover- ing a distance of about Si miles, arrived at head- quarters about 4-30.
